topic: AA Amyloidosis secondary to chronic arthritis

guidelinesKept: Consensus recommendations on the diagnosis and treatment of AA amyloidosis.

page.mentor_intro: AA (secondary/reactive) amyloidosis results from sustained overproduction of serum amyloid A (SAA) protein by hepatocytes during chronic systemic inflammation (rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, adult-onset Still's disease, or chronic infection). Insoluble amyloid fibrils deposit in tissues, predominantly causing nephrotic-range proteinuria, progressive renal failure, and hepatosplenomegaly, while cardiac involvement is rare compared to AL or ATTR amyloidosis. Diagnosis requires Congo red staining of tissue biopsies (abdominal fat pad, rectum, or kidney) showing apple-green birefringence under polarized light and positive anti-SAA immunohistochemistry. Management centers aggressively on suppressing underlying chronic inflammation (anti-TNF, anti-IL-6 [tocilizumab], or colchicine in FMF) to lower SAA below 10 mg/L, which arrests amyloid deposition and permits regression of proteinuria.

teaching_points.claim: AA amyloidosis is driven by chronic elevation of acute-phase reactant serum amyloid A (SAA); sustained suppression of SAA to < 10 mg/L halts renal progression and improves survival.
Renal involvement is the primary clinical manifestation (> 90% of cases), presenting initially as asymptomatic albuminuria progressing to nephrotic syndrome and end-stage kidney disease.
Biopsy confirmation using Congo red stain demonstrates characteristic apple-green birefringence under cross-polarized light, with immunohistochemistry differentiating AA from AL and ATTR amyloidosis.

Targeted biologic therapies suppressing chronic inflammation (IL-6 receptor antagonist tocilizumab or TNF inhibitors in inflammatory arthritis) produce dramatic biochemical and renal remissions in AA amyloidosis.

sources.title: Consensus recommendations on the diagnosis and treatment of AA amyloidosis.
AA amyloidosis: clinical characteristics and treatment outcomes.

uncertainties: Target SAA threshold (< 10 mg/L vs < 4 mg/L) necessary to achieve histological regression of renal amyloid deposits.
Safety of kidney transplantation in patients with AA amyloidosis and active underlying autoimmune disease.
mcq_angles: Differentiating AA from AL amyloidosis: AA presents with prominent nephrotic syndrome and hepatomegaly, but rarely severe cardiomyopathy; AL frequently presents with restrictive cardiomyopathy and macroglossia.
Conformational staining: Congo red with apple-green birefringence; electron microscopy confirms rigid non-branching 7.5-10 nm fibrils.
Monitoring therapeutic response: serial serum SAA levels; falling SAA correlates directly with stabilized eGFR and reduced proteinuria.

topic: Abatacept in RA: T-cell co-stimulation blockade, seropositive advantage, safety profile

guidelinesKept: 2021 American College of Rheumatology Guideline for the Treatment of Rheumatoid Arthritis.

page.mentor_intro: Abatacept is a soluble recombinant fusion protein consisting of the extracellular domain of human CTLA-4 linked to the modified Fc portion of human IgG1 (CTLA-4-Ig). It selectively modulates T-cell co-stimulation by binding to CD80 and CD86 on antigen-presenting cells, thereby blocking CD28 interaction on T cells and inhibiting T-cell activation. In the landmark AMPLE trial (first head-to-head biologic comparison in RA), subcutaneous abatacept demonstrated non-inferior clinical efficacy to adalimumab with comparable radiographic inhibition, but with fewer injection-site reactions and fewer serious infections. Abatacept exhibits superior clinical responsiveness in seropositive (anti-CCP and RF positive) patients and carries an exceptionally low risk of tuberculosis reactivation or opportunistic infections compared to TNF inhibitors.

teaching_points.claim: The landmark head-to-head AMPLE trial proved subcutaneous abatacept is non-inferior to adalimumab in achieving ACR20 response (64.8% vs 63.4%) and inhibiting radiographic progression at 2 years.
Abatacept selectively binds CD80/CD86 on antigen-presenting cells to prevent CD28 co-stimulation, uniquely dampening adaptive T-cell priming without broad systemic lymphopenia.
Clinical efficacy is significantly higher in seropositive patients (high-titer anti-CCP and RF), reflecting targeted suppression of autoantibody-generating T-cell help.

ACR guidelines recommend abatacept as an optimal first-line biologic choice in RA patients with a history of serious infections, recurrent cellulitis, or latent TB due to its favorable infectious safety profile.

sources.title: Subcutaneous abatacept versus adalimumab for rheumatoid arthritis: 2-year results of the AMPLE trial.

uncertainties: Comparative retention rate of abatacept vs JAK inhibitors in triple-therapy-refractory seropositive RA.

mcq_angles: Mechanism: CTLA-4-Ig binds CD80/CD86 on APCs, competing with CD28 co-stimulatory receptor on T cells.
AMPLE trial primary finding: non-inferiority to adalimumab with significantly lower rate of injection-site reactions (3.8% vs 9.1%).
Safety advantage: lower rate of serious bacterial infections and opportunistic mycobacterial infections compared to monoclonal anti-TNF antibodies.

topic: Abdominal aortic aneurysm: surveillance thresholds, EVAR vs open repair

guidelinesKept: European Society for Vascular Surgery (ESVS) 2019 Clinical Practice Guidelines on the Management of Abdominal Aorto-iliac Artery Aneurysms.

page.mentor_intro: Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is defined as an infrarenal aortic diameter >= 3.0 cm (or > 50% increase over normal). Rupture carries > 80% overall mortality. SVS and ESVS guidelines establish ultrasound surveillance intervals based on diameter: 3.0-3.9 cm (every 3 years), 4.0-4.9 cm (annually), and 5.0-5.4 cm (every 3-6 months). Elective repair is indicated at diameter >= 5.5 cm in men, >= 5.0 cm in women, or with rapid expansion (> 1.0 cm/year or > 0.5 cm in 6 months), or symptomatic aneurysms. Landmark trials (EVAR-1, DREAM, OVER) proved that Endovascular Aneurysm Repair (EVAR) significantly reduces 30-day perioperative mortality compared to open surgical repair (1.2-1.7% vs 4.7-5.0%), but this early survival benefit converges by 2-3 years, with EVAR carrying higher lifetime re-intervention rates for endoleaks (especially Type I and III) requiring lifelong CT/ultrasound surveillance.

teaching_points.claim: Elective threshold for repair is >= 5.5 cm in men and >= 5.0 cm in women, or rapid growth > 1.0 cm/year or > 0.5 cm in 6 months (SVS/ESVS guidelines).
Landmark trials (EVAR-1, DREAM) demonstrated a 3-fold lower 30-day operative mortality with EVAR compared to open surgical repair (1.7% vs 4.7%).

Long-term trial follow-up out to 10-15 years shows convergence of all-cause mortality between EVAR and open repair, with EVAR having significantly higher rates of secondary rupture and re-intervention for endoleaks.

Classification of endoleaks: Type I (attachment cuff leak; requires urgent repair), Type II (collateral lumbar/IMA back-bleeding; observe unless sac expands), Type III (graft fabric/modular disconnection; requires urgent repair).

mcq_angles: Repair threshold differences: 5.5 cm in men vs 5.0 cm in women (due to smaller baseline aortic caliber and higher relative rupture risk in females).
Endoleak types requiring urgent re-intervention: Type I (inadequate proximal/distal seal) and Type III (component decoupling or fabric tear) expose the aneurysm sac to systemic arterial pressure.
Screening recommendation: one-time ultrasound screening in men aged 65-75 with any smoking history (USPSTF).

topic: Abdominal compartment syndrome: diagnosis, decompressive laparotomy

guidelinesKept: Updated consensus definitions and clinical practice guidelines from the World Society of the Abdominal Compartment Syndrome (WSACS).

page.mentor_intro: Abdominal compartment syndrome (ACS) is defined by the WSACS consensus as a sustained intra-abdominal pressure (IAP) > 20 mmHg (with or without an abdominal perfusion pressure [APP = MAP - IAP] < 60 mmHg) associated with new or worsening single- or multiple-organ dysfunction. Intra-abdominal hypertension (IAH) is defined as sustained IAP >= 12 mmHg. Measurement of bladder pressure via an indwelling Foley catheter at end-expiration in the supine position is the gold standard diagnostic method. High IAP compresses the IVC (lowering venous return and cardiac output), impedes renal vein and parenchymal perfusion (oliguria and acute tubular necrosis), and elevates hemidiaphragms (peak airway pressures rise, producing hypercapnia and hypoxemia). Medical therapy encompasses nasogastric/colonic decompression, paracentesis of ascites, neuromuscular blockade, and judicious fluid management; refractory ACS is a surgical emergency mandating decompressive laparotomy with temporary open abdominal closure.

teaching_points.claim: WSACS consensus defines ACS as sustained IAP > 20 mmHg associated with new-onset organ failure; IAH is defined as sustained IAP >= 12 mmHg.
Transvesical bladder pressure measurement at end-expiration instilling 20-25 mL sterile saline with transducer zeroed at mid-axillary line is the clinical gold standard.

ACS pathophysiology produces a triad of cardiovascular collapse (decreased preload, elevated SVR), respiratory compromise (high peak airway pressures), and oliguric renal failure resistant to fluid challenges.
Emergency surgical decompressive laparotomy is the definitive life-saving intervention for refractory ACS (IAP > 20 mmHg with worsening organ dysfunction failing medical decompression).

sources.title: Updated consensus definitions and clinical practice guidelines from the World Society of the Abdominal Compartment Syndrome (WSACS).

uncertainties: Optimal timing and criteria for secondary temporary abdominal wall closure and prevention of giant ventral hernias.
Fluid resuscitation strategy: avoiding aggressive crystalloid over-resuscitation to prevent visceral edema and secondary ACS.
mcq_angles: Formula for Abdominal Perfusion Pressure: APP = Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) - Intra-Abdominal Pressure (IAP); maintaining APP >= 60 mmHg correlates with renal survival.
Renal impact: IAP > 15-20 mmHg directly compresses renal parenchyma and renal veins, causing severe oliguria mimicking hypovolemia; fluid boluses worsen bowel edema and worsen IAP.
Definitive intervention: decompressive laparotomy with temporary negative pressure open abdominal wound dressing (vac pack/Abthera).

A patient with severe acute necrotizing pancreatitis developing rising lactate and oliguria whose bladder pressure is 24 mmHg, undergoing urgent surgical decompression.

guidelinesKept: FIGO classification system (PALM-COEIN) for causes of abnormal uterine bleeding in nongravid women of reproductive age.
ACOG Committee Opinion No. 557: Management of Abnormal Uterine Bleeding in Nonpregnant Reproductive-Age Women.

page.mentor_intro: Abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) in non-pregnant reproductive-age women is classified according to the FIGO PALM-COEIN system into structural causes (Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, Malignancy/hyperplasia) and non-structural causes (Coagulopathy, Ovulatory dysfunction, Endometrial, Iatrogenic, Not otherwise classified). Initial workup requires pelvic transvaginal ultrasound, complete blood count, and endometrial biopsy in women aged >= 45 years (or < 45 with risk factors: obesity, nulliparity, chronic anovulation/PCOS, tamoxifen, Lynch syndrome). First-line medical therapy for ovulatory or non-structural AUB is the 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine system (LNG-IUS; Mirena), which reduces menstrual blood loss by > 70-90%, followed by oral tranexamic acid, combined oral contraceptives, or cyclical oral progestins. Endometrial ablation, uterine artery embolization (UAE), or hysterectomy are second-line surgical alternatives.

teaching_points.claim: The FIGO PALM-COEIN classification categorizes AUB etiologies into structural (PALM: polyp, adenomyosis, leiomyoma, malignancy) and non-structural (COEIN: coagulopathy, ovulatory, endometrial, iatrogenic, not classified).

ACOG guidelines mandate endometrial tissue sampling to rule out hyperplasia/cancer in any woman aged >= 45 with AUB, or < 45 with chronic unopposed estrogen (PCOS, obesity) or failed medical management.

The 52 mg levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (LNG-IUS) is the most effective medical therapy, reducing menstrual blood loss by > 70-90% and outperforming oral agents in quality-of-life improvements.

Acute severe AUB in hemodynamically stable patients is managed medically with high-dose oral tranexamic acid (1.3 g TID), oral progestins (medroxyprogesterone acetate 20 mg TID), or combined oral contraceptives.

mcq_angles: PALM vs COEIN categorization: PALM causes are visually identified on imaging/histopathology; COEIN causes are functional/systemic without discrete structural lesions.
Endometrial biopsy age cutoff: age >= 45 years is the standard threshold for mandatory biopsy in AUB.

Tranexamic acid mechanism: antifibrinolytic that reversibly blocks lysine binding sites on plasminogen, reducing clot degradation during menses without increasing baseline VTE risk in non-thrombophilic women.

topic: Absence seizures and juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME) therapeutic profiles

guidelinesKept: ILAE consensus on the diagnosis and management of idiopathic generalized epilepsies.

page.mentor_intro: Childhood Absence Epilepsy (CAE) and Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy (JME) are idiopathic generalized epilepsies (IGEs) characterized by bilateral, synchronous 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges on EEG (CAE) or rapid 4-6 Hz polyspike-and-wave discharges (JME). Ethosuximide is the drug of first choice for pure absence seizures: the landmark NIH randomized controlled trial proved ethosuximide and valproic acid have superior seizure freedom rates (~53-58%) compared to lamotrigine (29%), with ethosuximide causing significantly fewer attentional/cognitive side effects. JME presents around puberty with morning myoclonic jerks (especially after sleep deprivation or alcohol), generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and occasional absence seizures; valproic acid is the most effective drug for JME across all seizure types, but lamotrigine or levetiracetam are preferred first-line alternatives in women of childbearing potential due to valproate teratogenicity. Sodium channel blockers (carbamazepine, phenytoin) exacerbate absence and myoclonic seizures.

teaching_points.claim: The landmark NIH double-blind trial demonstrated that ethosuximide and valproate achieve superior 16-week seizure freedom in absence epilepsy compared to lamotrigine, with ethosuximide having the best cognitive/attentional profile.

In Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy (JME), broad-spectrum agents (valproate, levetiracetam, lamotrigine) control multiple seizure types; valproate is the most potent but restricted in females of reproductive age due to teratogenicity and neurodevelopmental harms.

Narrow-spectrum sodium channel blockers (carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, vigabatrin) are strictly contraindicated in absence epilepsy and JME as they worsen absence seizures and precipitate status myoclonicus.

EEG hallmarks: pure absence shows generalized, symmetric 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges provoked by hyperventilation; JME exhibits 4-6 Hz polyspike-and-wave discharges triggered by photic stimulation and sleep deprivation.

sources.title: Ethosuximide, valproic acid, and lamotrigine in childhood absence epilepsy (NIH RCT).
ILAE consensus on the diagnosis and management of idiopathic generalized epilepsies.

uncertainties: Long-term remission and discontinuation criteria for ethosuximide in CAE (often remits by adolescence) vs JME (usually requires lifelong pharmacotherapy).
Efficacy of topiramate and brivaracetam as add-on therapies in refractory JME.
mcq_angles: Drug of choice contrast: Ethosuximide for pure absence (T-type calcium channel blocker; ineffective for GTCs); Valproate for JME (controls myoclonus, GTCs, and absence).
Drugs to avoid: Carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, and phenytoin worsen both absence and myoclonus.
Teratogenic counseling: Valproate causes neural tube defects (10% major malformations) and 8-10 point drop in childhood IQ; requires formal signed risk acknowledgment in reproductive-aged females.

guidelinesKept: Tokyo Guidelines 2018: diagnostic criteria and severity assessment of acute cholecystitis.

page.mentor_intro: Acute acalculous cholecystitis (AAC) is an acute necroinflammatory gallbladder disease occurring without cholelithiasis, accounting for ~5-10% of acute cholecystitis cases but carrying 30-50% mortality. It typically arises in critically ill ICU patients, severe trauma, extensive burns, sepsis, major surgery, or prolonged total parenteral nutrition (TPN). Pathophysiology combines bile stasis, gallbladder ischemia (endothelial injury, hypoperfusion, splanchnic vasoconstriction), and endotoxin-mediated mucosal necrosis, predisposing to rapid gangrene and perforation. Ultrasound and CT criteria include gallbladder wall thickening (> 3 mm), pericholecystic fluid, intramural gas, and subserosal halo sign without gallstones. Initial management requires broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and prompt gallbladder decompression: percutaneous cholecystostomy (PC) is the preferred minimally invasive intervention in critically ill unstable patients, reserving laparoscopic or open cholecystectomy for stable candidates or those with gallbladder perforation/gangrene.

teaching_points.claim: AAC occurs in critically ill, burned, trauma, or post-cardiac surgery patients through a combination of bile stasis (TPN, fasting) and microvascular ischemia.
Ultrasound and contrast CT diagnostic criteria include gallbladder wall thickening >= 3.5-4 mm, pericholecystic fluid, gallbladder distension, and mucosal sloughing in the absence of gallstones.

Tokyo Guidelines (TG18) recommend ultrasound-guided percutaneous transhepatic cholecystostomy (PTC) as the definitive or stabilizing procedure of choice in critically ill patients unfit for emergent surgery.

Antibiotic therapy must cover enteric Gram-negative bacilli, Enterococcus, and anaerobes (e.g. piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem); cholecystostomy catheters are typically maintained for 4-6 weeks until mature tract formation before removal.

uncertainties: Optimal timing of interval elective cholecystectomy vs permanent tube removal in patients stabilized after percutaneous cholecystostomy.

mcq_angles: Risk factor profile: AAC occurs in hospitalized ICU patients (TPN, septic shock, mechanical ventilation); calculous cholecystitis occurs primarily in outpatients.
Percutaneous cholecystostomy tract maturity: tube must remain in place for >= 4-6 weeks to allow fibrous tract formation, preventing bile peritonitis upon removal.
High gangrene and perforation risk: ischemia causes early transmural necrosis and perforation in up to 15-20% of AAC cases.

guidelinesKept: 2015/2016 EULAR recommendations for cardiovascular risk management in patients with rheumatoid arthritis and other forms of inflammatory joint disorders.

page.mentor_intro: Systemic autoimmune and chronic inflammatory diseases (Rheumatoid Arthritis, Systemic Lupus Erythematosus, Psoriatic Arthritis, Ankylosing Spondylitis) confer a 2- to 3-fold higher risk of premature atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), rivaling diabetes mellitus as an independent cardiovascular risk equivalent. Chronic circulating pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IL-6, interferon-alpha) trigger endothelial dysfunction, vascular smooth muscle proliferation, macrophage foam-cell activation, oxidation of LDL, and destabilization of coronary fibrous caps. EULAR guidelines mandate a 1.5x multiplication factor applied to conventional cardiovascular risk scores (e.g. SCORE2, Framingham) in patients with RA who have disease duration >= 10 years, seropositivity (RF or anti-CCP), or extra-articular manifestations. Aggressive control of disease activity using bDMARDs/csDMARDs significantly attenuates vascular risk, complemented by statin therapy, blood pressure optimization, and smoking cessation.

teaching_points.claim: EULAR recommendations mandate multiplying calculated cardiovascular risk scores by 1.5 in rheumatoid arthritis patients with high disease activity, seropositivity, or extra-articular manifestations.

Chronic systemic inflammation drives endothelial injury, increases circulating adhesion molecules (ICAM-1, VCAM-1), promotes dense necrotic core lipid plaques, and doubles premature myocardial infarction rates.
Aggressive disease suppression with methotrexate and biologic DMARDs (anti-TNF, anti-IL-6) reduces vascular inflammation and decreases incident cardiovascular events by 20-30%.
Statin therapy provides lipid-lowering and pleiotropic anti-inflammatory vascular plaque stabilization, safe in combination with DMARDs under transaminase monitoring.

uncertainties: Comparative impact of JAK inhibitors on lipid subfractions and major adverse cardiovascular events (ORAL Surveillance trial implications) vs TNF inhibitors.
Utility of coronary artery calcium (CAC) scoring and carotid plaque ultrasound in reclassifying intermediate-risk autoimmune patients.
mcq_angles: EULAR 1.5x multiplier: applies to RA if disease duration > 10 years, RF or anti-CCP positive, or extra-articular features present.

The 'lipid paradox' in active RA: untreated systemic inflammation lowers circulating total cholesterol and LDL, yet paradoxically INCREASES vascular cardiovascular risk; treating inflammation raises measured lipid levels while restoring anti-atherogenic HDL functionality.
Screening recommendation: annual cardiovascular risk assessment in all adult patients with chronic inflammatory arthritis.

topic: ACE inhibitors and ARBs in cardiovascular disease: renal monitoring, hyperkalaemia

guidelinesKept: KDIGO 2021 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Blood Pressure in Chronic Kidney Disease.
2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure.

page.mentor_intro: Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS) inhibitors - ACE inhibitors and Angiotensin Receptor Blockers (ARBs) - are foundational therapies for hypertension, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), post-myocardial infarction, and proteinuric chronic kidney disease (diabetic and non-diabetic). By blocking angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar vasoconstriction, they decrease intraglomerular hydrostatic pressure, which provides long-term nephron protection and slows GFR decline, but causes an acute, predictable, hemodynamic decline in eGFR. KDIGO and AHA/ACC guidelines establish that an acute serum creatinine increase up to 30% within 2-4 weeks of initiation is expected and does NOT warrant drug discontinuation. Routine monitoring of serum creatinine and potassium is required 1-2 weeks post-initiation. True hyperkalemia (> 5.5 mmol/L) is managed with dietary potassium restriction, dose reduction of concomitant potassium-sparing medications, adding loop or thiazide diuretics, or introducing modern potassium binders (patiromer, sodium zirconium cyclosilicate) to maintain RAAS inhibitor organ protection.

teaching_points.claim: KDIGO and ACC/AHA guidelines establish that an acute serum creatinine elevation <= 30% from baseline upon RAAS inhibitor initiation reflects benign intraglomerular hemodynamics and should NOT prompt discontinuation.
Serum creatinine and potassium should be measured 1-2 weeks following initiation or dose escalation of ACE inhibitors or ARBs.

Routine combination therapy of an ACE inhibitor with an ARB or direct renin inhibitor is strictly contraindicated due to elevated risks of hyperkalemia, syncope, and acute kidney injury without cardiovascular benefit (ONTARGET and ALTITUDE trials).

Modern gastrointestinal potassium binders (patiromer, sodium zirconium cyclosilicate) enable continuation and optimization of guideline-directed RAAS inhibitors in heart failure and CKD patients with recurrent hyperkalemia.

sources.title: KDIGO 2021 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Blood Pressure in Chronic Kidney Disease.

2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure.

mcq_angles: Acceptable creatinine rise threshold: up to 30% rise above baseline is expected (due to efferent arteriolar vasodilation reducing intraglomerular pressure); withhold only if rise exceeds 30% or potassium exceeds 5.5-6.0 mmol/L.
Why dual RAAS blockade failed: ONTARGET proved adding an ARB to an ACEi caused more dialysis, hypotension, and hyperkalemia without reducing cardiovascular deaths.
The 36-hour washout rule: transitioning from an ACEi to ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) mandates a 36-hour washout to prevent life-threatening bradykinin-mediated angioedema.

guidelinesKept: ACG Clinical Guideline: Diagnosis and Management of Achalasia.

page.mentor_intro: Achalasia is a primary esophageal motility disorder characterized by incomplete lower esophageal sphincter (LES) relaxation and absent esophageal peristalsis due to autoimmune loss of inhibitory nitric oxide/VIP-producing ganglion cells in the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus. Diagnosis is confirmed by High-Resolution Manometry (HRM) according to the Chicago Classification v4.0, defining three subtypes based on panesophageal pressurization: Type I (classic, no pressurization), Type II (panesophageal pressurization; highest therapeutic success > 90%), and Type III (spastic, premature contractions). Definitive treatment aims to mechanically disrupt the LES and encompasses Per-Oral Endoscopic Myotomy (POEM), Laparoscopic Heller Myotomy with partial fundoplication (LHM), and Graded Pneumatic Dilation (PD; serial 30, 35, 40 mm balloons). POEM provides superior dysphagia relief for Type III spastic achalasia and comparable long-term success to LHM for Types I and II, but carries higher rates of post-procedure gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) requiring daily proton pump inhibitor therapy.

teaching_points.claim: High-Resolution Manometry (Chicago Classification) is the gold standard diagnostic tool, classifying achalasia into Type I (classic), Type II (panesophageal pressurization), and Type III (spastic).
POEM achieves excellent dysphagia relief (> 90%) across all subtypes and is the treatment of choice for Type III (spastic) achalasia due to the ability to perform a long proximal esophageal myotomy.
Laparoscopic Heller Myotomy combined with partial fundoplication (Dor or Toupet) provides durable 5-10 year clinical success with lower rates of post-procedure reflux compared to POEM.

Pneumatic dilation with graded balloon sizes (30, 35, 40 mm) achieves success comparable to myotomy in older adults with Type II achalasia, but carries a 1-3% perforation risk requiring emergency surgical backup.

sources.title: ACG Clinical Guideline: Diagnosis and Management of Achalasia.

uncertainties: Management of post-POEM GERD: surveillance endoscopy and endoluminal anti-reflux procedures (transoral incisionless fundoplication [TIF]).
Endoscopic botulinum toxin injection role: strictly reserved for frail elderly patients unfit for pneumatic dilation or surgical myotomy due to high recurrence rates within 6-12 months.
mcq_angles: Chicago Classification subtype responsiveness: Type II (best prognosis, > 95% response to any modality); Type III (worst to PD/Heller, best treated with POEM); Type I (intermediate).
Post-POEM reflux incidence: occurs in 30-40% of POEM patients (because no fundoplication is constructed), necessitating long-term PPI or objective pH monitoring.
Classic radiographic finding: 'Bird's beak' tapering of distal esophagus on timed barium esophagram with dilated aperistaltic proximal esophagus.
case_hooks: A 34-year-old male with dysphagia to both solids and liquids and regurgitation whose manometry shows IRP 28 mmHg with panesophageal pressurization (Type II achalasia).

guidelinesKept: 2020 American Heart Association Guidelines for Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation and Emergency Cardiovascular Care.

page.mentor_intro: Advanced Cardiovascular Life Support (ACLS) guidelines from the AHA and ERC structure adult cardiac arrest resuscitation around rapid rhythm identification, high-quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), and prompt defibrillation for shockable rhythms. Shockable rhythms (Ventricular Fibrillation [VF] and Pulseless Ventricular Tachycardia [pVT]) mandate immediate unsynchronized defibrillation (120-200 J biphasic), resumption of CPR for 2 minutes, and IV/IO epinephrine 1 mg administered after the second shock, alternating with amiodarone (300 mg first dose, 150 mg second dose) or lidocaine (1-1.5 mg/kg first dose, 0.5-0.75 mg/kg second dose) after the third shock (ALPS trial). Non-shockable rhythms (Asystole and Pulseless Electrical Activity [PEA]) require immediate epinephrine 1 mg as early as possible and urgent investigation of reversible etiologies using the 'H's and T's' framework (Hypovolemia, Hypoxia, Hydrogen ion acidosis, Hypo/hyperkalemia, Hypothermia, Tension pneumothorax, Tamponade, Toxins, Thrombosis PE/coronary).

teaching_points.claim: AHA/ERC guidelines mandate high-quality CPR: chest compression rate 100-120/min, depth 5-6 cm (2-2.4 inches), complete chest recoil, and minimizing interruptions (chest compression fraction > 60-80%).

In shockable rhythms (VF/pVT), amiodarone (300 mg initial, 150 mg second dose) and lidocaine (1-1.5 mg/kg initial) achieve equivalent survival-to-hospital-discharge rates in refractory cardiac arrest (ALPS trial).
In non-shockable rhythms (asystole/PEA), early administration of epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO within 5 minutes of arrest significantly increases return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) and survival.

Targeted Temperature Management (TTM) in comatose post-cardiac arrest patients targeting strict normothermia (36-37.5 C) to actively prevent fever is non-inferior to 33 C hypothermia in survival and functional recovery (TTM-2 trial).

sources.title: 2020 American Heart Association Guidelines for Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation and Emergency Cardiovascular Care.

Hypothermia versus Normothermia after Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest (TTM-2 trial).

uncertainties: Utility of double sequential external defibrillation (DSED) and vector change (VC) defibrillation in refractory ventricular fibrillation (DOSE VF trial).
Role of point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) during pulse checks to differentiate true PEA from pseudo-PEA without interrupting compressions.
mcq_angles: Epinephrine timing divergence: Shockable (give after the 2nd shock has failed); Non-shockable (give immediately as soon as IV/IO access is established).
End-tidal CO2 (ETCO2) monitoring: ETCO2 < 10 mmHg after 20 minutes of high-quality CPR suggests very low probability of ROSC; abrupt sustained rise to 35-40 mmHg is an early indicator of ROSC.
ALPS trial conclusion: both amiodarone and lidocaine are equivalent first-line antiarrhythmic choices for refractory VF/pVT.

A 71-year-old with PEA arrest whose bedside POCUS reveals massive right ventricular dilation and D-shaped septum, treated empirically for pulmonary embolism.

topic: Acromegaly: IGF-1 elevation, GH suppression test, somatostatin analogues, pegvisomant

guidelinesKept: Acromegaly: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline.
AACE and ACE consensus guidelines for the management of acromegaly.

page.mentor_intro: Acromegaly is a chronic systemic endocrine disease caused by excessive growth hormone (GH) secretion, in > 98% from a benign pituitary somatotroph adenoma. Elevated serum Insulin-like Growth Factor 1 (IGF-1) is the screening test of choice. Confirmation requires an Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT; 75 g oral glucose), where failure to suppress nadir GH < 1.0 ug/L (or < 0.4 ug/L with ultrasensitive assays) confirms autonomous GH hypersecretion. Transsphenoidal pituitary adenomectomy is the first-line definitive therapy, achieving biochemical cure in > 70-85% of microadenomas and 40-50% of macroadenomas. For persistent or recurrent disease, first-line medical therapy is first-generation long-acting Somatostatin Receptor Ligands (SRLs: octreotide LAR, lanreotide autogel; targeting SSTR2). Second-line therapies for SRL-resistant disease include the growth hormone receptor antagonist pegvisomant (normalizes IGF-1 in > 90% without lowering GH), pasireotide LAR (multi-receptor SRL targeting SSTR5; carries high hyperglycemia risk), or cabergoline (dopamine agonist for modest IGF-1 elevation).

teaching_points.claim: Endocrine Society guidelines establish serum IGF-1 as the initial diagnostic test of choice; confirmation requires lack of GH suppression (< 1.0 ug/L or < 0.4 ug/L) during a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test.
Transsphenoidal surgery is the primary definitive treatment of choice, performed by an expert neurosurgeon to achieve rapid decompression of visual pathways and biochemical cure.
First-generation somatostatin receptor ligands (octreotide LAR, lanreotide) normalize IGF-1 and control tumor volume in ~40-50% of surgical non-cured patients by targeting SSTR2.

Pegvisomant, a recombinant GH receptor antagonist, normalizes serum IGF-1 in > 90% of patients refractory to somatostatin analogues by blocking peripheral GH action without shrinking pituitary tumors.

sources.title: Acromegaly: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline.
AACE and ACE consensus guidelines for the management of acromegaly.

uncertainties: Monitoring tumor volume with serial pituitary MRI in patients treated with pegvisomant monotherapy (which blocks peripheral IGF-1 without pituitary antiproliferative effects).
Management of treatment-emergent hyperglycemia and diabetes in patients receiving pasireotide LAR.
mcq_angles: Diagnostic algorithm: Elevated age- and sex-adjusted IGF-1 -> Confirm with 75 g OGTT (failure of GH to suppress to < 1.0 ug/L) -> Pituitary MRI with gadolinium.
Biochemical targets of cure: Normal age-adjusted serum IGF-1 AND random GH < 1.0 ug/L (or post-OGTT GH < 0.4 ug/L).
Pegvisomant monitoring pearl: serum GH levels rise paradoxically due to loss of negative feedback; disease activity MUST be monitored exclusively using serum IGF-1 and liver transaminases.
case_hooks: A 42-year-old male with coarse facial features, increasing shoe size, and carpal tunnel syndrome found to have IGF-1 680 ng/mL and non-suppressed GH 4.2 ug/L during OGTT.
A patient with residual macroadenoma after transsphenoidal surgery on lanreotide who achieves complete IGF-1 normalization following the addition of pegvisomant.

guidelinesKept: 2023 ESC Guidelines for the management of acute coronary syndromes.

page.mentor_intro: Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS) encompasses ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI), Non-ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (NSTEMI), and Unstable Angina (UA), defined by myocardial ischemia with or without high-sensitivity cardiac troponin (hs-cTn) elevation. STEMI mandates immediate primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with door-to-balloon time < 90 minutes (or fibrinolysis within 120 minutes if PCI is unavailable). NSTEMI requires validated risk stratification (GRACE score > 140) to direct early invasive coronary angiography (< 24 hours). ESC and AHA/ACC guidelines mandate dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) combining aspirin with a potent P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor 90 mg BID or prasugrel 10 mg daily in PCI) over clopidogrel (PLATO and TRITON-TIMI 38 trials), anticoagulation with unfractionated heparin, bivalirudin, or enoxaparin, high-intensity statin therapy (atorvastatin 80 mg), beta-blockers in reduced LVEF, and early ACE inhibitors.

teaching_points.claim: STEMI mandates emergency primary PCI with target door-to-balloon time < 90 minutes, or fibrinolytic therapy within 10 minutes of ECG if primary PCI transfer time exceeds 120 minutes.

In NSTEMI, an early invasive coronary angiographic strategy (< 24 hours) is recommended for high-risk patients (GRACE score > 140, dynamic ST changes, elevated troponins) to reduce recurrent ischemia and hospitalizations.
Potent P2Y12 inhibitors (prasugrel or ticagrelor) are superior to clopidogrel in ACS, significantly reducing ischemic death and stent thrombosis (TRITON-TIMI 38 and PLATO trials).
Prasugrel demonstrated superior reduction in ischemic events without increased bleeding compared to ticagrelor in invasive ACS in the randomized ISAR-REACT 5 trial.

sources.title: 2023 ESC Guidelines for the management of acute coronary syndromes.
Prasugrel versus clopidogrel in patients with acute coronary syndromes (TRITON-TIMI 38).
Ticagrelor versus clopidogrel in patients with acute coronary syndromes (PLATO).
Ticagrelor or Prasugrel in Patients with Acute Coronary Syndromes (ISAR-REACT 5).

uncertainties: Optimal timing of DAPT de-escalation (e.g. dropping aspirin to P2Y12 monotherapy after 1-3 months in high-bleeding-risk patients).
Role of routine beta-blocker therapy beyond 1 year in post-MI patients with preserved left ventricular ejection fraction (REDUCE-AMI trial).
mcq_angles: Prasugrel contraindications: prior stroke or TIA (absolute contraindication; increased intracranial hemorrhage), age >= 75 years, or weight < 60 kg (requires dose reduction to 5 mg).
Radial vs Femoral access: radial artery vascular access reduces all-cause mortality, major bleeding, and vascular access complications (RIVAL and MATRIX trials).
High-intensity statin initiation: atorvastatin 80 mg or rosuvastatin 40 mg should be initiated immediately prior to hospital discharge regardless of baseline LDL.
case_hooks: A 56-year-old male presenting with crushing chest pain, 3 mm ST elevations in V1-V4, undergoing emergent radial primary PCI of proximal LAD with prasugrel and aspirin.
A 68-year-old female with NSTEMI, troponin 450 ng/L, GRACE score 155, scheduled for invasive angiography within 24 hours on ticagrelor and enoxaparin.

guidelinesKept: Official American Thoracic Society/Centers for Disease Control and Prevention/Infectious Diseases Society of America Clinical Practice Guidelines: Treatment of Drug-Susceptible Tuberculosis.

page.mentor_intro: Active pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, presenting with chronic cough, hemoptysis, fevers, drenching night sweats, weight loss, and upper lobe cavitary or nodular infiltrates on chest radiography. Diagnosis is confirmed via rapid molecular testing (Xpert MTB/RIF assay on sputum), sputum acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smear, and mycobacterial culture. Standard first-line therapy for drug-susceptible TB consists of a 6-month regimen: a 2-month intensive phase with 4 drugs (Rifampin [RIF], Isoniazid [INH], Pyrazinamide [PZA], and Ethambutol [EMB] - 'RIPE'), followed by a 4-month continuation phase with Rifampin and Isoniazid (2RH). Pyridoxine (vitamin B6; 25-50 mg daily) must be co-administered with isoniazid to prevent dose-dependent peripheral neuropathy. Baseline visual acuity and red-green color discrimination must be verified before starting ethambutol to detect optic neuritis; baseline and serial hepatic transaminases must be monitored for drug-induced liver injury (PZA > INH > RIF).

teaching_points.claim: ATS/CDC/IDSA guidelines recommend a 6-month regimen for drug-susceptible pulmonary TB: 2 months of daily RIPE (rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) followed by 4 months of daily RH (rifampin, isoniazid).
Rapid molecular testing (Xpert MTB/RIF) achieves sensitivity > 90% and simultaneously detects rpoB gene mutations conferring rifampin resistance within 2 hours.

Pyridoxine (vitamin B6, 25-50 mg daily) must be co-prescribed with isoniazid to prevent sensory peripheral neuropathy, particularly in diabetics, alcoholics, pregnant women, and malnourished patients.

Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) rules: discontinue all hepatotoxic drugs (PZA, INH, RIF) if transaminases rise >= 3x upper limit of normal with jaundice/nausea, or >= 5x ULN in asymptomatic patients.

sources.title: Official American Thoracic Society/Centers for Disease Control and Prevention/Infectious Diseases Society of America Clinical Practice Guidelines: Treatment of Drug-Susceptible Tuberculosis.

uncertainties: Adoption of 4-month rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimens (TBTC Study 31) for drug-susceptible pulmonary TB in non-pregnant individuals aged >= 12 years.
Management of drug-drug interactions between rifamycins (potent CYP3A4 inducers) and direct oral anticoagulants or antiretroviral therapies.
mcq_angles: Adverse effect monitoring: Ethambutol = retrobulbar optic neuritis (check visual acuity and Ishihara red-green color plates; discontinue if vision deteriorates); Pyrazinamide = hyperuricemia and acute gout; Isoniazid = peripheral neuropathy (prevent with vitamin B6).

DILI re-challenge protocol: once transaminases drop < 2x ULN, reintroduce drugs sequentially: Rifampin first, then Isoniazid, reserving Pyrazinamide last (or dropping PZA and extending continuation phase).
Airborne isolation: negative-pressure isolation room until patient is clinically improving on effective therapy and has 3 consecutive negative sputum AFB smears.
case_hooks: A 31-year-old immigrant presenting with 6 weeks of productive cough, night sweats, and right upper lobe cavitation, confirmed MTB positive and rifampin sensitive on Xpert.
A patient on RIPE therapy presenting at week 3 with dark urine, jaundice, AST 380 U/L, and ALT 440 U/L, requiring immediate cessation of hepatotoxic agents.

guidelinesKept: WSES guidelines for management of acute abdomen in the emergency department.
Antimicrobial therapy for intra-abdominal infections: international consensus.

page.mentor_intro: The acute abdomen encompasses rapid-onset, severe abdominal pain reflecting life-threatening surgical emergencies (perforated viscus, acute peritonitis, bowel obstruction, acute mesenteric ischemia, ruptured ectopic pregnancy, or ruptured AAA). Diagnostic evaluation prioritizes hemodynamic stability, early resuscitation, and structured clinical evaluation: localized peritoneal signs (involuntary guarding, percussion tenderness, rebound) mandate emergent surgical consultation. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis is the diagnostic gold standard, offering sensitivity and specificity > 95% for identifying surgical pathology. Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) rapidly detects hemoperitoneum (FAST), abdominal aortic aneurysm rupture, and acute cholecystitis at the bedside. Analgesia with IV opioids should NOT be withheld as it facilitates physical examination without masking surgical pathology.

teaching_points.claim: Contrast-enhanced abdominal/pelvic CT is the diagnostic imaging modality of choice, achieving sensitivity > 95% and significantly reducing negative laparotomy rates.
Early administration of intravenous opioid analgesia does NOT obscure abdominal examination or impede diagnostic accuracy, and is standard of care (WSES consensus).
Peritoneal signs (involuntary abdominal rigidity, focal rebound tenderness, percussion pain) warrant emergent surgical evaluation for peritonitis or hollow viscus perforation.

Immediate empiric broad-spectrum parenteral antibiotics covering enteric Gram-negative bacilli and anaerobes must be administered within 1 hour of identifying gastrointestinal perforation or peritonitis.

A 72-year-old on anticoagulation presenting with severe lower abdominal pain and diffuse guarding without fever, diagnosed with ruptured rectus sheath hematoma.

topic: Acute and chronic pain assessment and opioid safety

guidelinesKept: CDC Clinical Practice Guideline for Prescribing Opioids for Pain - United States, 2022.
Management of Postoperative Pain: A Clinical Practice Guideline From the American Pain Society.

page.mentor_intro: Pain assessment requires validated multidimensional scales and careful clinical differentiation between nociceptive, neuropathic, and nociplastic mechanisms. In acute pain, multimodal analgesia combining acetaminophen, NSAIDs (unless contraindicated by CKD, peptic ulcer, or cardiovascular disease), regional/neuraxial anesthesia, and non-pharmacologic interventions maximizes pain control while minimizing opioid requirements ('opioid-sparing strategy'). For chronic non-cancer pain, CDC guidelines emphasize non-opioid pharmacotherapies (gabapentinoids, SNRIs, tricyclics, topical agents) and non-pharmacologic modalities (CBT, physical therapy). When opioids are necessary, clinicians should prescribe immediate-release formulations at the lowest effective dose for <= 3-7 days in acute pain; for chronic therapy, clinicians should assess opioid risk tools (ORT), check prescription drug monitoring programs (PDMP), avoid concurrent benzodiazepines (which quadruple fatal overdose risk), and co-prescribe take-home naloxone when daily morphine milligram equivalents (MME) exceed 50.

teaching_points.claim: CDC and APS guidelines emphasize multimodal analgesia combining non-opioid medications (acetaminophen, NSAIDs) and regional blocks as first-line strategy to minimize opioid exposure.
Concurrent prescription of opioids and benzodiazepines quadruples the risk of fatal respiratory depression and is strongly discouraged unless strictly clinically necessary.
For acute pain requiring opioids, immediate-release formulations at the lowest effective dose should be prescribed for <= 3 to 7 days to prevent long-term physical dependence.

Take-home naloxone should be co-prescribed whenever opioid dosages equal or exceed 50 Morphine Milligram Equivalents (MME)/day, or in patients with sleep apnea, renal/hepatic dysfunction, or substance use history.

sources.title: CDC Clinical Practice Guideline for Prescribing Opioids for Pain - United States, 2022.

Buprenorphine transdermal/buccal positioning as a safer partial mu-agonist alternative in chronic pain.
mcq_angles: Benzodiazepine + Opioid lethal synergy: dual sedation blunts respiratory drive and hypercapnic ventilatory response, causing nocturnal fatal apnea.
MME calculation: converting opioid regimens to oral morphine milligram equivalents; threshold >= 50 MME/day mandates naloxone co-prescription and closer surveillance.
Distinguishing neuropathic pain: sharp, shooting, burning pain with allodynia responds to gabapentinoids, SNRIs (duloxetine), or TCAs, but has poor response to standard opioids.

guidelinesKept: 2015 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of pericardial diseases.

page.mentor_intro: Acute pericarditis is diagnosed clinically by the presence of at least 2 of 4 cardinal ESC criteria: 1) sharp, pleuritic chest pain improved by sitting upright and leaning forward, 2) pericardial friction rub on auscultation, 3) widespread concave-upward ST-segment elevation with PR depression on ECG, and 4) new or worsening pericardial effusion. Viral infections (Coxsackie, echovirus, SARS-CoV-2) are the most common cause in high-resource settings. ESC guidelines mandate combination therapy with high-dose NSAIDs (e.g. ibuprofen 600-800 mg TID or aspirin 750-1000 mg TID) PLUS weight-adjusted oral colchicine (0.5 mg daily if < 70 kg, 0.5 mg BID if >= 70 kg) for 3 months in acute pericarditis (ICAP trial) and 6 months in recurrent pericarditis (CORP trials). Colchicine inhibits tubulin polymerization and leukocyte chemotaxis, halving recurrence rates from 37% to 16%. Systemic corticosteroids are second-line agents strictly reserved for NSAID contraindications, autoimmune etiologies, or pregnancy, as early corticosteroid use independently increases the risk of chronic recurrence.

teaching_points.claim: ESC 2015 guidelines establish diagnosis by >= 2 of 4 criteria: pleuritic chest pain, pericardial rub, widespread ST elevation with PR depression, and pericardial effusion.
The landmark ICAP trial proved that adding colchicine to standard NSAID therapy halves the rate of recurrent or persistent pericarditis from 37.5% to 16.7% (NNT = 5).
Weight-adjusted colchicine dosing (0.5 mg daily if < 70 kg, or 0.5 mg BID if >= 70 kg) is maintained for 3 months for first-episode acute pericarditis and 6 months for recurrences.

Systemic corticosteroids should be avoided as first-line therapy because early steroid exposure independently promotes recurrence and chronicity; rilonacept (IL-1 inhibitor) is approved for refractory recurrent pericarditis.

sources.title: 2015 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of pericardial diseases.
A Randomized Trial of Colchicine for Acute Pericarditis (ICAP).

uncertainties: Optimal tapering schedule of colchicine and NSAIDs guided by serial high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP) normalization.
Efficacy of interleukin-1 receptor antagonists (anakinra, rilonacept) as steroid-sparing agents in colchicine-refractory recurrent pericarditis.
mcq_angles: ECG distinction: Acute pericarditis features diffuse concave-upward ST elevation with widespread PR depression and PR elevation in aVR (Spodick sign); STEMI features localized convex ST elevation with reciprocal ST depression and no PR depression.
Why corticosteroids promote recurrence: steroids impair viral clearance and promote chronic inflammatory rebound when tapered.
Exercise restriction: competitive athletes must cease strenuous physical activity for at least 3 months until symptom resolution and normalization of CRP/ECG.

A patient with third episode of recurrent pericarditis dependent on prednisone who achieves rapid remission and complete steroid cessation on rilonacept.

topic: Acute aortic dissection diagnosis and management

guidelinesKept: 2014 ESC Guidelines on the diagnosis and treatment of aortic diseases.
2022 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Aortic Disease.

page.mentor_intro: Acute Aortic Syndromes (AAS) encompass Acute Aortic Dissection (AAD), Intramural Hematoma (IMH), and Penetrating Atherosclerotic Ulcer (PAU), presenting with acute, tearing or ripping chest/back pain and severe hypertension. Stanford classification determines emergency management: Type A involves the ascending aorta (surgical emergency requiring immediate open surgical graft replacement to prevent pericardial tamponade, aortic rupture, or coronary malperfusion); Type B involves the descending aorta distal to the left subclavian artery (managed with medical anti-impulse therapy, reserving Thoracic Endovascular Aortic Repair [TEVAR] for complicated dissection: malperfusion, refractory pain, rapid expansion, or rupture). Initial medical therapy aims to reduce aortic wall shear stress (anti-impulse therapy): IV short-acting beta-blockers (esmolol, labetalol) must be initiated FIRST to lower heart rate < 60 bpm, followed by vasodilators (nitroprusside, nicardipine) to target systolic blood pressure 100-120 mmHg. Giving vasodilators before beta-blockers precipitates reflex tachycardia and accelerates dissection tear propagation.

teaching_points.claim: Stanford classification directs treatment: Type A (ascending aorta) is a surgical emergency with 1-2% hourly mortality requiring immediate operative repair; Type B is managed medically unless complicated.

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography angiography (CTA) of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis is the imaging modality of choice, providing rapid full-length aortic visualization and branch vessel assessment.
Emergency medical therapy requires anti-impulse control: intravenous beta-blockade (esmolol or labetalol) MUST precede vasodilators to lower heart rate < 60 bpm and SBP 100-120 mmHg.

Thoracic Endovascular Aortic Repair (TEVAR) is the standard of care for complicated Type B aortic dissection (visceral/limb malperfusion, refractory pain/hypertension, rupture, or aneurysm expansion).

sources.title: 2014 ESC Guidelines on the diagnosis and treatment of aortic diseases.
2022 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Aortic Disease.

uncertainties: Role of routine pre-emptive TEVAR in uncomplicated Type B dissection with high-risk anatomical features (entry tear > 10 mm, false lumen diameter > 22 mm).

guidelinesKept: Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA) Global Strategy for Asthma Management and Prevention.

page.mentor_intro: Acute severe asthma exacerbation is characterized by progressive dyspnea, wheezing, chest tightness, and airflow obstruction, quantified by Peak Expiratory Flow (PEF) < 50% predicted or personal best. Initial therapy mandates repetitive or continuous inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonists (SABA; albuterol 4-8 puffs or 2.5-5 mg nebulized) combined with inhaled ipratropium bromide (500 ug nebulized q20min x 3 doses), which reduces hospital admissions by 30%. Systemic corticosteroids (oral prednisone 40-50 mg daily for 5-7 days, or IV methylprednisolone 60-80 mg in severe cases) must be administered early within 1 hour of presentation to accelerate resolution of airway inflammation. In severe exacerbations unresponsive to initial nebulization, single-dose intravenous magnesium sulfate (2 g IV over 20 min) provides safe, potent bronchodilation and reduces hospitalizations. Controlled oxygen therapy should target SpO2 93-95% (avoiding hyperoxia, which worsens V/Q mismatch and hypercapnia). A 'normal' or rising PaCO2 (> 40 mmHg) or silent chest signals respiratory muscle fatigue and impending fatal respiratory arrest.

teaching_points.claim: GINA guidelines mandate immediate repetitive SABA plus ipratropium bromide nebulization, which significantly reduces hospital admissions compared to SABA monotherapy.
Systemic corticosteroids administered within 1 hour of emergency department presentation accelerate airflow recovery, prevent relapses, and reduce hospitalization rates.
Intravenous magnesium sulfate (2 g IV over 20 minutes) is indicated in acute severe asthma with PEF < 50% failing initial bronchodilators, significantly improving FEV1 and reducing admission.

A 'normal' or elevated PaCO2 (> 40-45 mmHg) in a tachypneic asthmatic is an ominous sign of respiratory muscle exhaustion, signaling impending arrest requiring ICU monitoring and preparation for intubation.

Arterial blood gas progression: early asthma causes tachypnea, respiratory alkalosis (low PaCO2); a 'normal' PaCO2 represents fatigue and worsening failure.

Ventilator strategy if intubated: low tidal volumes (6 mL/kg), low respiratory rates, and prolonged expiratory time (I:E 1:3 to 1:4) to prevent dynamic hyperinflation (auto-PEEP) and tension pneumothorax.

guidelinesKept: Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) Practice Guidelines for the Management of Bacterial Meningitis.
ESCMID guideline on diagnosis and treatment of acute bacterial meningitis.

page.mentor_intro: Acute bacterial meningitis is a life-threatening CNS infection presenting with the classic triad of fever, neck stiffness (nuchal rigidity, positive Kernig/Brudzinski signs), and altered mental status. Most common community pathogens in adults are Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis; Listeria monocytogenes must be covered in adults >= 50 years, alcoholics, or immunocompromised individuals. Empiric therapy in adults < 50 is IV ceftriaxone (2 g q12h) plus vancomycin (15-20 mg/kg q8-12h); adults >= 50 require the addition of IV ampicillin (2 g q4h) to cover Listeria. Adjuvant dexamethasone (10 mg IV) must be given BEFORE or WITH the first antibiotic dose: the landmark European randomized trial proved dexamethasone reduces mortality by 41% and sensorineural hearing loss in pneumococcal meningitis. Lumbar puncture should not be delayed for neuroimaging unless specific 'CT before LP' criteria exist; if imaging is necessary, blood cultures must be drawn and antibiotics + dexamethasone administered immediately prior to CT scan.

teaching_points.claim: Adjuvant intravenous dexamethasone (10 mg q6h for 4 days) initiated before or with the first antibiotic dose significantly reduces mortality and hearing loss in pneumococcal meningitis (European trial).
Empiric antimicrobial regimen: ceftriaxone 2 g q12h plus vancomycin for all adults; add ampicillin 2 g q4h in adults >= 50 years or immunocompromised hosts to cover Listeria monocytogenes.

CT of the head prior to lumbar puncture is indicated ONLY if specific high-risk features exist: immunocompromised state, history of CNS disease, new-onset seizures, papilledema, abnormal consciousness, or focal neurologic deficit.
If CT head is required before LP, blood cultures must be drawn immediately and empiric antibiotics plus dexamethasone administered WITHOUT waiting for CT completion.

guidelinesKept: ACEP Clinical Policy: Critical Issues in the Evaluation and Management of Adult Patients Presenting to the Emergency Department With Acute Agitation.

page.mentor_intro: Acute behavioural disturbance (ABD) and severe agitation in the emergency and acute inpatient setting represent medical emergencies that threaten patient and staff safety. Most common causes include acute delirium, intoxication (sympathomimetics, alcohol, synthetic cannabinoids), sedative withdrawal, severe psychiatric psychosis, metabolic derangements, and traumatic brain injury. Clinical management follows a staged de-escalation hierarchy: environmental adaptation and verbal de-escalation are attempted first. When non-pharmacologic measures fail and physical danger exists, parenteral pharmacotherapy is deployed: for delirium and undifferentiated agitation, low-dose atypical antipsychotics (haloperidol 2.5-5 mg IM or olanzapine 5-10 mg IM) are first-line. For stimulant toxicity or alcohol withdrawal, intravenous or intramuscular benzodiazepines (lorazepam 1-2 mg or midazolam 2.5-5 mg) are the treatments of choice. For violent, hyperactive excited delirium, intramuscular ketamine (3-4 mg/kg IM) achieves rapid sedation within 5 minutes under strict airway monitoring.

teaching_points.claim: A structured stepwise approach begins with non-pharmacologic de-escalation, reserving chemical sedation for patients presenting immediate physical danger to themselves or staff.
Benzodiazepines (lorazepam, midazolam) are the first-line sedatives for agitation driven by sympathomimetic intoxication (cocaine, methamphetamines) or alcohol withdrawal.
Antipsychotics (haloperidol, olanzapine, droperidol) provide effective sedation for psychotic agitation and delirium, but require ECG monitoring for QTc prolongation.
Intramuscular ketamine (3-4 mg/kg IM) produces rapid, reliable dissociation within 3-5 minutes in extreme, life-threatening violent agitation failing other agents, under dedicated airway monitoring.

Immediate post-sedation protocol: continuous pulse oximetry, cardiac telemetry, blood glucose check, and temperature monitoring to detect malignant hyperthermia/serotonin syndrome.

page.mentor_intro: Acute cholecystitis and acute cholangitis represent common biliary infections governed by the international Tokyo Guidelines (TG18). Acute cholecystitis is defined by local inflammation (Murphy's sign, RUQ tenderness), systemic inflammation (fever, elevated CRP/WBC), and confirmatory imaging (ultrasound showing gallbladder wall thickening >= 4 mm, pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy's sign). Laparoscopic cholecystectomy performed early within 72 hours of symptom onset (or during index admission) is the gold standard, achieving shorter hospital stays and fewer complications than delayed surgery. Acute cholangitis is a medical emergency caused by biliary tract obstruction (primarily choledocholithiasis) with bacterial superinfection, presenting with Charcot's triad (fever, jaundice, RUQ pain) or Reynolds' pentad (adding hypotension and altered mental status in septic shock). TG18 mandates immediate resuscitation, empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics, and emergency biliary decompression via Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) within 24 hours (or emergent < 12 hours for severe Grade III cholangitis).

teaching_points.claim: Tokyo Guidelines 2018 (TG18) recommend early laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 72 hours of symptom onset as the optimal treatment of choice for acute cholecystitis.
Acute cholangitis is diagnosed by systemic inflammation (fever, elevated WBC/CRP), cholestasis (jaundice, elevated transaminases/alkaline phosphatase), and biliary dilation on imaging.
Severe (Grade III) acute cholangitis with organ dysfunction mandates immediate fluid resuscitation, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, and urgent biliary drainage by ERCP within 12 hours.

In high-risk surgical patients with acute cholecystitis unfit for emergency surgery, ultrasound-guided percutaneous transhepatic gallbladder drainage (PTGBD) provides effective temporary or definitive decompression.

Timing of cholecystectomy: early surgery (< 72 hours) avoids dense inflammatory adhesions that develop after 7-10 days, reducing conversion rate to open surgery.

TG18 mandates immediate resuscitation, empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics, and emergency biliary decompression via Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) within 24 hours (or emergent < 12 hours for severe Grade III cholangitis).

teaching_points.claim: Tokyo Guidelines 2018 (TG18) recommend early laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 72 hours of symptom onset as the optimal treatment of choice for acute cholecystitis.
Acute cholangitis is diagnosed by systemic inflammation (fever, elevated WBC/CRP), cholestasis (jaundice, elevated transaminases/alkaline phosphatase), and biliary dilation on imaging.
Severe (Grade III) acute cholangitis with organ dysfunction mandates immediate fluid resuscitation, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, and urgent biliary drainage by ERCP within 12 hours.

In high-risk surgical patients with acute cholecystitis unfit for emergency surgery, ultrasound-guided percutaneous transhepatic gallbladder drainage (PTGBD) provides effective temporary or definitive decompression.

guidelinesKept: NICE Guideline NG103: Delirium: prevention, diagnosis and management in healthcare settings.

page.mentor_intro: Acute confusion (delirium) is an acute, fluctuating neurocognitive disturbance characterized by inattention, altered level of consciousness, and disorganized thinking, triggered by underlying acute medical illness, surgery, or toxidrome. Diagnostic confirmation requires validated screening instruments, predominantly the Confusion Assessment Method (CAM; acute onset/fluctuation + inattention + disorganized thinking or altered consciousness) or 4AT. Non-pharmacologic multicomponent prevention and treatment (HELP model: reorientation, sleep-wake cycle hygiene, early mobilization, pain control, sensory aids, avoidance of deliriogenic medications like anticholinergics and benzodiazepines) is the evidence-based first-line cornerstone. Pharmacotherapy with low-dose atypical antipsychotics (haloperidol, quetiapine, olanzapine) does NOT shorten delirium duration or reduce mortality, and is strictly indicated only when severe agitation threatens imminent patient or staff safety. Formal mental capacity assessment must be decision-specific and time-specific, assessing the ability to understand, retain, weigh information, and communicate a choice.

teaching_points.claim: Diagnosis requires validated bedside tools; the Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) requires features 1 (acute onset/fluctuating course) AND 2 (inattention), PLUS either 3 (disorganized thinking) OR 4 (altered level of consciousness).
Non-pharmacological multicomponent bundles (Hospital Elder Life Program [HELP]: early mobilization, hydration, cognitive reorientation, sleep protocols) reduce delirium incidence by > 30-40%.

Randomized clinical trials (MIND-USA trial) proved that routine antipsychotic administration (haloperidol or ziprasidone) does not alter delirium duration, ICU length of stay, or 30-day mortality compared to placebo.

Mental capacity is legally presumed unless proven otherwise, must be assessed specifically for the particular decision at that exact moment, and requires structured assessment of understanding, retaining, weighing, and communicating decisions.

guidelinesKept: 2023 ESC Guidelines for the management of acute coronary syndromes.

page.mentor_intro: Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS) management centers on rapid risk stratification, coronary revascularization, and potent antithrombotic therapy. Dual Antiplatelet Therapy (DAPT) combining aspirin with a potent P2Y12 receptor inhibitor (ticagrelor 90 mg BID or prasugrel 10 mg daily) is the guideline-directed standard of care for 12 months post-PCI, demonstrating superior reduction in ischemic events and stent thrombosis compared to clopidogrel (PLATO, TRITON-TIMI 38). In the randomized head-to-head ISAR-REACT 5 trial, prasugrel was superior to ticagrelor in reducing composite death, MI, or stroke (6.9% vs 9.3%) without increasing major bleeding. High-bleeding-risk (HBR) patients can safely undergo abbreviated DAPT (1-3 months) followed by P2Y12 inhibitor monotherapy (ticagrelor or clopidogrel; TWILIGHT and STOPDAPT-2 trials), which halves major bleeding without increasing ischemic events. Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors (eptifibatide, tirofiban) are reserved for thrombotic bailout during PCI.

teaching_points.claim: Prasugrel and ticagrelor are significantly superior to clopidogrel in ACS, reducing ischemic death and stent thrombosis (TRITON-TIMI 38 and PLATO trials).
The head-to-head ISAR-REACT 5 trial demonstrated that a prasugrel-based strategy significantly reduced ischemic events compared to ticagrelor without increasing major bleeding in ACS.

In high-bleeding-risk patients undergoing PCI, dropping aspirin after 1-3 months and continuing P2Y12 inhibitor monotherapy significantly reduces major bleeding without increasing stent thrombosis (TWILIGHT trial).

Triple antithrombotic therapy (OAC + DAPT) in patients with atrial fibrillation undergoing PCI should be minimized: transition to dual therapy (DOAC + clopidogrel) at hospital discharge reduces bleeding by > 40% (AUGUSTUS trial).

guidelinesKept: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure.

page.mentor_intro: Acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF) requires aggressive, early decongestion to relieve elevated ventricular filling pressures and systemic congestion. Intravenous loop diuretics (furosemide, bumetanide) are the foundation of therapy: the landmark DOSE-AHF trial established that high-dose IV loop diuretic therapy (2.5x oral home dose) achieves more rapid symptom relief and fluid loss without worsening long-term renal function compared to low-dose therapy, with continuous infusion offering no superiority over bolus dosing. Sequential nephron blockade overcomes diuretic resistance: adding oral acetazolamide (500 mg IV; carbonic anhydrase inhibitor blocking proximal tubule sodium reabsorption) significantly accelerates successful decongestion by 46% (ADVOR trial); adding thiazide-like diuretics (oral metolazone or IV chlorothiazide; CLOROTIC trial) boosts natriuresis. SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) initiated early during index hospitalization improve decongestion and reduce cardiovascular mortality and readmissions (EMPULSE trial).

teaching_points.claim: The landmark DOSE-AHF trial showed that high-dose loop diuretic therapy (2.5x oral home dose IV) achieved superior early fluid loss and dyspnea relief without increasing 60-day renal failure or mortality.
Adding intravenous acetazolamide (500 mg daily) to loop diuretics significantly accelerates successful complete decongestion by 46% without increasing renal adverse events (ADVOR trial).
Adding a thiazide diuretic (CLOROTIC trial: oral hydrochlorothiazide added to IV furosemide) significantly enhances weight loss and diuresis in patients with loop diuretic resistance.

In-hospital initiation of SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin) in acute decompensated heart failure produces significant clinical benefit, weight reduction, and lower 90-day all-cause mortality (EMPULSE trial).

mcq_angles: DOSE-AHF findings: High-dose bolus (2.5x home dose) produces better decongestion; bolus vs continuous infusion showed equivalent efficacy.

Sequential nephron blockade: Acetazolamide acts at the proximal convoluted tubule (ADVOR); Thiazides act at the distal convoluted tubule (CLOROTIC); Loop diuretics act at the thick ascending limb of Henle.

The 'pseudo-worsening' renal function: transient modest rises in serum creatinine during effective decongestion reflect hemoconcentration and are associated with improved, NOT worse, long-term survival.
case_hooks: A 68-year-old on furosemide 40 mg PO daily admitted with pulmonary edema, starting IV furosemide 100 mg (2.5x home dose) with spot urine sodium 82 mmol/L at 2 hours.
A patient with refractory volume overload on furosemide 120 mg IV BID who achieves rapid negative fluid balance after adding IV acetazolamide 500 mg daily.

topic: Acute Disseminated Encephalomyelitis (ADEM): paediatric predominance, MRI characteristics

guidelinesKept: International Pediatric Multiple Sclerosis Study Group (IPMSSG) consensus definitions for demyelinating disorders of the central nervous system.

page.mentor_intro: Acute Disseminated Encephalomyelitis (ADEM) is an acute, immune-mediated, monophasic inflammatory demyelinating disease of the central nervous system, predominantly affecting children and young adults typically 1-3 weeks following a viral illness or vaccination. Clinical presentation combines encephalopathy (altered behavior, lethargy, or coma - a mandatory diagnostic feature in pediatric consensus criteria) with multifocal neurologic deficits (ataxia, cranial nerve palsies, hemiparesis, optic neuritis). Brain and spine MRI with gadolinium is the imaging modality of choice, demonstrating large, bilateral, asymmetric, poorly marginated, fluffy hyperintensities on T2/FLAIR predominantly involving cerebral white matter, deep gray nuclei (thalami, basal ganglia), and spinal cord, with punctate or open-ring enhancement. Serum myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) antibodies are positive in > 50-60% of pediatric ADEM cases. First-line therapy is high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone (30 mg/kg/day, up to 1 g daily for 3-5 days) followed by an oral prednisone taper; intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG 2 g/kg over 2-5 days) or plasma exchange (PLEX) are second-line rescue therapies.

First-line therapy is high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g daily for 3-5 days in adults, 30 mg/kg/day in children) followed by a 4- to 6-week oral taper, achieving complete functional recovery in > 70-80%.

topic: Acute gout attack in hospital: colchicine contraindications, IV corticosteroids, IL-1 inhibition

guidelinesKept: 2020 American College of Rheumatology Guideline for the Management of Gout.

page.mentor_intro: Acute gouty arthritis is an intensely painful inflammatory arthritis driven by the deposition of monosodium urate (MSU) crystals in synovial fluid and periarticular tissues, triggering the NLRP3 inflammasome and interleukin-1beta (IL-1beta) release. Definite diagnosis requires synovial fluid aspiration demonstrating needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals under polarized light (yellow when parallel to the compensator axis). First-line therapies for acute flares are low-dose oral colchicine (1.2 mg initial loading dose, followed by 0.6 mg 1 hour later, then 0.6 mg once or twice daily; AGREE trial), oral NSAIDs (e.g. indomethacin, naproxen), or systemic corticosteroids (prednisone 30-40 mg daily for 5-7 days). In hospitalized patients, oral colchicine and NSAIDs are frequently contraindicated by acute kidney injury, chronic kidney disease (eGFR < 30 mL/min), or anticoagulant therapy; in this setting, systemic corticosteroids (oral, IV, or intra-articular) are the first-line therapy of choice. Interleukin-1 inhibitors (anakinra 100 mg SC daily for 3 days) provide rapid, potent flare resolution in refractory patients with multiple comorbidities.

teaching_points.claim: ACR guidelines establish low-dose colchicine (1.2 mg followed by 0.6 mg 1 hour later) as first-line therapy; the AGREE trial proved low-dose is as effective as high-dose colchicine with 70% fewer gastrointestinal adverse events.

Systemic corticosteroids (oral prednisone 30-40 mg daily or IV methylprednisolone) are first-line for acute gout in hospitalized patients where NSAIDs and colchicine are contraindicated by CKD, AKI, or bleeding risk.
Urate-lowering therapy (allopurinol, febuxostat) should NOT be stopped during an acute gout flare; continuation maintains serum urate stability and avoids precipitating prolonged rebound flares.

Interleukin-1 inhibitors (anakinra 100 mg SC daily for 3 days) achieve rapid clinical pain relief in patients with frequent flares where colchicine, NSAIDs, and corticosteroids are contraindicated or ineffective.

guidelinesKept: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure.

page.mentor_intro: Acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF) requires aggressive, early decongestion to relieve elevated ventricular filling pressures and systemic congestion. Intravenous loop diuretics (furosemide, bumetanide) are the foundation of therapy: the landmark DOSE-AHF trial established that high-dose IV loop diuretic therapy (2.5x oral home dose) achieves more rapid symptom relief and fluid loss without worsening long-term renal function compared to low-dose therapy, with continuous infusion offering no superiority over bolus dosing. Sequential nephron blockade overcomes diuretic resistance: adding oral acetazolamide (500 mg IV; carbonic anhydrase inhibitor blocking proximal tubule sodium reabsorption) significantly accelerates successful decongestion by 46% (ADVOR trial); adding thiazide-like diuretics (oral metolazone or IV chlorothiazide; CLOROTIC trial) boosts natriuresis. SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) initiated early during index hospitalization improve decongestion and reduce cardiovascular mortality and readmissions (EMPULSE trial).

teaching_points.claim: The landmark DOSE-AHF trial showed that high-dose loop diuretic therapy (2.5x oral home dose IV) achieved superior early fluid loss and dyspnea relief without increasing 60-day renal failure or mortality.
Adding intravenous acetazolamide (500 mg daily) to loop diuretics significantly accelerates successful complete decongestion by 46% without increasing renal adverse events (ADVOR trial).
Adding a thiazide diuretic (CLOROTIC trial: oral hydrochlorothiazide added to IV furosemide) significantly enhances weight loss and diuresis in patients with loop diuretic resistance.

In-hospital initiation of SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin) in acute decompensated heart failure produces significant clinical benefit, weight reduction, and lower 90-day all-cause mortality (EMPULSE trial).

guidelinesKept: 2019 AHA/ASA Guidelines for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke.

page.mentor_intro: Acute ischemic stroke management is defined by rapid reperfusion to salvage the ischemic penumbra. Intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase (0.9 mg/kg, max 90 mg; NINDS trial) or tenecteplase (0.25 mg/kg, max 25 mg; EXTEND-IA TNK trial) is indicated within 4.5 hours of symptom onset in eligible patients after intracranial hemorrhage is excluded on non-contrast CT head. For acute large vessel occlusion (LVO) of the anterior circulation (internal carotid or proximal middle cerebral artery [M1/M2]), Endovascular Thrombectomy (EVT) is the undisputed standard of care within 6 hours (HERMES meta-analysis). Furthermore, landmark trials revolutionized late-window therapy: the DAWN trial (6 to 24 hours using clinical-core mismatch on diffusion MRI or CT perfusion) and DEFUSE-3 trial (6 to 16 hours using perfusion-core mismatch: ischemic core < 70 mL, mismatch ratio >= 1.8) proved that EVT dramatically improves functional independence (mRS 0-2: 45-49% vs 13-17%; NNT ~2-3) in selected patients with salvageable penumbral tissue out to 24 hours.

teaching_points.claim: Intravenous thrombolysis (alteplase 0.9 mg/kg or tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg) administered within 4.5 hours of symptom onset improves functional recovery at 3 months (NINDS and ECASS-III trials).

Endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) for large vessel anterior circulation occlusions within 6 hours of onset achieves functional independence in 46% of patients compared to 27% with medical therapy (HERMES meta-analysis, NNT = 2.6).
The landmark DAWN trial proved that mechanical thrombectomy performed between 6 and 24 hours based on clinical-infarct core mismatch achieves marked functional independence (49% vs 13%, NNT = 2.8).

The DEFUSE-3 trial demonstrated that EVT performed between 6 and 16 hours in patients selected by CT perfusion or diffusion MRI (ischemic core < 70 mL, mismatch ratio >= 1.8) significantly reduces disability and 90-day mortality.

mcq_angles: Blood pressure thresholds: prior to IV thrombolysis, BP must be lowered < 185/110 mmHg; during and for 24 hours after thrombolysis/thrombectomy, maintain BP < 180/105 mmHg (using labetalol or nicardipine).

DAWN and DEFUSE-3 late-window criteria: patients waking up with stroke (wake-up stroke) or presenting > 6 hours qualify for EVT up to 24 hours if advanced CT perfusion/MRI reveals small core with large salvageable penumbra.
Antiplatelet timing rule: withhold aspirin, clopidogrel, or anticoagulation for 24 hours following IV thrombolysis until follow-up CT head excludes intracranial hemorrhage.

A 71-year-old female who awoke with left-sided hemiparesis (wake-up stroke, 11 hours since last seen normal) whose CT perfusion reveals 18 mL core and 95 mL penumbra, undergoing successful DAWN-protocol EVT.

guidelinesKept: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Kidney Injury.

page.mentor_intro: Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) is an abrupt decline in glomerular filtration rate defined by KDIGO consensus as an increase in serum creatinine by >= 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours, a >= 1.5-fold increase over baseline within 7 days, or urine output < 0.5 mL/kg/h for >= 6 hours. Clinical evaluation categorizes etiology into prerenal (volume depletion, renal hypoperfusion), intrinsic renal (acute tubular necrosis [ATN], acute interstitial nephritis [AIN], glomerulonephritis), and postrenal (urinary tract obstruction). Urinalysis with microscopic sediment examination is essential: muddy brown granular casts indicate ATN, white cell casts/eosinophils suggest AIN, dysmorphic red cells and RBC casts signal glomerulonephritis, and bland sediment points to prerenal azotemia. Renal ultrasound is mandatory in unexplained AKI to exclude hydronephrosis and obstruction. Management prioritizes restoring euvolemia with balanced crystalloids, discontinuing nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, contrast), and initiating renal replacement therapy for urgent refractory complications (AEIOU: Acidosis pH < 7.15, Electrolytes K+ > 6.5, Ingestion toxins, Overload pulmonary edema, Uremia encephalopathy/pericarditis).

teaching_points.claim: KDIGO consensus criteria stage AKI from Stage 1 (creatinine 1.5-1.9x baseline or urine < 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6-12h) to Stage 3 (creatinine 3.0x baseline, >= 4.0 mg/dL, or anuria >= 12h).
Urinary sediment microscopy provides high diagnostic accuracy: muddy brown granular casts are pathognomonic for acute tubular necrosis (ATN); red cell casts indicate acute glomerulonephritis.
Balanced crystalloids (Lactated Ringer's, Plasma-Lyte) reduce the risk of major adverse kidney events (MAKE) compared to 0.9% normal saline in hospitalized patients (SMART and SALT-ED trials).

Urgent indications for renal replacement therapy follow the 'AEIOU' mnemonic: refractory Acidemia (pH < 7.15), refractory Hyperkalemia (K+ > 6.5 mmol/L), Intoxications, volume Overload, and Uremic pericarditis/encephalopathy.

Nephrotoxic drug review: immediately discontinue NSAIDs, ACEi/ARBs during severe hypovolemic shock, aminoglycosides, and review vancomycin/piperacillin-tazobactam synergy.
