page.mentor_intro: Adult-Onset Still's Disease (AOSD) is a diagnosis of exclusion requiring rigorous elimination of occult infections, hematologic malignancies (especially lymphoma), and other systemic autoimmune diseases. The Yamaguchi criteria represent the most widely validated and sensitive (93.5%) diagnostic framework, requiring at least five criteria with at least two major criteria: high quotidian fever (>= 39°C for >= 1 week), arthralgias/arthritis (>= 2 weeks), typical evanescent non-pruritic salmon-pink maculopapular rash, and leukocytosis (>= 10,000/uL with >= 80% granulocytes). Marked hyperferritinemia (> 5x ULN) with decreased glycosylated ferritin (< 20%) provides substantial corroborative diagnostic confirmation.

teaching_points.claim: Under the validated Yamaguchi criteria, diagnosis requires >= 5 criteria (with at least 2 major criteria): Major criteria include fever >= 39°C lasting >= 1 week, arthralgia/arthritis >= 2 weeks, typical salmon-pink maculopapular rash, and leukocytosis >= 10,000/uL (>= 80% neutrophils).
Minor Yamaguchi criteria include sore throat, lymphadenopathy and/or splenomegaly, abnormal liver enzymes (transaminitis), and negative antinuclear antibody (ANA) and rheumatoid factor (RF).

The Fautrel criteria introduced biological markers into diagnostic classification, incorporating extreme hyperferritinemia and glycosylated ferritin <= 20%, which provides high diagnostic specificity (98.5%) for AOSD.

A drop in the proportion of glycosylated ferritin (< 20%, normal 50-80%) in the setting of severe hyperferritinemia strongly supports AOSD and helps differentiate it from other systemic inflammatory or neoplastic disorders.

topic: Adult-onset Stills disease AOSD: quotidian fever, salmon rash, ferritin, IL-1 inhibition

page.mentor_intro: The clinical hallmark of Adult-Onset Still's Disease (AOSD) is the striking triad of high spiking quotidian fevers, an evanescent salmon-pink maculopapular rash that parallels febrile spikes, and extreme hyperferritinemia (frequently > 3,000 to > 50,000 ug/L). The most severe, life-threatening complication of AOSD is Macrophage Activation Syndrome (MAS), also known as secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (sHLH), characterized by uncontrolled cytokine storm, hemophagocytosis, paradoxical drop in ESR (due to consumptive hypofibrinogenemia), acute cytopenias, transaminitis, and coagulopathy, requiring emergency high-dose pulse corticosteroids and anakinra.

teaching_points.claim: The rash of AOSD is characteristically an evanescent, non-pruritic or mildly pruritic salmon-pink macular or maculopapular eruption, predominantly appearing on the trunk and proximal extremities during high evening fever spikes and disappearing as temperature normalizes.

Extreme hyperferritinemia (> 5-to-10-fold upper limit of normal, often exceeding 10,000 ug/L) reflects massive reticuloendothelial histiocyte activation and directly correlates with disease activity and response to treatment.

Macrophage Activation Syndrome (MAS/sHLH) develops in 10-15% of AOSD patients; laboratory clues include acute fall in erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) with rising CRP, sudden bicytopenia/pancytopenia, hypofibrinogenemia, elevated triglycerides, and hyperferritinemia > 10,000 ug/L.

Emergency management of AOSD-associated MAS mandates high-dose intravenous pulse methylprednisolone (1 g/day for 3 days) combined with high-dose intravenous or subcutaneous anakinra (100-200 mg every 6-8 hours) to arrest the fatal cytokine cascade.

topic: adult septic shock corticosteroids vasopressors mortality randomized trial

page.mentor_intro: The role of adjunctive corticosteroid therapy in adult septic shock was clarified by two landmark randomized controlled trials published simultaneously in 2018: the ADRENAL trial (3,800 patients) and the APROCCHSS trial (1,241 patients). While ADRENAL evaluated continuous intravenous hydrocortisone (200 mg/day) monotherapy and demonstrated faster shock resolution and shorter mechanical ventilation without 90-day mortality benefit, APROCCHSS evaluated hydrocortisone (50 mg IV q6h) plus oral fludrocortisone (50 ug daily) in severe shock and demonstrated a statistically significant 90-day all-cause mortality reduction (43.0% vs 49.1%). The 2021 Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines recommend low-dose corticosteroids in patients with persistent vasopressor dependency.

teaching_points.claim: The landmark ADRENAL trial (3,800 patients, Venkatesh et al., NEJM) showed that continuous hydrocortisone (200 mg/day for 7 days) significantly accelerated shock resolution (median 3 vs 4 days), shortened time to ICU discharge, and reduced blood transfusion requirements, though 90-day mortality was not significantly different (27.9% vs 28.8%).

The French APROCCHSS trial (1,241 patients with severe septic shock, Annane et al., NEJM) demonstrated that combined hydrocortisone (50 mg IV q6h) plus oral fludrocortisone (50 ug daily) significantly reduced 90-day all-cause mortality from 49.1% to 43.0% (hazard ratio 0.88, p=0.03).

The 2021 Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines issue a weak recommendation for low-dose corticosteroid therapy (IV hydrocortisone 200 mg/day) in adult septic shock patients who have an ongoing requirement for vasopressor therapy (norepinephrine or epinephrine >= 0.25 ug/kg/min) for at least 4 hours.

Neither trial reported an increase in secondary hospital-acquired infections or gastrointestinal bleeding with low-dose corticosteroids, although hydrocortisone was associated with higher rates of manageable hyperglycemia.

page.mentor_intro: The therapeutic paradigm for advanced/metastatic melanoma has been revolutionized by immune checkpoint blockade targeting PD-1 and CTLA-4. In the benchmark CheckMate 067 trial, dual checkpoint inhibition with nivolumab plus ipilimumab achieved unprecedented durable 6.5-year overall survival (49% vs 42% for nivolumab alone and 23% for ipilimumab alone), with median overall survival reaching 72.1 months. While dual therapy yields the highest response rates (58%) and intracranial control, it induces severe Grade 3/4 immune-related adverse events (irAEs) in 59% of patients, necessitating proactive monitoring, prompt high-dose corticosteroid intervention, and careful risk-benefit stratification against anti-PD-1 monotherapy.

teaching_points.claim: In the landmark phase 3 CheckMate 067 trial (Wolchok et al., NEJM), nivolumab plus ipilimumab achieved a median overall survival of 72.1 months and a 6.5-year overall survival rate of 49%, establishing dual checkpoint blockade as the most potent frontline regimen.

Nivolumab monotherapy in CheckMate 067 demonstrated robust efficacy with a 6.5-year survival rate of 42% and a substantially lower rate of Grade 3/4 treatment-related adverse events (24%) compared to combination therapy (59%).

The randomized phase 3 KEYNOTE-006 trial established pembrolizumab (anti-PD-1) superiority over ipilimumab in both treatment-naive and previously treated advanced melanoma, prolonging progression-free and overall survival with significantly lower toxicity.

Immune-related adverse events (colitis, hepatitis, hypophysitis, pneumonitis, myocarditis) require protocolized grading and prompt high-dose systemic corticosteroids (prednisone 1-2 mg/kg/day or IV methylprednisolone); refractory colitis responds rapidly to infliximab or vedolizumab.

page.mentor_intro: The treatment landscape of locally advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma has been fundamentally transformed by the antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) enfortumab vedotin paired with the anti-PD-1 inhibitor pembrolizumab. In the practice-changing EV-302 phase 3 trial, enfortumab vedotin plus pembrolizumab nearly doubled median overall survival compared to traditional platinum-based chemotherapy (gemcitabine plus cisplatin or carboplatin), establishing a new frontline standard of care regardless of cisplatin eligibility. In patients receiving initial platinum chemotherapy, the JAVELIN Bladder 100 trial proved that switch maintenance avelumab significantly extends survival in those without disease progression.

teaching_points.claim: In the global phase 3 EV-302 / KEYNOTE-A39 trial (Powles et al., NEJM), enfortumab vedotin combined with pembrolizumab nearly doubled median overall survival (31.5 vs 16.1 months; hazard ratio for death 0.47, p<0.001) compared with platinum-based chemotherapy.

The landmark JAVELIN Bladder 100 randomized trial proved that avelumab maintenance therapy (anti-PD-L1) significantly prolonged median overall survival (21.4 vs 14.3 months, HR 0.69) in patients with advanced urothelial carcinoma whose disease did not progress after 4-6 cycles of first-line platinum-gemcitabine chemotherapy.

Enfortumab vedotin targets Nectin-4 to deliver the microtubule-disrupting cytotoxic payload monomethyl auristatin E (MMAE); cardinal toxicities require rigorous monitoring for peripheral neuropathy, severe cutaneous adverse reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), and hyperglycemia.

For patients with advanced urothelial carcinoma harboring susceptible FGFR3 or FGFR2 genetic alterations who progress after platinum chemotherapy, the oral FGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor erdafitinib demonstrates proven survival extension over single-agent chemotherapy.

page.mentor_intro: Agitation in hospitalized adult medical and surgical patients represents a clinical emergency reflecting underlying delirium, substance intoxication or withdrawal, toxic-metabolic encephalopathy, or acute exacerbation of psychiatric illness. Systematic clinical evaluation utilizing the Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale (RASS) objectively gauges severity. The initial approach prioritizes environmental optimization, de-escalation, addressing uncomfortable physical triggers (pain, urinary retention, hypoxia, constipation), and minimizing deliriogenic restraints. When severe aggression endangers the patient or staff, structured pharmacological calming (rapid tranquilization with oral or parenteral atypical antipsychotics) is implemented with continuous airway and vital sign monitoring.

teaching_points.claim: Structured bedside agitation scoring using validated tools such as the Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale (RASS; ranging from +4 combative to -5 unarousable) allows objective titration of behavioral and pharmacological calming interventions.

NICE Guideline NG103 emphasizes that non-pharmacological interventions—reorientation, reassurance, family presence, lighting regulation, noise reduction, and pain control—are the mandatory first-line strategy for agitated delirium in hospital inpatients.

In the multicenter TREC randomized trials of rapid tranquilization in emergency settings, intramuscular olanzapine or haloperidol plus promethazine achieved rapid tranquility within 15-30 minutes with significantly lower risks of respiratory depression than parenteral benzodiazepines.

Physical restraints are an intervention of absolute last resort, carry high risks of strangulation, blunt trauma, and worsening agitation, and mandate continuous 1-on-1 nursing observation and regular vital sign checks every 15 minutes.

topic: Air embolism: venous vs arterial, Trendelenburg positioning, hyperbaric oxygen

page.mentor_intro: Vascular air embolism is a rare but catastrophic iatrogenic or barotraumatic event categorized into Venous Air Embolism (VAE; entrainment into systemic venous circulation or right heart) and Arterial Air Embolism (AAE; air entering pulmonary veins, left heart, or systemic arteries, leading to cerebral or coronary occlusions). VAE occurs during central venous catheter placement/removal, neurosurgical operations in the sitting position, or laparoscopic insufflation, precipitating right ventricular outflow tract 'air lock' and cardiovascular collapse. Immediate management requires stopping air ingress, 100% high-flow oxygen, Durant maneuver (left lateral decubitus and Trendelenburg positioning), and urgent hyperbaric oxygen (HBOT) therapy.

teaching_points.claim: Venous air embolism entering the right ventricle creates a mechanical 'air lock' obstructing the pulmonary artery, producing acute pulmonary hypertension, acute cor pulmonale, profound hypotension, and sudden drop in end-tidal CO2 (EtCO2).

Immediate bedside rescue positioning for suspected venous air embolism is the Durant maneuver: placing the patient in the left lateral decubitus and Trendelenburg position, which traps the air bubble at the apex of the right ventricle away from the pulmonary outflow tract.

Administration of 100% inspired oxygen accelerates bubble reabsorption by washing out systemic nitrogen, creating a steep nitrogen concentration gradient from the bubble into blood and reducing bubble volume.

Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT at 2.8 to 3.0 atmospheres absolute) is the definitive treatment of choice for arterial gas embolism and severe venous embolism with neurological or hemodynamic impairment, rapidly compressing bubble diameter (Boyle's law) and restoring microvascular tissue perfusion.

page.mentor_intro: Systematic airway management requires structured pre-intubation difficult airway assessment and adherence to validated rescue algorithms to avoid the dreaded 'cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate' (CICO) scenario. The 4th National Audit Project (NAP4) in the United Kingdom revealed that poor airway assessment, failure to plan for difficult intubation, and persistent repeated laryngoscopy attempts are the leading causes of catastrophic airway brain damage and death. The 2015 Difficult Airway Society (DAS) guidelines structure unanticipated difficult tracheal intubation into four sequential plans: Plan A (facemask and video-laryngoscopy), Plan B (second-generation supraglottic airway device [SAD]), Plan C (facemask oxygenation and waking the patient), and Plan D (emergency front-of-neck access [FONA]).

teaching_points.claim: The NAP4 major airway complications audit demonstrated that unrecognized esophageal intubation, repeated blind attempts at laryngoscopy, and delay in performing surgical cricothyroidotomy were major causes of fatal airway outcomes.

The 2015 Difficult Airway Society (DAS) guidelines structure failed intubation into a strict sequential protocol: Plan A (tracheal intubation with video-laryngoscopy, maximum 3+1 attempts); Plan B (maintaining oxygenation with a 2nd generation supraglottic airway device); Plan C (facemask oxygenation); Plan D (emergency front-of-neck access).

Second-generation supraglottic airway devices (e.g., i-gel, ProSeal LMA) are superior to first-generation LMAs because of higher seal pressures (> 30 cmH2O) and a separate gastric drainage port that reduces pulmonary aspiration risk.

Plan D (Emergency Front-of-Neck Access / FONA) mandates a scalpel-bougie-tube cricothyroidotomy (stab incision through the cricothyroid membrane, coude-tip bougie insertion, and railroading a 6.0 mm cuffed endotracheal tube), which is faster and more reliable than needle/cannula techniques.

topic: Airway management in the ICU: RSI, video-laryngoscopy, difficult airway

guidelinesKept: Difficult Airway Society guidelines for the management of tracheal intubation in critically ill adults.

page.mentor_intro: Endotracheal intubation in the intensive care unit is a high-risk procedure carrying a 10-to-20-fold higher incidence of life-threatening complications (severe hypoxemia, cardiovascular collapse, cardiac arrest) compared to elective operating room intubations. The landmark DEVICE trial (Prekker et al., NEJM) definitively established that video-laryngoscopy significantly improves first-pass intubation success (85.1% vs 70.8%) compared to direct laryngoscopy in critically ill adults. Structured ICU intubation bundles—comprising pre-oxygenation with HFNC or NIV, hemodynamic optimization, mandatory video-laryngoscopy, neuromuscular blockade, and capnography confirmation—mitigate peri-intubation morbidity.

teaching_points.claim: In the multicenter randomized DEVICE trial (1,417 critically ill patients, Prekker et al., NEJM), video-laryngoscopy resulted in a higher rate of successful intubation on the first attempt compared with direct laryngoscopy (85.1% vs 70.8%; absolute difference 14.2 percentage points, p<0.001).

The French MACMAN randomized trial demonstrated that video-laryngoscopy did not improve first-pass intubation when performed by highly experienced operators with standard Mac blades, highlighting that operator familiarity and blade geometry (hyperangulated vs standard) dictate performance.

DAS and Intensive Care Society (ICS) guidelines for management of the critically ill airway recommend mandatory pre-oxygenation with non-invasive ventilation (NIV) or high-flow nasal oxygen, aggressive fluid and vasopressor pre-loading, and continuous waveform capnography.

Peri-intubation cardiovascular collapse occurs in up to 30% of critically ill patients; prophylactic pre-induction initiation of peripheral norepinephrine or push-dose vasopressors significantly reduces severe hypotension and cardiac arrest during induction.

page.mentor_intro: Malignant central airway obstruction (CAO) is a life-threatening complication occurring in up to 20-30% of advanced lung cancers and metastatic malignancies (esophagus, thyroid, melanoma, breast). Patients present with stridor, severe dyspnea, wheezing mistakenly treated as asthma, recurrent post-obstructive pneumonias, or hemoptysis. Emergency management requires high-dose corticosteroids, heliox (helium-oxygen mixture) to reduce airway resistance in laminar flow, and emergent multidisciplinary interventional pulmonology consultation. Rigid bronchoscopy is the optimal platform to secure the airway, de-bulk endobronchial tumor via ablative modalities (electrocautery, APC, cryotherapy), and deploy self-expanding metallic or silicone tracheobronchial stents.

teaching_points.claim: American College of Chest Physicians (CHEST) guidelines recommend rigid bronchoscopy under general anesthesia as the preferred diagnostic and therapeutic interventional modality for severe malignant central airway obstruction.

Immediate mechanical airway recanalization is achieved via rigid bronchoscope core-out debridement combined with immediate ablative thermal modalities (argon plasma coagulation [APC], electrocautery, or contact diode laser).

Airway stenting with silicone (Dumon) or self-expanding covered metallic stents (SEMS) provides immediate structural stabilization for extrinsic airway compression or mixed endobronchial/extrinsic obstruction, restoring airway lumen in > 90% of cases.

In the multicenter AQuIRE registry study (Ost et al., Chest), therapeutic bronchoscopy for malignant CAO resulted in immediate, statistically significant improvements in dyspnea, health-related quality of life, and lung function, with complication rates < 4% in experienced centers.

guidelinesKept: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Kidney Injury.

page.mentor_intro: Acute kidney injury (AKI) diagnosis and management focuses on early detection, etiology identification, avoidance of compounding toxicities, and fluid stewardship. Under KDIGO recommendations, identifying AKI early via paired serum creatinine and hourly urine output monitoring mandates implementation of the KDIGO Stage-based Care Bundle. In resuscitating patients at risk of or suffering from AKI, the landmark SMART and SALT-ED randomized trials demonstrated that balanced crystalloids (Plasma-Lyte or Lactated Ringer's) significantly reduce Major Adverse Kidney Events at 30 days (MAKE30) compared to 0.9% normal saline, avoiding hyperchloremia-induced renal arteriolar vasoconstriction.

teaching_points.claim: In the landmark SMART trial of 15,802 critically ill adults (Semler et al., NEJM), intravenous resuscitation with balanced crystalloids significantly lowered the 30-day incidence of Major Adverse Kidney Events (MAKE30: death, new RRT, or persistent renal dysfunction) compared with 0.9% saline (14.3% vs 15.4%, p=0.04).

The companion SALT-ED trial in non-critically ill emergency department patients confirmed that balanced crystalloids reduced MAKE30 compared to saline (4.7% vs 5.6%), driven particularly by lower rates of acute renal replacement therapy in high-risk baseline subgroups.

KDIGO guidelines recommend discontinuing all potential nephrotoxic medications (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, amphotericin B, vancomycin where alternatives exist) and holding RAAS inhibitors during acute hypotension and volume depletion.

In severe AKI with fluid overload, diuretics (loop diuretics alone or combined with metolazone/acetazolamide) do not improve renal recovery or survival, but facilitate fluid balance and buy time while deciding on renal replacement therapy initiation.

page.mentor_intro: Accurate diagnosis and staging of acute kidney injury under the KDIGO consensus criteria requires serial assessment of both serum creatinine and hourly urine output. Urine output criteria frequently detect AKI earlier than serum creatinine, which requires 24 to 48 hours of accumulation to cross diagnostic thresholds. The Acute Disease Quality Initiative (ADQI) consensus emphasizes that combining functional staging (creatinine and urine output) with structural injury biomarkers (TIMP-2, IGFBP7, NGAL) defines subclinical AKI, guiding risk-adapted monitoring and preventing secondary iatrogenic insult.

teaching_points.claim: KDIGO diagnostic criteria define AKI by any of the following: rise in serum creatinine by >= 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours; rise in creatinine >= 1.5 times baseline within 7 days; or urine volume < 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 consecutive hours.

Oliguria criteria (< 0.5 mL/kg/h) provide earlier identification of AKI than creatinine in critically ill patients, and persistent oliguria beyond 12 hours independently predicts 30-day mortality even with minor creatinine increments.

KDIGO Stage 3 criteria include: serum creatinine >= 3.0 times baseline; serum creatinine >= 4.0 mg/dL (>= 353.6 umol/L); initiation of renal replacement therapy; or in patients < 18 years, a decrease in eGFR to < 35 mL/min/1.73m2.

The ADQI 23 consensus recommendations advocate incorporating damage biomarkers to refine staging: identifying 'biomarker positive / function negative' patients with subclinical AKI who carry elevated risks of prolonged hospitalization and progression.

page.mentor_intro: Sepsis-associated acute kidney injury (S-AKI) arises from intrarenal microvascular shunting, endothelial injury, and inflammatory metabolic reprogramming rather than simple gross hypoperfusion. Management emphasizes balanced crystalloids over 0.9% saline, early norepinephrine targeting MAP >= 65-70 mmHg (80-85 mmHg in chronic hypertension), avoiding nephrotoxins, and KDIGO-guided RRT initiation.

teaching_points.claim: Balanced crystalloids reduce the composite incidence of death, new persistent renal replacement therapy, or persistent renal dysfunction compared to 0.9% saline in critically ill septic patients (SMART trial).

KDIGO guidelines define S-AKI using consensus serum creatinine and urine output criteria, staging severity from Stage 1 (1.5-1.9x baseline or urine < 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6-12h) to Stage 3 (3x baseline, creatinine >= 4.0 mg/dL, or anuria >= 12h).

Routine early accelerated initiation of renal replacement therapy without conventional urgent indications does not improve survival and significantly increases dialytic complications and vascular access line infections (STARRT-AKI trial).

Restoring renal perfusion pressure with norepinephrine targeting MAP 65-70 mmHg optimizes medullary microcirculation; higher targets (80-85 mmHg) provide benefit only in patients with chronic pre-existing hypertension (SEPSISPAM trial).

page.mentor_intro: Acute kidney disease (AKD) describes the critical window between 7 and 90 days post-insult where acute injury either resolves or progresses to permanent chronic kidney disease. Standard of care includes post-discharge nephrology follow-up within 90 days, blood pressure optimization, monitoring proteinuria, and reassessing cardioprotective medications.

teaching_points.claim: ADQI 24 consensus defines acute kidney disease (AKD) as persistent kidney dysfunction lasting 7 to 90 days after an initial AKI episode.
Post-AKI survivors experience a 3-fold higher long-term risk of incident end-stage kidney disease and accelerated cardiovascular mortality.
Timely post-discharge nephrology evaluation within 90 days of severe AKI is associated with a 24% relative reduction in 1-year all-cause mortality.
Careful re-initiation of RAAS inhibitors after recovery from hemodynamic AKI reduces secondary cardiovascular events and mortality without increasing recurrent AKI.

page.mentor_intro: Severe alcohol-associated hepatitis carries up to 30-50% 1-month mortality. It is defined by Maddrey Discriminant Function (mDF) >= 32 or MELD > 20. Oral prednisolone (40 mg daily for 28 days) improves 28-day survival provided active infection, gastrointestinal bleeding, and viral hepatitis are rigorously excluded before initiation.

teaching_points.claim: AASLD guidelines recommend oral prednisolone 40 mg daily for 28 days in patients with severe alcohol-associated hepatitis (mDF >= 32 or MELD > 20).
The Lille Model assessed on day 7 calculates corticosteroid responsiveness; a score >= 0.45 indicates non-response and warrants stopping steroids to avoid fatal fungal or bacterial sepsis.
Pentoxifylline does not improve 28-day or 6-month survival in severe alcoholic hepatitis and is no longer recommended (STOPAH trial).

Early liver transplantation in highly selected patients with first-episode severe alcoholic hepatitis non-responsive to medical therapy achieves post-transplant survival comparable to other indications.

uncertainties: Optimal selection criteria and duration of alcohol abstinence for early liver transplantation in non-responders.
Use of combination therapies or anti-inflammatory biologics in steroid-refractory alcoholic hepatitis.
mcq_angles: Calculating Maddrey DF (4.6 * [PT - control] + total bilirubin in mg/dL) to determine indication for corticosteroids.
Interpreting the Day 7 Lille score threshold of 0.45 to discontinue futile steroids.
Screening for occult spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, urinary tract infection, and bacteremia before giving corticosteroids.
case_hooks: A 46-year-old with heavy drinking history presenting with deep jaundice (bilirubin 22 mg/dL), AST 240, ALT 85, and prolonged PT (DF = 48).
A patient on Day 7 of prednisolone whose bilirubin has increased from 18 to 23 mg/dL, with a Lille score of 0.62.
page.gaps: Reviewers should cross-reference local early liver transplant evaluation pathways and infection screening protocols.

page.mentor_intro: Alcoholic hepatitis presents with rapid-onset jaundice, tender hepatomegaly, AST:ALT ratio > 2:1 (rarely exceeding 400 IU/L), and systemic inflammation. Core therapy requires intensive nutrition (1.2-1.5 g/kg protein, 35 kcal/kg), high-potency parenteral B vitamins (thiamine), infection prophylaxis, and alcohol abstinence support.

teaching_points.claim: EASL guidelines emphasize enteral nutritional support providing 35-40 kcal/kg/day and 1.2-1.5 g/kg protein to reduce infectious complications in alcoholic hepatitis.
Aminotransferase elevations in alcoholic hepatitis typically display AST:ALT > 2:1 with absolute values almost always < 500 IU/L due to hepatic pyridoxal-5-phosphate deficiency.
Parenteral thiamine must be administered immediately prior to any glucose infusion to prevent precipitation of acute Wernicke encephalopathy.
Ascites and hepatic encephalopathy in acute alcoholic hepatitis require standard spironolactone/furosemide and lactulose/rifaximin titration.

uncertainties: Efficacy of granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) in improving liver regeneration and reducing 90-day mortality.
Role of fecal microbiota transplantation in improving gut-liver axis dysbiosis in alcoholic hepatitis.
mcq_angles: Characteristic laboratory findings: AST:ALT > 2 with transaminases < 300-400 IU/L, leukocytosis, and elevated INR.
Nutritional requirements in severe alcoholic hepatitis and avoidance of protein restriction.
Mandatory baseline diagnostic paracentesis to exclude spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in jaundiced cirrhotic ascites.

page.mentor_intro: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is diagnosed using DSM-5-TR criteria and quantified with validated screening tools (AUDIT-C). Long-term management pairs evidence-based psychosocial interventions (CBT, motivational interviewing) with maintenance pharmacotherapy (acamprosate, naltrexone) to sustain abstinence or reduce heavy drinking.

teaching_points.claim: APA practice guidelines recommend offering either acamprosate or oral naltrexone as first-line pharmacotherapy for patients with moderate-to-severe alcohol use disorder.
AUDIT-C screening with scores >= 4 in men and >= 3 in women identifies hazardous drinking with high sensitivity and specificity in outpatient settings.
Combining pharmacotherapy with structured medical management or cognitive behavioral therapy yields higher abstinence rates than medication alone (COMBINE study).
Routine laboratory monitoring with GGT, MCV, and carbohydrate-deficient transferrin (CDT) provides objective biochemical markers of ongoing alcohol consumption.

uncertainties: Comparative effectiveness of abstinence-oriented versus heavy-drinking-reduction endpoints in clinical trial design.
Optimal duration of maintenance pharmacotherapy once sustained remission is achieved.
mcq_angles: Identifying first-line maintenance pharmacotherapy for AUD: acamprosate and naltrexone.
Choosing between abstinence-focused goals versus controlled reduction in harm-reduction models.
Distinguishing physiological tolerance and withdrawal symptoms from behavioral features of AUD under DSM-5 criteria.

page.mentor_intro: Acamprosate and naltrexone are first-line pharmacological options for alcohol use disorder. Acamprosate modulates glutamatergic NMDA and GABA transmission, is excreted renally, and is preferred in patients with liver disease. Naltrexone blocks mu-opioid receptors, reduces alcohol reward/craving, but is contraindicated in acute hepatitis, liver failure, and concurrent opioid use.

teaching_points.claim: Naltrexone (oral 50 mg daily or monthly depot intramuscular extended-release 380 mg) significantly reduces the risk of return to heavy drinking.
Naltrexone is strictly contraindicated in patients currently taking prescription opioids or undergoing opioid detoxification, as it precipitates severe acute opioid withdrawal.
Acamprosate (666 mg three times daily) modulates NMDA hyperglutamatergic states, promotes abstinence maintenance, and is safe in advanced liver disease because it lacks hepatic metabolism.
Acamprosate dose must be reduced in moderate renal impairment (CrCl 30-50 mL/min) and is contraindicated when CrCl < 30 mL/min.

uncertainties: Precision pharmacogenetics: whether OPRM1 Asn40Asp (A118G) polymorphism reliably predicts enhanced clinical response to naltrexone.
Efficacy of simultaneous combination of acamprosate plus naltrexone over individual monotherapy.
mcq_angles: Selecting acamprosate over naltrexone in a patient with Child-Pugh class B cirrhosis.
Recognizing naltrexone contraindication in patients with chronic pain managed with opioid analgesics.
Managing gastrointestinal side effects (nausea, diarrhea) of acamprosate and naltrexone during treatment initiation.

page.gaps: Verify renal dosing adjustment tables for acamprosate and toxicological screening prior to naltrexone initiation.

page.mentor_intro: Chronic alcohol use disorder commonly leads to hepatic fibrosis and metabolic brain injury. Wernicke encephalopathy is a medical emergency caused by thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, classic triad of confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia (nystagmus/lateral rectus palsy) occurring in only one-third of cases. Prompt IV thiamine prevents progression to irreversible Korsakoff psychosis.

teaching_points.claim: Wernicke encephalopathy is a clinical diagnosis requiring high-dose intravenous thiamine (500 mg IV three times daily for 3-5 days) before any enteral or parenteral carbohydrates.
Caine criteria diagnostic sensitivity for Wernicke encephalopathy requires 2 of: dietary deficiency, oculomotor abnormalities, cerebellar dysfunction, and altered mental state.
Alcohol-related cirrhosis requires systematic hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) screening with ultrasound +/- AFP every 6 months and endoscopic variceal screening.
Sustained alcohol abstinence is the single most powerful determinant of survival and portal pressure reduction across all stages of alcohol-related liver disease.

uncertainties: Optimal oral thiamine maintenance dosing and bioavailability following completion of high-dose intravenous treatment.
Reversibility of cognitive deficits in Korsakoff syndrome with long-term nutritional and cognitive rehabilitation.
mcq_angles: Why IV thiamine must precede glucose infusion: glucose metabolism consumes scarce remaining thiamine pyrophosphate cofactors in pyruvate dehydrogenase.
Classic MRI brain findings in Wernicke encephalopathy: symmetric hyperintensity in mammillary bodies, medial thalami, and periaqueductal gray.
Clinical distinction between Wernicke encephalopathy (acute, reversible) and Korsakoff syndrome (chronic, anterograde amnesia with confabulation).
case_hooks: A 55-year-old homeless male brought to the ED with confusion, horizontal nystagmus, and broad-based ataxia after a multi-week drinking binge.
A cirrhotic patient admitted for decompensated ascites whose nurse asks whether a 5% dextrose infusion can be started before the thiamine arrives.
page.gaps: Ensure local emergency department protocol mandates IV thiamine in triage for all malnourished or alcohol-dependent patients.

page.mentor_intro: Alcohol withdrawal syndrome (AWS) ranges from mild tremulousness to life-threatening delirium tremens and withdrawal seizures. Long-acting benzodiazepines (diazepam, chlordiazepoxide) are standard of care, administered preferably via symptom-triggered protocols (CIWA-Ar) rather than fixed schedules. In hepatic cirrhosis, short-acting agents without active metabolites (lorazepam, oxazepam) avoid drug accumulation.

teaching_points.claim: Symptom-triggered benzodiazepine administration guided by CIWA-Ar scores achieves equivalent clinical control with significantly lower total medication dose and shorter hospital stay.
Diazepam and chlordiazepoxide provide smoother withdrawal control due to long-acting active metabolites (desmethyldiazepam), reducing withdrawal seizure frequency.

In patients with severe liver failure or cirrhosis, lorazepam or oxazepam (LOT drugs: Lorazepam, Oxazepam, Temazepam) are preferred because they undergo direct glucuronidation without phase I hepatic metabolism.
Alcohol withdrawal seizures typically occur 12-48 hours after alcohol reduction, are generalized tonic-clonic, and are treated with benzodiazepines, not standard phenytoin.

uncertainties: Use of adjunctive alpha-2 agonists (clonidine, dexmedetomidine) for autonomic hyperactivity without masking ongoing neurocognitive deterioration.
Role of gabapentin or carbamazepine as monotherapy in mild-to-moderate outpatient alcohol withdrawal.
mcq_angles: Choosing lorazepam or oxazepam in patients with decompensated alcoholic cirrhosis or acute liver injury.
Why phenytoin is ineffective for alcohol withdrawal seizures (the underlying mechanism is GABA down-regulation and NMDA up-regulation, not an epileptic focus).
Timing of symptom-triggered CIWA-Ar assessments and intervention threshold (CIWA-Ar >= 8-10 points).

page.gaps: Reviewers should confirm nurses are validated in CIWA-Ar scoring and that telemetry is available for heavy withdrawal protocols.

page.mentor_intro: Delirium tremens (DT) is a severe medical emergency characterized by profound delirium, hallucinations, agitation, fever, and severe autonomic instability, typically developing 48-96 hours after alcohol cessation. Management in the ICU mandates aggressive intravenous sedation (high-dose benzodiazepines or phenobarbital protocols), airway protection, and correction of electrolyte abnormalities (hypomagnesemia, hypokalemia).

teaching_points.claim: Delirium tremens carries up to 5-15% mortality without intensive care; mortality is driven by hyperthermia, cardiac arrhythmias, and aspiration pneumonia.
Phenobarbital monotherapy or protocolized combination with benzodiazepines achieves faster symptom control, lower intubation rates, and decreased ICU length of stay in severe refractory withdrawal.
Dexmedetomidine reduces sympathetic overdrive and tachycardia as an adjunctive sedative, but does not prevent seizures or delirium and cannot substitute for GABAergic agents.
Severe hypomagnesemia and hypophosphatemia are common in severe withdrawal and must be corrected aggressively to prevent refractory seizures and refractory hypokalemia.

uncertainties: Exact dosing protocols for intravenous phenobarbital load (10 mg/kg vs incremental 130-260 mg doses) in non-intubated patients.
Long-term neurocognitive sequelae following prolonged ICU delirium tremens.
mcq_angles: Distinguishing alcoholic hallucinosis (clear sensorium, occurs 12-24h post-cessation) from delirium tremens (global delirium, profound disorientation, 48-96h).
Why antipsychotics (e.g. haloperidol) must not be used as monotherapy: they lower seizure threshold and worsen autonomic temperature dysregulation.
Criteria for ICU admission: failure of high-dose benzodiazepines (> 50-100 mg diazepam equivalent in 1 hour), severe hemodynamic instability, or status epilepticus.
case_hooks: A 52-year-old 3 days post-laparotomy who becomes wildly agitated, diaphoretic, pyrexic (38.8C), and sees insects crawling on the ICU ceiling.
A patient with delirium tremens who has received 120 mg of IV diazepam in 2 hours with persistent severe tachycardia (HR 145) and tremor.
page.gaps: Confirm ICU protocol availability for phenobarbital loading and continuous intravenous infusions with endotracheal intubation readiness.

guidelinesKept: Working Group Consensus on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis (ISHAM).

page.mentor_intro: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) is a hypersensitivity response to Aspergillus fumigatus colonization in patients with asthma or cystic fibrosis. Diagnostic criteria include total serum IgE > 1000 IU/mL, positive Aspergillus-specific IgE or skin test, eosinophilia, and central bronchiectasis on HRCT. Treatment combines systemic oral corticosteroids with antifungal therapy (itraconazole) or T2 biologics.

teaching_points.claim: ISHAM criteria require total serum IgE > 1000 IU/mL, elevated Aspergillus-specific IgE or positive skin prick test, along with peripheral eosinophilia or central bronchiectasis.
Oral itraconazole (200 mg twice daily with therapeutic drug monitoring) combined with oral corticosteroids increases response rates and reduces steroid exposure.
High-attenuation mucus (HAM) on high-resolution chest CT is pathognomonic for ABPA and signifies higher relapse rates.
Biologic therapies targeting IL-4/IL-13 (dupilumab), IL-5 (mepolizumab), or IgE (omalizumab) provide significant steroid-sparing efficacy in recurrent or steroid-dependent ABPA.

uncertainties: Optimal duration of antifungal therapy (4 months vs 12 months) in preventing long-term bronchiectasis progression.
Positioning of T2-targeted biologics as upfront monotherapy without prolonged high-dose oral corticosteroids.
mcq_angles: Recognizing elevated total IgE (> 1000 IU/mL) as the mandatory entry criterion for ABPA diagnosis.
Identifying high-attenuation mucus (mucus plugs denser than paraspinal muscle) on non-contrast chest CT.
Selecting therapeutic drug monitoring for oral itraconazole (target trough > 1.0-2.0 ug/mL) to ensure adequate gastrointestinal absorption.
case_hooks: A 36-year-old with severe asthma presenting with recurrent cough, expectoration of brown mucus plugs, total IgE 3,400 IU/mL, and eosinophils 1,200/uL.
An adult with cystic fibrosis showing fleeting bilateral infiltrates and worsening spirometry despite standard antibiotic therapy.
page.gaps: Verify availability of serum Aspergillus fumigatus-specific IgG/IgE assays and azole therapeutic drug monitoring.

page.mentor_intro: Allergic rhinitis is an IgE-mediated chronic inflammatory disease of the upper airway. Moderate-to-severe symptoms are managed first-line with intranasal corticosteroids (INCS) or combination INCS and intranasal antihistamines (e.g. fluticasone/azelastine). Allergen immunotherapy (SLIT or SCIT) is the only disease-modifying intervention for IgE-confirmed refractory disease.

teaching_points.claim: AAO-HNS guidelines recommend intranasal corticosteroids as first-line monotherapy for patients with clinically significant allergic rhinitis affecting quality of life.
Fixed-dose combination of intranasal corticosteroid and intranasal antihistamine (fluticasone propionate/azelastine) provides faster and superior symptom relief compared to either agent alone.
Oral first-generation sedating antihistamines (e.g. diphenhydramine, chlorpheniramine) should be avoided due to sedation, anticholinergic side effects, and cognitive impairment.
Allergen-specific immunotherapy (sublingual or subcutaneous) induces immune tolerance, reduces medication requirements, and prevents new allergen sensitizations.

uncertainties: Comparative long-term clinical efficacy and adherence of sublingual immunotherapy (SLIT) tablets versus subcutaneous injections (SCIT).
Role of biologics (e.g. dupilumab, omalizumab) in severe refractory allergic rhinitis with concurrent nasal polyposis.
mcq_angles: Selecting intranasal corticosteroids over oral antihistamines as the most effective monotherapy for nasal congestion.
Advising patients on proper INCS spray technique (direct nozzle away from nasal septum towards outer ear to avoid epistaxis/septal perforation).
Recognizing rhinitis medicamentosa resulting from rebound hyperemia after > 3-5 days of topical alpha-adrenergic decongestants (oxymetazoline).
case_hooks: A 24-year-old student with seasonal sneezing, severe nasal congestion, and conjunctival itching who complains that oral cetirizine is not clearing his congestion.
A 35-year-old presenting with continuous severe nasal blockage after using over-the-counter xylometazoline spray multiple times daily for 6 weeks.
page.gaps: Confirm referral criteria to allergy clinics for skin prick testing or specific IgE validation prior to immunotherapy initiation.

page.mentor_intro: Allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (allo-HCT) offers curative potential for high-risk acute leukemias, myelodysplastic syndromes, and marrow failure syndromes via the graft-versus-leukemia (GVL) effect. Post-transplant care focuses on conditioning toxicity, acute and chronic graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) prevention/treatment, and infectious surveillance (CMV, EBV, invasive molds).

teaching_points.claim: EBMT/ELN guidelines recommend allogeneic HCT in first complete remission for acute myeloid leukemia with intermediate- or adverse-risk cytogenetics and molecular features.
Post-transplant cyclophosphamide (PTCy) on days +3 and +4 significantly reduces severe acute and chronic GVHD, enabling successful haploidentical and mismatched unrelated donor transplants.
Pre-emptive antiviral therapy with letermovir prophylaxis reduces clinically significant cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection in CMV-seropositive HCT recipients without myelosuppression.

Chronic GVHD diagnosis requires diagnostic clinical signs (e.g. lichen planus-like skin changes, sclerotic skin, fasciitis) or distinctive signs confirmed by histology according to NIH consensus criteria.

uncertainties: Positioning targeted maintenance therapies (FLT3 inhibitors, IDH inhibitors, azacitidine) post-allo-HCT to prevent molecular relapse.
Comparative efficacy of ruxolitinib versus belumosudil as second-line treatment for steroid-refractory chronic GVHD.
mcq_angles: Recognizing acute GVHD clinical triad: maculopapular erythematous rash, secretory diarrhea with crampy pain, and cholestatic hyperbilirubinemia.
Mechanism of post-transplant cyclophosphamide: selectively eliminates rapidly proliferating alloreactive donor T cells while sparing non-alloreactive memory T cells and regulatory T cells.
Distinguishing sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (veno-occlusive disease: weight gain, painful hepatomegaly, jaundice within 3 weeks) from acute liver GVHD.
case_hooks: A 45-year-old on Day +28 post-matched unrelated donor transplant developing a confluent erythematous rash over 60% of body surface area and 1,200 mL watery diarrhea daily.
A post-allograft patient on cyclosporine who presents with rising CMV viral load (> 2,500 IU/mL) requiring pre-emptive valganciclovir therapy.
page.gaps: Reviewers should verify local institutional SOPs for HLA donor selection, conditioning intensity (MAC vs RIC), and chimerism monitoring.

page.mentor_intro: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (AATD) is an autosomal codominant genetic disorder characterized by low circulating levels of AAT (a serine protease inhibitor protecting lung elastin). Homozygosity for the Z allele (Pi*ZZ) predisposes to early-onset panacinar emphysema (predominating in lower lung zones) and liver cirrhosis from misfolded polymer accumulation in hepatocytes.

teaching_points.claim: ATS/ERS guidelines recommend screening for AATD in all patients with COPD, unexplained liver disease, or persistent adult-onset asthma with incompletely reversible airflow obstruction.
Serum AAT concentration < 11 umol/L (< 57 mg/dL) combined with protein phenotyping (isoelectric focusing) or SERPINA1 genotyping confirms severe deficiency.
Intravenous AAT augmentation therapy (60 mg/kg weekly) significantly slows the loss of lung density assessed by chest computed tomography densitometry in patients with FEV1 35-70% (RAPID trial).

Hepatic disease in AATD results from toxic gain-of-function due to intracellular retention of Z-AAT protein polymers (PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules) and is not corrected by IV augmentation.

uncertainties: Efficacy and cost-effectiveness of AAT augmentation therapy in non-smoking patients with mild airflow limitation (FEV1 > 70%).
Efficacy of emerging RNA interference (RNAi) therapies (e.g. fazirsiran) designed to silence hepatic Z-AAT mRNA and reverse fibrosis.
mcq_angles: Characteristic radiographic finding: panacinar emphysema with marked lower lobe predominance in a non-smoker under 45 years of age.
Liver biopsy hallmark: periodic acid-Schiff (PAS)-positive, diastase-resistant globules in periportal hepatocytes.
Primary indication for IV augmentation therapy: documented Pi*ZZ phenotype, serum AAT < 11 umol/L, non-smoker, and FEV1 35-70% predicted.
case_hooks: A 38-year-old lifetime non-smoker presenting with progressive exertional dyspnea, FEV1/FVC ratio 0.52, and bibasilar hyperlucency on chest radiography.
A 50-year-old with Pi*ZZ genotype presenting with elevated transaminases and hepatomegaly, inquiring if augmentation therapy will heal his liver.
page.gaps: Ensure national registry enrolment criteria and pre-authorization requirements for weekly IV augmentation are highlighted.

page.mentor_intro: Alport syndrome is an inherited progressive type IV collagen nephropathy caused by pathogenic variants in COL4A3, COL4A4, or COL4A5 genes. It presents with persistent microscopic hematuria in childhood, progressive proteinuria, hypertension, progressive renal failure, high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, and anterior lenticonus. Early ACE inhibitor therapy significantly delays progression to end-stage kidney disease.

teaching_points.claim: International consensus guidelines recommend early initiation of ACE inhibitors at the onset of persistent microalbuminuria (or at diagnosis in males with X-linked Alport syndrome) to delay end-stage kidney disease by decades.

X-linked inheritance due to COL4A5 mutations accounts for approximately 85% of cases; affected hemizygous males universally develop ESRD, whereas heterozygous females exhibit variable clinical phenotypes.
Renal biopsy electron microscopy demonstrates characteristic irregular thinning, thickening, and longitudinal splitting/lamellation ('basket-weave' appearance) of the glomerular basement membrane.
Post-transplant anti-GBM nephritis occurs in 3-5% of transplanted Alport patients due to alloimmunization against normal collagen alpha-3/4/5(IV) chains in the donor kidney.

uncertainties: Long-term efficacy of add-on SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin/empagliflozin) on top of maximally tolerated ACEi/ARB in Alport syndrome.
Genotype-phenotype correlations: predicting ESRD timing based on missense versus truncating/nonsense COL4A5 mutations.
mcq_angles: Characteristic clinical triad: persistent microscopic hematuria, bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, and ocular abnormalities (anterior lenticonus, macular flecks).
Pathognomonic electron microscopic finding: basket-weave lamellation and split lamina densa of the GBM.
Timing of ACE inhibitor initiation: do not wait for overt proteinuria; start at diagnosis in affected males or persistent microalbuminuria.
case_hooks: A 14-year-old boy evaluated for asymptomatic microscopic hematuria whose maternal uncle developed kidney failure and required hearing aids in his twenties.
A 26-year-old male with Alport syndrome on lisinopril whose 24-hour urine protein has risen to 1.8 g/day, seeking guidance on second-line antiproteinuric therapy.

page.mentor_intro: Inherited collagen IV nephropathies span a continuum from benign familial hematuria (thin basement membrane nephropathy) to severe X-linked or autosomal recessive Alport syndrome. Genetic testing for COL4A3, COL4A4, and COL4A5 distinguishes benign non-progressive heterozygous carriers from individuals at high risk for progressive proteinuria, glomerulosclerosis, and extra-renal sensorineural deafness.

teaching_points.claim: Thin basement membrane nephropathy (TBMN), commonly caused by heterozygous COL4A3 or COL4A4 mutations, presents with isolated microscopic hematuria and a benign long-term renal prognosis in the absence of proteinuria.
Next-generation sequencing multigene panels have replaced routine renal biopsy as the preferred first-line diagnostic investigation for suspected inherited collagen IV disorders.
Heterozygous females with X-linked Alport syndrome (COL4A5) have a lifelong risk of developing proteinuria (up to 75%) and ESRD (up to 15-30% by age 60), requiring lifelong annual monitoring.
SGLT2 inhibitors confer additive antiproteinuric and renoprotective effects when added to maximum tolerated renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system blockade.

uncertainties: Distinguishing pathogenic variants from variants of uncertain significance (VUS) in COL4A3/COL4A4 in adult-onset focal segmental glomerulosclerosis.
Role of dual endothelin-angiotensin receptor antagonists (spartansentan) in slowing progression in progressive collagen IV glomerulopathies.
mcq_angles: Differentiating thin basement membrane nephropathy (diffuse uniform thinning of GBM < 250 nm, normal hearing, normal renal function) from Alport syndrome.
Managing pregnant women who are heterozygous carriers of X-linked Alport syndrome: risk of pre-eclampsia and passing mutation to male offspring.
Genetic counseling: male-to-male transmission never occurs in X-linked inheritance (COL4A5), but 100% of daughters of affected males are obligate carriers.

A patient misdiagnosed with steroid-resistant focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) whose genetic panel identifies a pathogenic heterozygous COL4A3 mutation.

guidelinesKept: 2019 Update to the 2018 Guidelines for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke (AHA/ASA).

page.mentor_intro: Intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase (0.9 mg/kg, max 90 mg; 10% bolus over 1 min, remainder over 60 min) or tenecteplase (0.25 mg/kg, max 25 mg) is the standard of care for acute ischemic stroke within 4.5 hours of symptom onset. Pre-treatment non-contrast head CT must exclude intracranial hemorrhage, and blood pressure must be safely lowered < 185/110 mmHg. Concurrently, patients with large vessel occlusion should be evaluated for endovascular thrombectomy.

teaching_points.claim: The landmark NINDS rt-PA Stroke Study demonstrated that patients treated with intravenous alteplase within 3 hours had a 30% higher likelihood of minimal or no disability at 3 months (mRS 0-1) despite a 6.4% symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage rate.

ECASS III trial demonstrated efficacy of alteplase extended to 4.5 hours from symptom onset in eligible patients without severe stroke (NIHSS > 25), age > 80 with previous stroke/diabetes, or oral anticoagulant use.
AHA/ASA guidelines require blood pressure to be maintained < 180/105 mmHg during and for 24 hours following intravenous thrombolysis to minimize hemorrhagic transformation.

In patients with acute large vessel occlusion (ICA or M1 segment MCA), mechanical thrombectomy is standard within 6 hours (and up to 24 hours selected by perfusion imaging via DAWN and DEFUSE-3 criteria), regardless of whether IV thrombolysis is given.

uncertainties: Non-inferiority and practical workflow benefits of tenecteplase over alteplase in routine real-world acute ischemic stroke protocols.
Safety of thrombolysis in patients on direct oral anticoagulants whose last dose was taken between 24 and 48 hours prior to onset.
mcq_angles: Blood pressure exclusion threshold for IV thrombolysis: SBP > 185 mmHg or DBP > 110 mmHg refractory to IV labetalol/nicardipine.
Managing acute orolingual angioedema (seen in 1-5% of patients, especially those on ACE inhibitors): stop infusion, give IV methylprednisolone, diphenhydramine, and prepare for emergent intubation.
Post-thrombolysis antiplatelet/anticoagulant timing: strictly avoid aspirin or heparin for 24 hours until follow-up CT/MRI excludes hemorrhage.
case_hooks: A 68-year-old presenting with acute right hemiparesis and aphasia (NIHSS 16) arriving at ED 75 minutes after witnessed onset, BP 178/96 mmHg.
A stroke patient 40 minutes into an alteplase infusion who develops sudden severe headache, vomiting, acute hypertension (BP 210/120), and declining GCS.
page.gaps: Verify institutional 'code stroke' door-to-needle benchmark (< 45 minutes) and rapid transfer protocols for endovascular thrombectomy.

topic: alzheimer s disease anti amyloid immunotherapy

guidelinesKept: Appropriate Use Criteria for Lecanemab in Early Alzheimer's Disease.

page.mentor_intro: Early Alzheimer's disease with confirmed amyloid-beta pathology is eligible for anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies (lecanemab, donanemab). These agents target protofibrillar or plaque amyloid-beta to slow cognitive decline, but mandate APOE genotyping and serial safety MRI monitoring for ARIA.

teaching_points.claim: Lecanemab slowed 18-month cognitive and functional decline (CDR-SB) by 27% compared to placebo in the CLARITY AD trial.
Appropriate Use Criteria mandate pre-treatment confirmation of amyloid pathology via CSF biomarkers or amyloid PET imaging.
Amyloid-related imaging abnormalities with edema (ARIA-E) occur in 12.6% of patients on lecanemab and 24% on donanemab, with highest risk in APOE e4 homozygotes.
Routine surveillance brain MRIs are required before infusions 5, 7, and 14 to detect asymptomatic ARIA-E and ARIA-H.

guidelinesKept: Indications for allogeneic stem cell transplantation: EBMT guidelines.

page.mentor_intro: Congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia (CAMT) is a severe marrow failure disorder characterized by isolated severe thrombocytopenia and absent megakaryocytes on bone marrow biopsy. CAMT is caused by biallelic loss-of-function MPL mutations (TPO receptor), typically progressing to aplastic anemia or leukemia; allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation is the definitive curative treatment.

teaching_points.claim: Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the MPL gene encoding the thrombopoietin receptor cause CAMT, leading to early marrow aplasia.
Bone marrow examination demonstrates selective absent or severely hypoplastic megakaryocytes with preserved erythroid and myeloid lineages in early stages.
Allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation performed prior to trilineage marrow failure or leukemic transformation achieves > 80% long-term cure.
In acquired amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia (AAT), immunosuppressive therapy with cyclosporine, ATG, or rituximab achieves remissions in autoantibody-mediated cases.

uncertainties: Optimal conditioning regimen intensity for CAMT.

mcq_angles: Distinguishing CAMT (absent radius syndrome / TAR has preserved megakaryocytes and absent radii; CAMT has normal radii).
Role of allogeneic stem cell transplantation as sole curative modality.
Initial bone marrow findings in CAMT vs immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP: abundant megakaryocytes).

page.mentor_intro: Acute myeloid leukemia transformed from myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN-blast phase / secondary AML) carries an aggressive clinical course and dismal prognosis. It is characterized by high rates of complex karyotype, TP53 mutations, and resistance to standard 7+3 chemotherapy. Management incorporates hypomethylating agents plus venetoclax or ruxolitinib as a bridge to allogeneic stem cell transplantation.

teaching_points.claim: Transformation to AML (blast phase, >= 20% blasts) occurs in 10-15% of myelofibrosis and 3-5% of polycythemia vera / essential thrombocythemia.
Standard cytarabine/anthracycline (7+3) induction yields low complete remission rates (< 20-30%) and high induction mortality in post-MPN AML.
Combination therapy with azacitidine and venetoclax produces composite remission in 40-50% of secondary AML, serving as an effective bridge to transplant.
Allogeneic stem cell transplantation is the only curative therapeutic option for patients with MPN in blast phase who achieve morphological remission.

topic: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS): El Escorial criteria, riluzole, non-invasive ventilation

guidelinesKept: EFNS/EAN Guidelines on the Clinical Management of ALS.

page.mentor_intro: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a neurodegenerative disorder causing progressive loss of upper and lower motor neurons. Diagnosis utilizes Revised El Escorial and Gold Coast criteria. Disease-modifying therapy includes riluzole (glutamate antagonist) and edaravone. Non-invasive ventilation (NIV) improves survival and quality of life when respiratory muscle weakness develops.

teaching_points.claim: Revised El Escorial and Gold Coast criteria establish diagnosis based on upper and lower motor neuron signs across progressive body regions.
Riluzole (50 mg orally twice daily) extends median survival by 2 to 3 months and reduces tracheostomy risk (Cochrane review).
Non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP) is the single most effective intervention for extending survival (median 7-12 months benefit) when FVC drops < 50% or SNIP < 40 cmH2O.
Percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) or radiologically inserted gastrostomy (RIG) should be placed before FVC falls below 50% to minimize procedural respiratory failure.

sources.title: EFNS/EAN Guidelines on the Clinical Management of ALS.

uncertainties: Effectiveness of early pre-symptomatic NIV in patients with preserved daytime FVC but nocturnal hypoventilation.
Targeted genetic therapies (tofersen) in SOD1-mutated familial ALS.
mcq_angles: Distinguishing ALS from cervical spondylotic myelopathy: tongue fasciculations and normal sensory exam confirm ALS.
Laboratory monitoring for riluzole: baseline and monthly hepatic transaminases for the first 3 months.
Screening for frontotemporal dementia (FTD) which co-occurs in 15% of ALS patients.

An ALS patient reporting morning headaches, fragmented sleep, and orthopnea whose sitting FVC is 46%.

guidelinesKept: British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines for the management of iron deficiency anaemia in adults.

page.mentor_intro: Anaemia evaluation begins with complete blood count, reticulocyte count, and peripheral smear to categorize microcytic (MCV < 80 fL), normocytic (80-100 fL), or macrocytic (> 100 fL) etiologies. In adults, iron deficiency requires systematic investigation of the gastrointestinal tract (coeliac serology, bidirectional endoscopy) to identify bleeding malignancies.

teaching_points.claim: British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines mandate bidirectional endoscopy (gastroscopy and colonoscopy) for unexplained iron deficiency anemia in men and postmenopausal women.
Serum ferritin < 30 ug/L is the most specific biochemical marker of absolute iron deficiency; ferritin < 100 ug/L indicates deficiency in the setting of chronic inflammation.
Oral iron supplementation given once daily or on alternate days achieves equivalent or superior fractional iron absorption compared to multiple daily doses due to hepcidin surges.
Intravenous iron (ferric carboxymaltose, ferric derisomaltose) is superior to oral iron in active inflammatory bowel disease, heart failure (FERRIC-HF), and chronic kidney disease.

page.mentor_intro: Anaemia of chronic disease (ACD / anaemia of inflammation) is a cytokine-driven normocytic or mildly microcytic anaemia. Interleukin-6 stimulates hepatic production of hepcidin, which degrades ferroportin, trapping iron in reticuloendothelial macrophages and enterocytes. Laboratory hallmark is low serum iron, low TIBC/transferrin, normal to elevated ferritin (> 100 ng/mL), and elevated hepcidin.

teaching_points.claim: Hepcidin-mediated internalization and degradation of ferroportin-1 prevents intestinal iron absorption and macrophage iron release, causing hypoferremia.
Differentiating pure ACD from combined ACD + iron deficiency: TSAT < 20% with ferritin 30-100 ug/L indicates concurrent true iron deficiency responsive to IV iron.
Treating the underlying inflammatory, infectious, or rheumatologic condition remains the primary and most effective therapy for ACD.
Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs) or hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors (HIF-PHIs) restore hemoglobin in chronic kidney disease ACD but require repletion of iron stores.

guidelinesKept: ESMO Clinical Practice Guideline for Anal Cancer.

page.mentor_intro: Squamous cell carcinoma of the anal canal is strongly associated with high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV types 16 and 18). Curative standard of care for localized disease (T1-T4, N0-N3) is definitive concurrent chemoradiotherapy (Nigro protocol: 5-fluorouracil or capecitabine + mitomycin C with external beam radiotherapy), preserving anal sphincter function in > 75% of patients.

teaching_points.claim: Definitive concurrent chemoradiation with 5-FU and mitomycin C provides 80% 5-year colostomy-free survival in localized anal squamous cell carcinoma.
ESMO and NCCN guidelines recommend IMRT (intensity-modulated radiation therapy) to minimize radiation dermatitis, proctitis, and pelvic bone marrow toxicity.
Abdominoperineal resection (APR) with permanent end colostomy is reserved strictly for persistent disease at 26 weeks post-CRT or biopsy-proven locoregional recurrence.

First-line systemic therapy for metastatic or unresectable recurrent anal carcinoma is carboplatin plus paclitaxel, with immune checkpoint inhibitors (retifanlimab, pembrolizumab) for refractory disease.

The Nigro regimen components: 5-FU (or capecitabine) plus mitomycin C combined with radiotherapy.
Post-treatment surveillance: digital rectal exam, anoscopy, and inguinal lymph node palpation every 3-6 months for 5 years.

guidelinesKept: Practice Guidelines for Acute Postoperative Pain Management: American Society of Anesthesiologists.

page.mentor_intro: Multimodal analgesia targets multiple pain pathways simultaneously using paracetamol, NSAIDs or selective COX-2 inhibitors, regional/neuraxial blocks, and non-opioid adjuvants (gabapentinoids, IV lidocaine, ketamine). This synergistic approach achieves superior dynamic pain control while minimizing opioid consumption and opioid-related adverse events.

teaching_points.claim: ASA and PROSPECT practice guidelines recommend scheduled multimodal non-opioid analgesia as the baseline for all postoperative pain management.
Combining paracetamol (1g IV/oral q6h) with an NSAID (e.g. ibuprofen or celecoxib) provides greater pain relief than either agent alone without added toxicity.
Perioperative intravenous lidocaine infusions in major abdominal surgery accelerate return of bowel function, reduce pain scores, and shorten hospital stay.
Low-dose ketamine (NMDA receptor antagonist) reduces postoperative opioid consumption and prevents opioid-induced hyperalgesia in opioid-tolerant surgical patients.

uncertainties: Risk-benefit balance of preoperative gabapentinoid loading regarding excessive sedation and respiratory depression.
Cardiovascular and renal safety of short-course (48-72h) perioperative COX-2 inhibitors.
mcq_angles: Mechanism of ketamine in chronic pain: non-competitive NMDA receptor blockade preventing central sensitization.
Opioid-sparing multimodal protocol components: scheduled paracetamol + NSAID + local infiltration + PRN weak opioid.
Contraindications to intravenous lidocaine: severe heart block, ventricular arrhythmias, and severe hepatic impairment.

guidelinesKept: World Allergy Organization Anaphylaxis Guidelines 2020 Update.

page.mentor_intro: Anaphylaxis is an acute, life-threatening systemic hypersensitivity reaction with rapid onset involving airway, breathing, circulation, or skin/mucosa. Intramuscular epinephrine (adrenaline) 1:1,000 (0.01 mg/kg, max 0.5 mg in adults; 0.3 mg auto-injector) into the mid-anterolateral thigh is the immediate, mandatory first-line therapy. Second-line antihistamines and steroids must never delay epinephrine.

teaching_points.claim: World Allergy Organization (WAO) guidelines mandate immediate intramuscular epinephrine (0.01 mg/kg, max 0.5 mg) in the mid-anterolateral thigh as the primary life-saving drug.
Antihistamines (H1/H2 blockers) and corticosteroids relieve cutaneous symptoms but do not treat airway obstruction, bronchospasm, or vascular collapse and must not delay epinephrine.
Biphasic anaphylactic reactions occur in 5-10% of cases, typically within 8 hours, warranting hospital observation for at least 4-8 hours post-resolution.
Serial serum total tryptase levels measured at 1-2 hours and > 24 hours post-event confirm mast cell degranulation (acute peak > 1.2 x baseline + 2 ug/L).

Refractory anaphylaxis in a patient on propranolol: administer IV glucagon (1-5 mg over 5 min) which bypasses beta-receptors via adenylate cyclase stimulation.
Discharge requirements: prescription of two epinephrine auto-injectors, personalized allergy action plan, and allergy clinic referral.

topic: Anaplastic thyroid cancer: rapid progression, multimodal treatment, dabrafenib

guidelinesKept: 2021 American Thyroid Association Guidelines for Management of Patients with Anaplastic Thyroid Cancer.

page.mentor_intro: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma (ATC) is an ultra-aggressive solid malignancy presenting with a rapidly enlarging anterior neck mass, dysphagia, stridor, and vocal cord paralysis. Immediate airway assessment, contrast-enhanced CT neck/chest, core biopsy, and rapid molecular testing for BRAF V600E are required within 48-72 hours. For BRAF-mutated ATC, dabrafenib plus trametinib induces dramatic rapid tumor regression.

teaching_points.claim: American Thyroid Association (ATA) guidelines mandate urgent multidisciplinary evaluation, vocal cord assessment, and reflex BRAF V600E testing within 2-3 days of suspected ATC.
Combined targeted therapy with dabrafenib (BRAF inhibitor) and trametinib (MEK inhibitor) achieves an 69% objective response rate in BRAF V600E-mutated ATC (ROAR trial).
In resectable disease without distant metastases, radical surgical resection with clear margins followed by adjuvant intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) improves locoregional control.
For BRAF wild-type ATC, cytotoxic chemotherapy (paclitaxel plus carboplatin) combined with radiation therapy or checkpoint inhibitors is standard.

uncertainties: Neoadjuvant dabrafenib/trametinib to convert initially unresectable BRAF-mutant ATC to complete surgical resection.
Role of frontline PD-1 inhibitors (pembrolizumab) added to chemoradiation in BRAF wild-type disease.
mcq_angles: Clinical presentation of ATC: elderly patient with rapidly growing rock-hard neck mass over weeks with hoarseness and dyspnea.
Molecular profiling urgency: BRAF V600E mutation occurs in 40-50% of ATC and dictates immediate targeted therapy.
Airway management priorities: avoid tracheostomy if possible unless acute imminent asphyxia, as it leads to tumor fungation and stoma bleeding.

topic: ANCA-associated vasculitis: GPA, MPA, EGPA: classification, renal involvement, ANCA serology

guidelinesKept: EULAR recommendations for the management of ANCA-associated vasculitis: 2022 update.

page.mentor_intro: ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV) encompasses Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA; PR3-ANCA), Microscopic Polyangiitis (MPA; MPO-ANCA), and Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (EGPA). Remission induction for organ- or life-threatening disease combines high-dose glucocorticoids with rituximab or cyclophosphamide. Avacopan (C5a receptor antagonist) enables significant glucocorticoid-sparing induction.

teaching_points.claim: EULAR 2022 recommendations establish rituximab (375 mg/m2 weekly x 4 or 1000 mg x 2) as equivalent to cyclophosphamide for induction and superior for relapsing disease.
Avacopan (30 mg twice daily), an oral complement C5a receptor antagonist, produces sustained remission at 52 weeks while significantly reducing glucocorticoid-related toxicity (ADVOCATE trial).

PEXIVAS trial demonstrated that routine plasma exchange does not reduce end-stage kidney disease or all-cause mortality, and a reduced-dose glucocorticoid regimen is non-inferior with fewer severe infections.
Maintenance of remission is best achieved with scheduled low-dose rituximab (500 mg every 6 months for at least 24-48 months) compared to azathioprine (MAINRITSAN trial).

guidelinesKept: 2023 Guideline for the Management of Patients With Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (AHA/ASA).
Critical care management of patients following aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage: Neurocritical Care Society.

page.mentor_intro: Aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH) is an acute neurosurgical emergency presenting with sudden thunderclap headache. Initial evaluation requires emergent non-contrast head CT within 6 hours (sensitivity > 99%); lumbar puncture for CSF xanthochromia is mandatory if CT is negative. Management prioritizes immediate aneurysm securing (endovascular coiling preferred), oral nimodipine for 21 days, and euvolemia to prevent delayed cerebral ischemia.

teaching_points.claim: AHA/ASA guidelines recommend immediate endovascular coiling over surgical clipping for ruptured aneurysms amenable to both modalities (ISAT trial).
Oral nimodipine (60 mg every 4 hours for 21 days) significantly reduces delayed cerebral ischemia and poor neurological outcome.
Blood pressure should be controlled with titratable IV infusions (labetalol, nicardipine) targeting SBP < 140-160 mmHg prior to aneurysm securing.
Maintenance of euvolemia is recommended; hypervolemic 'triple-H' therapy is no longer recommended due to cardiopulmonary complications.

mcq_angles: Non-contrast head CT sensitivity within 6 hours vs requirement for lumbar puncture looking for spectrophotometric xanthochromia at 12 hours.
Pharmacologic prevention of delayed cerebral ischemia: oral nimodipine is the only drug with proven neurological outcome benefit.

guidelinesKept: The international WAO/EAACI guideline for the management of hereditary angioedema - the 2021 revision.

page.mentor_intro: Angioedema is asymmetric swelling of the deep dermis and subcutaneous or submucosal tissues. It is critical to differentiate histamine-mediated angioedema (associated with urticaria/pruritus, responds to epinephrine, antihistamines, and steroids) from bradykinin-mediated angioedema (ACE-inhibitor induced or hereditary angioedema [HAE]). Bradykinin-mediated angioedema lacks urticaria and does NOT respond to antihistamines or steroids.

teaching_points.claim: WAO/EAACI guidelines recommend icatibant (bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist) or plasma-derived C1-inhibitor concentrate for acute attacks of hereditary angioedema.
ACE inhibitor-induced angioedema is caused by impaired bradykinin degradation; ACE inhibitors must be permanently discontinued, and ARBs should be avoided in acute severe airway presentation.
Hereditary angioedema (HAE) Type 1 (85%) has low C4 and low antigenic/functional C1-INH; Type 2 (15%) has low C4, normal antigenic but low functional C1-INH.
Emergent airway protection (fiberoptic intubation or cricothyroidotomy) takes precedence over pharmacotherapy in progressive laryngeal edema.

mcq_angles: Screening test of choice for HAE: serum C4 level (consistently low even during remission; sensitivity > 95%).
Why steroids and epinephrine fail in bradykinin angioedema: pathology is vascular permeability driven by bradykinin B2 receptors.

topic: angiotensin ii for catecholamine refractory vasodilatory shock

guidelinesKept: Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2021.

page.mentor_intro: Catecholamine-refractory vasodilatory shock is characterized by persistent severe hypotension and inadequate organ perfusion despite high-dose norepinephrine and vasopressin. Synthetic human angiotensin II acts through the AT1 receptor, providing a non-adrenergic vasoconstrictor mechanism. Management includes early hydrocortisone, vasopressin (0.03 units/min), and angiotensin II in refractory shock.

teaching_points.claim: ATHOS-3 randomized trial demonstrated that synthetic human angiotensin II significantly increased mean arterial pressure and reduced background catecholamine requirements in vasodilatory shock.
Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines recommend adding vasopressin (0.03 U/min) rather than escalating norepinephrine to high levels (> 0.25 mcg/kg/min).
Patients with high baseline serum renin concentrations or acute kidney injury receiving renal replacement therapy experience the greatest survival benefit from angiotensin II.
Thromboembolic events occur more frequently with angiotensin II, warranting mandatory concurrent pharmacological venous thromboembolism prophylaxis.

sources.title: Angiotensin II for the Treatment of Vasodilatory Shock (ATHOS-3 Trial).
Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2021.
Angiotensin II in septic shock: current evidence and practical clinical use.

uncertainties: Optimal physiological biomarkers for selecting patients who derive mortality benefit from angiotensin II.
Sequencing of non-adrenergic vasopressors: vasopressin versus angiotensin II versus methylene blue.
mcq_angles: The adrenergic sparing effect: adding vasopressin or angiotensin II prevents excessive beta-1 tachycardia and myocardial ischemia from extreme norepinephrine doses.
Surviving Sepsis Campaign recommendation on corticosteroids: IV hydrocortisone 200 mg/day indicated only if shock persists despite norepinephrine >= 0.25 mcg/kg/min and vasopressin.
Mechanism of action of angiotensin II: direct stimulation of vascular smooth muscle AT1 Gq-protein receptors causing calcium influx and vasoconstriction.
case_hooks: A 55-year-old with septic shock requiring norepinephrine 0.5 mcg/kg/min, vasopressin 0.03 U/min, and epinephrine whose lactate is 6.2 mmol/L.
An ICU patient with septic shock and dialysis-dependent AKI initiated on angiotensin II infusion.

guidelinesKept: 2022 EULAR recommendations for the management of axial spondyloarthritis.
2019 ACR/SAA/SPARTAN Guideline for the Treatment of Axial Spondyloarthritis.

page.mentor_intro: Ankylosing spondylitis (radiographic axial spondyloarthritis) is a chronic inflammatory arthritis predominantly affecting the axial skeleton and sacroiliac joints. It presents with inflammatory back pain (morning stiffness > 30 minutes, improvement with exercise, pain at night) in individuals < 45 years. First-line therapy is continuous full-dose NSAIDs; active disease refractory to NSAIDs is treated with TNF inhibitors or IL-17A inhibitors.

teaching_points.claim: ASAS/EULAR 2022 recommendations recommend continuous NSAIDs at maximum tolerated doses as first-line medical therapy for active axial spondyloarthritis.
TNF inhibitors (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab, golimumab, certolizumab) or IL-17A inhibitors (secukinumab, ixekizumab) achieve significant disease reduction (ASAS40) in active AS.
Conventional synthetic DMARDs (methotrexate, sulfasalazine) are ineffective for pure axial spinal disease, although sulfasalazine is useful for prominent peripheral arthritis.
JAK inhibitors (upadacitinib, tofacitinib) are approved oral options for active radiographic and non-radiographic axSpA refractory to bDMARDs.

sources.title: 2022 EULAR recommendations for the management of axial spondyloarthritis.
2019 ACR/SAA/SPARTAN Guideline for the Treatment of Axial Spondyloarthritis.

uncertainties: Comparative effectiveness of IL-17A inhibitors vs TNF inhibitors on radiographic syndesmophyte progression.
Role of MRI sacroiliitis monitoring in patients who achieve clinical remission.
mcq_angles: Features of inflammatory vs mechanical back pain: age < 45, insidious onset, improvement with exercise, no improvement with rest, pain at night.
Extra-skeletal manifestations of AS: acute anterior uveitis (most common, 30%), psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, and aortic regurgitation / conduction blocks.
Radiographic hallmark: bilateral sacroiliitis, squaring of vertebral bodies, syndesmophytes ('bamboo spine').

guidelinesKept: The American Society of Colon and Rectal Surgeons Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Management of Hemorrhoids.

page.mentor_intro: Common benign anorectal disorders include hemorrhoidal disease, anal fissures, anorectal abscesses, and fistula-in-ano. Thrombosed external hemorrhoids present with acute severe pain and a bluish perianal lump (excised within 72h). Acute anal fissures present with tearing pain during defecation and bright red rectal bleeding (treated with topical nitroglycerin or diltiazem). Anorectal abscesses require prompt incision and drainage.

teaching_points.claim: ASCRS guidelines recommend dietary fiber supplementation (25-35g daily) and water intake as the cornerstone of conservative therapy for hemorrhoids.
Rubber band ligation is the most effective outpatient procedure for Grade I to III internal hemorrhoids that fail medical management.
Topical calcium channel blockers (2% diltiazem) or topical nitrates (0.4% nitroglycerin) are first-line for chronic anal fissure, healing 65-75% without fecal incontinence risk.
Anorectal abscesses require prompt surgical incision and drainage; routine antibiotics do not prevent fistula formation unless systemic sepsis or immunosuppression is present.
