page.mentor_intro: Anterior mediastinal masses encompass the classic '4 Ts': Thymoma/thymic carcinoma, Teratoma (germ cell tumors), Thyroid (substernal goiter), and Terrible lymphoma. Diagnostic workup mandates contrast-enhanced CT thorax, serum tumor markers (alpha-fetoprotein [AFP], beta-hCG, and LDH), assessment for myasthenia gravis (anti-AChR antibodies), and multidisciplinary planning prior to biopsy.

teaching_points.claim: Serum tumor markers (AFP and beta-hCG) must be drawn before any biopsy or invasive procedure to evaluate for non-seminomatous germ cell tumors.
Preoperative screening for anti-acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibodies is mandatory in suspected thymoma to prevent post-intubation myasthenic crisis.
Primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma (PMLBCL) and classic Hodgkin lymphoma present with rapid bulky anterior masses in young adults, treated with DA-EPOCH-R or ABVD.
Complete surgical resection (thymectomy) is the mainstay of treatment for non-invasive and locally advanced resectable thymomas (Masaoka-Koga stage I-II).

guidelinesKept: 2022 ESC Guidelines on cardio-oncology.

page.mentor_intro: Anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity (doxorubicin, epirubicin) causes cumulative dose-dependent myocardial injury through topoisomerase II-beta inhibition, reactive oxygen species generation, and irreversible cardiomyocyte apoptosis. Surveillance relies on baseline and serial echocardiography with global longitudinal strain (GLS). Cardioprotection with dexrazoxane or neurohormonal blockade (ACEi/beta-blockers) is indicated in high-risk patients.

teaching_points.claim: ESC 2022 Cardio-Oncology guidelines define cancer therapy-related cardiac dysfunction (CTRCD) by a decrease in LVEF >= 10 percentage points to < 50%, or a relative reduction in global longitudinal strain (GLS) > 15%.
Cumulative lifetime doxorubicin dose is the strongest risk factor: heart failure incidence rises sharply above 400-500 mg/m2.
Dexrazoxane (iron-chelating topoisomerase II-beta inhibitor) significantly reduces anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity without compromising oncological efficacy in high-risk patients.
Guideline-directed neurohormonal blockade (carvedilol, enalapril) initiated for early subclinical strain deterioration or asymptomatic LVEF drop prevents progression to clinical heart failure.

Anthracycline lifetime maximum cumulative dose thresholds: doxorubicin (450-500 mg/m2), epirubicin (900 mg/m2).

topic: Antibiotic prophylaxis for infective endocarditis: high-risk procedures and patients

guidelinesKept: 2023 ESC Guidelines for the management of endocarditis.
Prevention of Viridans Group Streptococcal Infective Endocarditis: An Update to the AHA Scientific Statement.

page.mentor_intro: Antibiotic prophylaxis for infective endocarditis (IE) is restricted to patients at the highest risk of adverse outcomes undergoing high-risk dental procedures involving manipulation of the gingival tissue, periapical region of teeth, or perforation of oral mucosa. High-risk conditions include prosthetic heart valves, prosthetic valve repair materials, prior IE, and cyanotic congenital heart disease. The standard prophylactic regimen is a single oral dose of amoxicillin 2g 30-60 minutes pre-procedure.

teaching_points.claim: ESC 2023 guidelines restrict antibiotic prophylaxis strictly to high-risk cardiac conditions undergoing dental procedures involving gingival or periapical manipulation.
High-risk cardiac categories: prosthetic valves (transcatheter or surgical), prosthetic rings/cords, previous IE, and unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease.
Standard regimen: oral amoxicillin 2g (or ampicillin 2g IV) administered 30-60 minutes before the procedure; for severe penicillin allergy, cephalexin 2g, azithromycin 500mg, or doxycycline 100mg.
Prophylaxis is NOT recommended for gastrointestinal, urological, respiratory, or routine skin procedures in the absence of established local infection.

uncertainties: Role of clindamycin in penicillin-allergic patients (AHA no longer recommends clindamycin due to fatal Clostridioides difficile risk).

mcq_angles: Identifying high-risk cardiac conditions qualifying for prophylaxis: prosthetic valve, prior endocarditis, unrepaired cyanotic CHD (native valve disease like mitral valve prolapse does NOT qualify).
Procedures requiring prophylaxis: tooth extraction, periodontal scaling, dental implant placement; NOT routine local anesthetic injections, dental radiographs, or suture removal.
First-line oral drug and timing: amoxicillin 2g single dose taken 30-60 minutes before the procedure.

guidelinesKept: Implementing an Antibiotic Stewardship Program: Guidelines by IDSA and SHEA.

page.mentor_intro: Antimicrobial stewardship programs (ASPs) optimize clinical outcomes while minimizing unintended consequences of antimicrobial use, including toxicity, selection of pathogenic organisms (such as Clostridioides difficile), and the emergence of antimicrobial resistance. Core strategies include pre-authorization, prospective audit with feedback, evidence-based guidelines, and diagnostic stewardship.

teaching_points.claim: CDC and IDSA guidelines emphasize prospective audit and feedback as the most effective stewardship intervention to optimize antibiotic prescribing.
Implementing hospital-based ASPs significantly reduces overall antibiotic consumption, hospital-onset Clostridioides difficile infection, and institutional resistance rates.
Diagnostic stewardship ensures appropriate collection of microbiological cultures before antimicrobial initiation, preventing contaminated or unindicated blood and urine cultures.
Facility-specific antibiograms updated annually guide empirical therapy based on local pathogen susceptibility patterns rather than national estimates.

guidelinesKept: ESMO Clinical Practice Guideline on Antibody-Drug Conjugates in Solid Tumors.

page.mentor_intro: Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) deliver potent cytotoxic payloads directly to tumor cells expressing specific surface antigens using a targeted monoclonal antibody, cleavable or non-cleavable linker, and chemotherapeutic payload (e.g. topoisomerase I inhibitors, auristatins, calicheamicins). Landmark examples include trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) in HER2+ and HER2-low cancers, and enfortumab vedotin in urothelial cancer.

teaching_points.claim: Trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) demonstrated significant progression-free and overall survival improvements over standard therapy in HER2-low metastatic breast cancer (DESTINY-Breast04).
Enfortumab vedotin (targeting Nectin-4) combined with pembrolizumab established a new first-line standard of care in advanced urothelial carcinoma (EV-302 trial).

Drug-induced interstitial lung disease (ILD) / pneumonitis is a class-defining toxicity of topoisomerase I payload ADCs (T-DXd, sacituzumab govitecan), requiring routine CT surveillance and prompt steroid treatment.
The 'bystander killing effect' occurs when membrane-permeable cleaved cytotoxic payloads diffuse into adjacent antigen-negative tumor cells, overcoming intratumoral target heterogeneity.

page.mentor_intro: Rituximab is a chimeric monoclonal antibody targeting CD20 on pre-B and mature B lymphocytes, mediating complement-dependent cytotoxicity and antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity. In rheumatology and nephrology, rituximab is standard of care for rheumatoid arthritis refractory to anti-TNF agents, ANCA-associated vasculitis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and primary membranous nephropathy.

teaching_points.claim: ACR guidelines recommend rituximab in rheumatoid arthritis patients with inadequate response to TNF inhibitors, particularly in seropositive (RF/anti-CCP positive) disease.
Rituximab is standard first-line remission induction therapy for primary membranous nephropathy, demonstrating superior long-term remission rates compared to cyclosporine (MENTOR trial).
Universal screening for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and anti-HBc total antibodies is mandatory prior to rituximab due to high risk of fatal hepatitis B reactivation.
Serum quantitative immunoglobulins (IgG/IgM) should be monitored at baseline and prior to each retreat course to detect persistent secondary hypogammaglobulinemia.

topic: anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation in chronic kidney disease

guidelinesKept: KDIGO 2023 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Cardiovascular Disease in Chronic Kidney Disease.
2024 ESC Guidelines for the management of atrial fibrillation.

page.mentor_intro: Atrial fibrillation is highly prevalent in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), significantly increasing stroke and bleeding risks. Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs: apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran) provide superior or non-inferior stroke prevention compared to warfarin in mild-to-moderate CKD (CrCl 30-50 mL/min). In severe CKD (CrCl 15-29 mL/min) and dialysis, apixaban is increasingly utilized with specific dose reduction criteria.

teaching_points.claim: KDIGO 2023 guidelines recommend DOACs over vitamin K antagonists (warfarin) in patients with non-valvular AF and CKD Stages 1-3, and consider DOACs in Stage 4 (CrCl 15-29 mL/min).
Apixaban requires dose reduction to 2.5 mg BID if the patient meets at least two of the following criteria: age >= 80 years, body weight <= 60 kg, or serum creatinine >= 1.5 mg/dL (133 umol/L).
Warfarin in advanced CKD and dialysis accelerates vascular calcification and calcific uremic arteriolopathy (calciphylaxis) by inhibiting vitamin K-dependent matrix Gla protein.
Dabigatran is 80% renally eliminated and is contraindicated when CrCl < 30 mL/min in European guidelines.

guidelinesKept: 2021 ESC/EACTS Guidelines for the management of valvular heart disease.

page.mentor_intro: Mechanical prosthetic heart valves mandate lifelong oral anticoagulation with vitamin K antagonists (warfarin) to prevent catastrophic valve thrombosis and thromboembolic stroke. Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are strictly contraindicated based on the RE-ALIGN trial, which demonstrated significantly higher thromboembolic and bleeding events with dabigatran.

teaching_points.claim: AHA/ACC and ESC guidelines establish vitamin K antagonists (warfarin) as the only approved anticoagulation for mechanical heart valves; DOACs are absolutely contraindicated.
The RE-ALIGN trial testing dabigatran in mechanical heart valves was halted early due to an excess of ischemic strokes, valve thrombosis, and major bleeding.
Target INR for mechanical aortic valves without thromboembolic risk factors is 2.5 (range 2.0-3.0); target INR for mechanical mitral valves or aortic valves with risk factors is 3.0 (range 2.5-3.5).
Low-dose aspirin (75-100 mg daily) is recommended in addition to warfarin only if there is a concomitant clinical indication (e.g. established atherosclerotic disease).

topic: Anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation: CHA2DS2-VASc scoring and DOAC selection

guidelinesKept: 2024 ESC Guidelines for the management of atrial fibrillation.

page.mentor_intro: Stroke prevention in non-valvular atrial fibrillation is guided by the CHA2DS2-VASc risk score. Oral anticoagulation is recommended for men with score >= 2 and women with score >= 3, and should be considered for men with score 1 and women with score 2. Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs: apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran, edoxaban) are preferred over warfarin due to a 50% reduction in intracranial hemorrhage.

teaching_points.claim: ESC 2024 guidelines recommend DOACs over warfarin as first-line stroke prevention for non-valvular atrial fibrillation (Class I, Level A).
CHA2DS2-VASc score assigns points: CHF (1), HTN (1), Age >= 75 (2), Diabetes (1), Stroke/TIA/thromboembolism (2), Vascular disease (1), Age 65-74 (1), Sex female (1).
Female sex is a risk modifier rather than an independent risk factor; a female with no other risk factors (CHA2DS2-VASc = 1) does NOT require anticoagulation.
Meta-analysis of landmark DOAC trials demonstrates a 19% relative reduction in stroke/systemic embolism and a 51% reduction in hemorrhagic stroke compared to warfarin.

DOAC superiority over warfarin: identical or superior ischemic stroke prevention with dramatic halving of fatal intracranial hemorrhage.

guidelinesKept: Antithrombotic Therapy in Patients With Cancer: ASCO Guideline Update.

page.mentor_intro: Cancer-associated thrombosis (CAT) carries high risks of both recurrent venous thromboembolism and major bleeding. International guidelines recommend direct oral anticoagulants (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban) or low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) for at least 6 months. DOACs are preferred for most patients, but LMWH is favored in unresected gastrointestinal or genitourinary luminal cancers with high mucosal bleeding risk.

teaching_points.claim: ASCO guidelines recommend DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban) as preferred first-line therapy for acute VTE in cancer patients without high mucosal bleeding risk.
In patients with unresected gastrointestinal or genitourinary luminal malignancies, LMWH is preferred over DOACs due to increased GI mucosal bleeding.
The CARAVAGGIO trial demonstrated that oral apixaban was non-inferior to subcutaneous dalteparin for recurrent VTE in cancer patients without an increase in major bleeding.
Anticoagulation should be continued beyond 6 months as long as the cancer remains active, the patient is receiving systemic chemotherapy, or metastatic disease persists.

guidelinesKept: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 196: Thromboembolism in Pregnancy.

page.mentor_intro: Pregnancy is a prothrombotic state with a 4- to 5-fold increased risk of venous thromboembolism. Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH: enoxaparin, dalteparin) is the anticoagulant of choice throughout pregnancy and the postpartum period because it does not cross the placenta. Warfarin is teratogenic in the first trimester (warfarin embryopathy), and DOACs cross the placenta and are strictly contraindicated.

teaching_points.claim: ACOG and RCOG guidelines mandate LMWH as the anticoagulant of choice for prevention and treatment of VTE in pregnancy and lactation.
Warfarin crosses the placental barrier and causes warfarin embryopathy (nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses, CNS defects) when taken between 6 and 12 weeks gestation.
Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) cross the placenta, have documented embryofetal toxicities in animal models, and are strictly contraindicated in pregnancy.
Peripartum management: therapeutic LMWH must be held at least 24 hours (and prophylactic LMWH held 12 hours) prior to planned induction or neuraxial anesthesia.

Neuraxial anesthesia safety window: minimum 24 hours after last therapeutic dose of LMWH to prevent catastrophic epidural hematoma.
Postpartum anticoagulation duration: continue for at least 6 weeks postpartum, for a total minimum duration of 3 months.

page.mentor_intro: Management of acute life-threatening bleeding or urgent surgery in anticoagulated patients requires specific reversal agents and supportive hemostatic resuscitation. Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran; andexanet alfa reverses apixaban and rivaroxaban; 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (4F-PCC) combined with IV vitamin K reverses warfarin (target INR < 1.5). topic: antidepressant sequential treatment steps depressed outpatients outcomes

guidelinesKept: Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients With Major Depressive Disorder (APA).

page.mentor_intro: Major depressive disorder (MDD) requires systematic stepwise pharmacotherapy guided by measurement-based care (e.g. PHQ-9). The landmark STAR*D trial demonstrated that approximately 33% of patients achieve remission with initial SSRI monotherapy (Step 1). Subsequent steps—switching classes (to bupropion, venlafaxine) or augmenting with bupropion, buspirone, lithium, or second-generation antipsychotics—achieve cumulative remission rates up to 67%.

teaching_points.claim: The STAR*D trial established that sequential treatment steps for treatment-resistant depression produce cumulative remission rates approaching 67%.
APA practice guidelines recommend evaluating antidepressant response at 4-8 weeks before modifying therapy (switching vs augmenting).
Augmentation of an SSRI/SNRI with an atypical antipsychotic (aripiprazole, quetiapine) or bupropion produces higher response rates than switching monotherapy in partial responders.
Ketamine and esketamine nasal spray provide rapid-onset antidepressant effects in treatment-resistant depression with acute suicidal ideation.

guidelinesKept: NICE Guideline NG217: Epilepsies in children, young people and adults.

page.mentor_intro: Antiseizure medication (ASM) selection is determined by seizure classification (focal vs generalized vs unclassified), patient demographics (age, childbearing potential), comorbidity profiles, and potential drug-drug interactions. Broad-spectrum ASMs (levetiracetam, lamotrigine, valproate, topiramate) are effective for both focal and generalized seizures. Sodium channel blockers (carbamazepine, phenytoin) treat focal seizures but can aggravate generalized absence or myoclonic seizures.

teaching_points.claim: SANAD II trials established lamotrigine as first-line for focal epilepsy, and valproate as superior to levetiracetam for generalized epilepsy in males.
Sodium valproate is strictly contraindicated in women of childbearing potential due to high teratogenicity (neural tube defects) and neurodevelopmental delays.
Narrow-spectrum sodium channel blockers (carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin) can exacerbate generalized absence and juvenile myoclonic epilepsy.
Levetiracetam has low drug interaction potential and broad efficacy, but requires monitoring for behavioral changes, agitation, and depressive mood swings.

topic: Antifungal agents: azoles, echinocandins, polyenes: mechanisms, spectrum, drug interactions

guidelinesKept: Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Candidiasis: 2016 Update by the Infectious Diseases Society of America.
Practice Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management of Aspergillosis: 2016 Update by the IDSA.

page.mentor_intro: Systemic antifungal therapy is organized into three major classes: polyenes (amphotericin B), azoles (fluconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole, isavuconazole), and echinocandins (caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin). Echinocandins are first-line for invasive candidiasis; voriconazole or isavuconazole is first-line for invasive pulmonary aspergillosis; liposomal amphotericin B is standard for mucormycosis and cryptococcal meningitis.

teaching_points.claim: IDSA guidelines recommend an echinocandin (caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin) as initial first-line therapy for candidemia and invasive candidiasis.
Voriconazole is the treatment of choice for invasive pulmonary aspergillosis, but requires therapeutic drug monitoring (target trough 1.5-5.0 ug/mL) and visual/hepatic monitoring.
Isavuconazole provides equivalent efficacy to voriconazole for invasive aspergillosis with significantly fewer drug-related adverse events and drug discontinuations (SECURE trial).
Liposomal amphotericin B (5-10 mg/kg daily) combined with urgent surgical debridement is the cornerstone of management for invasive mucormycosis.

Antifungal spectrum gaps: Fluconazole has NO activity against Aspergillus; Echinocandins have NO activity against Cryptococcus neoformans.

guidelinesKept: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Glomerular Diseases.

page.mentor_intro: Anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) disease (Goodpasture disease) is a rare, severe autoimmune vasculitis mediated by pathogenic autoantibodies against the non-collagenous-1 (NC1) domain of the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen. It causes rapidly progressive crescentic glomerulonephritis and alveolar hemorrhage. Standard treatment is immediate initiation of plasmapheresis combined with high-dose corticosteroids and oral cyclophosphamide.

teaching_points.claim: KDIGO guidelines mandate immediate daily plasma exchange (for 14 days or until anti-GBM antibodies are undetectable) plus high-dose steroids and cyclophosphamide.
Renal prognosis is directly correlated with serum creatinine at presentation; patients presenting with dialysis-dependence and 100% cellular crescents rarely recover native kidney function.
Renal biopsy immunofluorescence demonstrates pathognomonic bright linear deposition of IgG (and often C3) along the glomerular capillary basement membrane.
Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia prophylaxis with co-trimoxazole is mandatory during cyclophosphamide immunosuppression.

sources.title: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Glomerular Diseases.

uncertainties: Role of targeted anti-CD20 therapy (rituximab) or imlifidase in refractory or severe anti-GBM disease.
Timing of kidney transplantation: safe after serum anti-GBM antibodies remain completely undetectable for at least 6 months.
mcq_angles: Diagnostic hallmark on immunofluorescence: linear IgG staining along the glomerular basement membrane.
Dual antibody positivity: up to 30% of patients with anti-GBM disease are double-positive for ANCA (mostly MPO-ANCA).
Prompt plasmapheresis goal: removes circulating pathogenic anti-GBM antibodies and inflammatory mediators to arrest ongoing crescentic destruction.

guidelinesKept: Consensus recommendations for the management of CAR T-cell toxicities.

page.mentor_intro: Interleukin-6 receptor (IL-6R) antagonist monoclonal antibodies (tocilizumab, sarilumab) block both soluble and membrane-bound IL-6 signaling. In rheumatology and immunology, anti-IL-6 therapy is standard of care for rheumatoid arthritis, giant cell arteritis (GiACTA trial), systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis, cytokine release syndrome (CRS) after CAR-T cell therapy, and severe hospitalized COVID-19.

teaching_points.claim: The GiACTA trial demonstrated that tocilizumab combined with a 26-week prednisone taper achieved 56% sustained remission at 52 weeks in giant cell arteritis compared to 14% with placebo.
Tocilizumab is the FDA-approved first-line therapy for severe or life-threatening chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell-induced cytokine release syndrome.
In hospitalized patients with severe COVID-19 hypoxia and systemic inflammation, tocilizumab significantly reduces 28-day mortality and progression to mechanical ventilation (RECOVERY trial).
Anti-IL-6 therapy completely suppresses hepatic C-reactive protein (CRP) synthesis; serum CRP cannot be used as an inflammatory marker to detect intercurrent bacterial infection.

guidelinesKept: Infectious Diseases Society of America 2023 Guidance on the Treatment of Antimicrobial-Resistant Gram-Negative Infections.

page.mentor_intro: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a top-tier global public health threat driven by the selective pressure of overuse and inappropriate antimicrobial prescribing in human health and agriculture. Pathogens of highest clinical priority ('ESKAPE': Enterococcus faecium, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Enterobacter species) cause severe hospital-acquired infections with limited therapeutic options.

teaching_points.claim: The WHO Global Antimicrobial Resistance Report identifies carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) and Acinetobacter baumannii as critical priority pathogens.
Gram-negative resistance mechanisms include carbapenemases (KPC, NDM, VIM, OXA-48), extended-spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBLs), and porin loss / efflux pumps.
Novel beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations (ceftazidime-avibactam, meropenem-vaborbactam, imipenem-relebactam, cefiderocol) provide targeted coverage for specific CRE classes.
Comprehensive infection prevention and control (hand hygiene, contact precautions, environmental disinfection) reduces horizontal nosocomial transmission of multidrug-resistant organisms.

topic: Antimicrobial stewardship: IV to oral switch, duration of therapy, procalcitonin-guided therapy

guidelinesKept: Implementing an Antibiotic Stewardship Program: Guidelines by IDSA and SHEA.

page.mentor_intro: Antimicrobial stewardship programs (ASPs) optimize clinical outcomes while minimizing unintended consequences of antimicrobial use, including toxicity, selection of pathogenic organisms (such as Clostridioides difficile), and the emergence of antimicrobial resistance. Core strategies include pre-authorization, prospective audit with feedback, evidence-based guidelines, and diagnostic stewardship.

teaching_points.claim: CDC and IDSA guidelines emphasize prospective audit and feedback as the most effective stewardship intervention to optimize antibiotic prescribing.
Implementing hospital-based ASPs significantly reduces overall antibiotic consumption, hospital-onset Clostridioides difficile infection, and institutional resistance rates.
Diagnostic stewardship ensures appropriate collection of microbiological cultures before antimicrobial initiation, preventing contaminated or unindicated blood and urine cultures.
Facility-specific antibiograms updated annually guide empirical therapy based on local pathogen susceptibility patterns rather than national estimates.

guidelinesKept: 2023 ACR/EULAR Antiphospholipid Syndrome Classification Criteria.
EULAR recommendations for the management of antiphospholipid syndrome in adults.

page.mentor_intro: Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is a systemic autoimmune thrombophilia characterized by vascular thrombosis (arterial, venous, or microvascular) and/or pregnancy morbidity in the presence of persistent antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, and anti-beta-2 glycoprotein I). Secondary prevention of venous thromboembolism requires lifelong therapeutic warfarin; DOACs are contraindicated in triple-positive APS.

teaching_points.claim: 2023 ACR/EULAR APS Classification Criteria incorporate modern weighted scoring across clinical domains (macrovascular, obstetric, microvascular) and laboratory antibody titers.
The TRAPS trial demonstrated that oral rivaroxaban was associated with an excess of arterial thrombotic events (mainly stroke) compared to warfarin in triple-positive APS.
Long-term therapeutic anticoagulation with warfarin targeting an INR of 2.0-3.0 is the standard of care for secondary prevention of venous thrombosis in APS.
Obstetric APS management requires combination low-dose aspirin (75-100 mg daily) and prophylactic-to-therapeutic LMWH throughout pregnancy and 6 weeks postpartum.

Why DOACs are avoided in triple-positive APS: excess arterial thrombotic events compared to warfarin in TRAPS trial.

topic: Antiphospholipid syndrome: Sapporo criteria, thrombosis, obstetric APS management

guidelinesKept: 2023 ACR/EULAR Antiphospholipid Syndrome Classification Criteria.
EULAR recommendations for the management of antiphospholipid syndrome in adults.

page.mentor_intro: Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is a systemic autoimmune thrombophilia characterized by vascular thrombosis (arterial, venous, or microvascular) and/or pregnancy morbidity in the presence of persistent antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, and anti-beta-2 glycoprotein I). Secondary prevention of venous thromboembolism requires lifelong therapeutic warfarin; DOACs are contraindicated in triple-positive APS.

teaching_points.claim: 2023 ACR/EULAR APS Classification Criteria incorporate modern weighted scoring across clinical domains (macrovascular, obstetric, microvascular) and laboratory antibody titers.
The TRAPS trial demonstrated that oral rivaroxaban was associated with an excess of arterial thrombotic events (mainly stroke) compared to warfarin in triple-positive APS.
Long-term therapeutic anticoagulation with warfarin targeting an INR of 2.0-3.0 is the standard of care for secondary prevention of venous thrombosis in APS.
Obstetric APS management requires combination low-dose aspirin (75-100 mg daily) and prophylactic-to-therapeutic LMWH throughout pregnancy and 6 weeks postpartum.

guidelinesKept: Consensus Development Conference on Antipsychotic Drugs and Obesity and Diabetes (ADA/APA).
Evidence-based guidelines for the pharmacological treatment of schizophrenia (BAP).

page.mentor_intro: Second-generation (atypical) antipsychotics are effective for schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and treatment-resistant depression, but carry significant cardiometabolic liabilities (weight gain, dyslipidemia, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, and accelerated cardiovascular mortality). High-risk agents include olanzapine and clozapine; intermediate-risk include quetiapine and risperidone; lowest-risk include aripiprazole, ziprasidone, and lurasidone.

teaching_points.claim: ADA/APA consensus guidelines mandate structured baseline and periodic metabolic monitoring: BMI and blood pressure at every visit; fasting glucose and lipid profile at 12 weeks, then annually.
Olanzapine and clozapine cause the greatest increases in adiposity, visceral fat, triglyceride levels, and incident diabetes through 5-HT2C, H1, and M3 receptor antagonism.
Metformin initiated early in antipsychotic treatment significantly attenuates drug-induced weight gain and improves insulin sensitivity.

Switching to a metabolic-neutral atypical antipsychotic (aripiprazole, lurasidone) or adding GLP-1 receptor agonists provides effective weight and glycemic reduction in established metabolic syndrome.

guidelinesKept: 2021 ESC/EACTS Guidelines for the management of valvular heart disease.

page.mentor_intro: Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) mandates antithrombotic therapy to balance the risks of leaflet thrombosis, thromboembolic stroke, and major bleeding. In patients without an underlying indication for oral anticoagulation, single antiplatelet therapy (aspirin 75-100 mg daily) is superior to dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT), achieving equivalent ischemic protection with significantly lower bleeding (POPular TAVI trial).

teaching_points.claim: The POPular TAVI trial (Cohort A) demonstrated that aspirin monotherapy significantly reduced bleeding without increasing stroke or thromboembolic events compared to DAPT after TAVR.
In patients with pre-existing indications for oral anticoagulation, oral anticoagulation alone without antiplatelet therapy reduces major bleeding (POPular TAVI Cohort B).
Subclinical leaflet thrombosis (hypoattenuating leaflet thickening, HALT) occurs in 10-15% of bioprosthetic valves on four-dimensional cardiac CT, and is resolved with oral anticoagulation.
ESC/EACTS and ACC/AHA guidelines recommend single antiplatelet therapy (aspirin) as the standard default antithrombotic strategy in patients without OAC indications.

guidelinesKept: Generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder in adults: management (NICE Guideline CG113).
Evidence-based pharmacotherapy of anxiety disorders (WFSBP).

page.mentor_intro: Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) and panic disorder are common psychiatric conditions characterized by excessive chronic worry, autonomic arousal, or sudden recurrent panic attacks with agoraphobia. First-line evidence-based treatments are cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and SSRIs (sertraline, escitalopram) or SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine). Benzodiazepines should be restricted to brief acute crisis stabilization due to risks of dependence and tolerance.

teaching_points.claim: NICE Guideline CG113 recommends CBT and SSRIs (sertraline as first-line) as the most effective long-term treatments for GAD and panic disorder.
Benzodiazepines are not recommended for long-term treatment of anxiety disorders due to tolerance, cognitive impairment, withdrawal rebound, and dependence.
Initial 'jitteriness / paradoxical anxiety' syndrome occurs during the first 1-2 weeks of SSRI initiation; start at half the standard starting dose and titrate gradually.
Pregabalin (alpha-2-delta ligand) is an approved non-benzodiazepine second-line option for generalized anxiety disorder with rapid onset of anxiolysis.

Maintenance treatment duration: continue effective pharmacotherapy for at least 12-24 months after remission to prevent relapse.

guidelinesKept: 2024 ESC Guidelines for the management of aortic diseases.
2021 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Evaluation and Diagnosis of Chest Pain.

page.mentor_intro: Acute aortic dissection is a life-threatening cardiovascular emergency resulting from an intimal tear that creates a false lumen in the aortic media. Stanford Type A involves the ascending aorta (mandates emergent open surgical repair). Stanford Type B involves only the descending aorta distal to the left subclavian artery (managed with medical anti-impulse therapy using IV beta-blockers, reserving TEVAR for complicated Type B).

teaching_points.claim: ESC and AHA/ACC guidelines mandate emergent cardiothoracic surgical repair for Stanford Type A aortic dissection to prevent fatal tamponade, rupture, or coronary malperfusion.

Initial medical management requires anti-impulse therapy: IV beta-blockers (esmolol, labetalol) to reduce heart rate < 60 bpm and shear stress (dP/dt), followed by vasodilators to achieve SBP 100-120 mmHg.
Vasodilators (nitroprusside, nicardipine) must NEVER be started before beta-blockade, as reflex sympathetic tachycardia increases aortic wall shear stress and propagates the tear.
Thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) is indicated for complicated Stanford Type B dissection (refractory pain, rapid expansion, organ malperfusion, rupture).

mcq_angles: Stanford classification: Type A = involves ascending aorta (surgical emergency); Type B = restricted to descending aorta distal to left subclavian artery.
The critical rule of anti-impulse therapy: IV beta-blocker FIRST (target HR < 60 bpm), then vasodilator (target SBP 100-120 mmHg) to avoid reflex tachycardia.
Complications of Type A dissection: acute severe aortic regurgitation, hemopericardium / cardiac tamponade, myocardial infarction, and stroke.

topic: Aortic stenosis: grading severity, low-flow low-gradient, intervention timing

guidelinesKept: 2021 ESC/EACTS Guidelines for the management of valvular heart disease.

page.mentor_intro: Severe aortic stenosis (AS) is defined on transthoracic echocardiography by an aortic valve area (AVA) <= 1.0 cm2 (or indexed AVA <= 0.6 cm2/m2), mean transvalvular gradient >= 40 mmHg, or peak jet velocity >= 4.0 m/s. Once symptoms (angina, syncope, dyspnea) develop, 2-year mortality exceeds 50% without valve intervention. Low-flow low-gradient AS requires dobutamine stress echocardiography or non-contrast cardiac CT calcium scoring.

teaching_points.claim: ESC and AHA/ACC guidelines define severe aortic stenosis by AVA <= 1.0 cm2, mean gradient >= 40 mmHg, or peak velocity >= 4.0 m/s.
Low-dose dobutamine stress echocardiography differentiates true severe AS from pseudo-severe AS in low-flow low-gradient AS with reduced LVEF.
In paradoxical low-flow low-gradient AS with preserved LVEF, non-contrast cardiac CT aortic valve calcium scoring confirms severity (threshold >= 2,000 in men, >= 1,200 in women).
Aortic valve replacement (SAVR or TAVR) is indicated in all symptomatic patients with severe AS, and in asymptomatic patients with LVEF < 50% or abnormal exercise testing.

mcq_angles: Classic triad of symptomatic severe AS: Dyspnea (heart failure, 2-year survival 50%), Syncope (exertional, 3-year survival), Angina (5-year survival).
Dobutamine stress echo assessment of contractile reserve: an increase in stroke volume >= 20% confirms contractile reserve and predicts lower procedural mortality.
Cardiac CT calcium score thresholds for severe AS: >= 2,000-3,000 AU in men; >= 1,200-1,600 AU in women.

guidelinesKept: 2021 ESC/EACTS Guidelines for the management of valvular heart disease.

page.mentor_intro: Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) has transformed the treatment of severe symptomatic aortic stenosis across all surgical risk categories (high, intermediate, and low surgical risk). Valve selection between transfemoral TAVR and surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) is made by the Heart Team, considering patient age (TAVR favored in age >= 75; SAVR favored in age < 65), life expectancy, anatomical suitability, and vascular access.

teaching_points.claim: The PARTNER 3 and Evolut Low Risk trials demonstrated that transfemoral TAVR was non-inferior or superior to surgical aortic valve replacement in low-risk elderly patients.
ESC/EACTS guidelines recommend TAVR in older patients (age >= 75 years) or those who are inoperable or high surgical risk (STS/EuroSCORE II > 8%).
Complications of TAVR include complete heart block requiring permanent pacemaker implantation (higher with self-expanding valves), vascular access site injury, paravalvular leak, and stroke.
Pre-procedural planning requires ECG-gated multislice cardiac CT of the aortic root and iliofemoral vasculature for valve sizing and access evaluation.

guidelinesKept: 2024 ESC Guidelines for the management of atrial fibrillation.

page.mentor_intro: Apixaban and rivaroxaban are direct factor Xa inhibitors widely prescribed for stroke prevention in non-valvular atrial fibrillation and treatment of venous thromboembolism. Apixaban is administered twice daily (12-hour half-life) and has the lowest renal elimination (~27%) among DOACs. Rivaroxaban is administered once daily with food (to ensure absorption of 15 mg and 20 mg doses) and is 35% renally cleared. Large observational comparative studies show lower gastrointestinal bleeding and mortality with apixaban.

teaching_points.claim: Large real-world observational comparative effectiveness studies consistently associate apixaban with lower rates of major bleeding and gastrointestinal hemorrhage compared to rivaroxaban.
Rivaroxaban 15 mg and 20 mg tablets must strictly be taken with food to achieve predictable oral bioavailability (bioavailability falls to 66% in the fasting state).
Apixaban requires twice-daily dosing to maintain steady-state anticoagulation, reducing peak-to-trough plasma fluctuations compared to once-daily rivaroxaban.
Both agents are substrate of CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, requiring dose adjustment or avoidance with strong dual inhibitors (ketoconazole, ritonavir) or inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine).

guidelinesKept: 2024 ESC Guidelines for the management of atrial fibrillation.

page.mentor_intro: The landmark ARISTOTLE trial compared the oral direct factor Xa inhibitor apixaban (5 mg twice daily, or 2.5 mg twice daily in select patients) with dose-adjusted warfarin in 18,201 patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation. Apixaban achieved significant superiority in preventing stroke or systemic embolism (21% reduction), major bleeding (31% reduction), and all-cause mortality (11% reduction).

teaching_points.claim: In the ARISTOTLE trial, apixaban was superior to warfarin in preventing stroke or systemic embolism (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.66-0.95; p < 0.001 for non-inferiority, p = 0.01 for superiority).
Apixaban significantly reduced major bleeding by 31% (HR 0.69; p < 0.001) and intracranial hemorrhage by 58% compared to warfarin.
Apixaban demonstrated a statistically significant 11% reduction in all-cause mortality (HR 0.89; p = 0.047), a landmark finding unique among pivotal DOAC trials.
Dose reduction to 2.5 mg twice daily is indicated if at least 2 of 3 criteria are met: age >= 80 years, body weight <= 60 kg, or serum creatinine >= 1.5 mg/dL.

guidelinesKept: Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of adult aplastic anaemia (BSH).

page.mentor_intro: Severe aplastic anaemia (SAA) is an immune-mediated bone marrow failure disorder characterized by profound pancytopenia and hypocellular bone marrow (cellularity < 25-30%) without dysplasia or fibrosis. In young, fit patients (< 40-50 years) with an HLA-matched sibling donor, upfront allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation is curative. For older patients or those lacking a matched sibling, immunosuppressive therapy (IST) with horse anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG), cyclosporine, and the thrombopoietin receptor agonist eltrombopag achieves > 80% response rates.

teaching_points.claim: British Society for Haematology guidelines define SAA by bone marrow cellularity < 25% and at least two of: neutrophils < 0.5 x 10^9/L, platelets < 20 x 10^9/L, or reticulocytes < 60 x 10^9/L (Camitta criteria).
First-line allogeneic HCT from an HLA-matched sibling donor cures > 85-90% of children and young adults with severe aplastic anaemia.
Adding eltrombopag to horse ATG and cyclosporine significantly increases complete and overall hematologic response rates (87% vs 66%) in treatment-naive SAA (RACE trial).
Horse ATG (ATGAM) is clinically superior to rabbit ATG (Thymoglobulin) for initial immunosuppressive therapy in SAA.

uncertainties: Efficacy and graft-versus-host disease rates with upfront matched unrelated donor (MUD) vs IST in adults aged 40-60.

mcq_angles: Camitta criteria for severe aplastic anemia: marrow cellularity < 25% plus 2 of: ANC < 0.5 x 10^9/L, Plt < 20 x 10^9/L, Retics < 60 x 10^9/L (ANC < 0.2 defines very severe AA).
Serum sickness prophylaxis and management during horse ATG: high-dose oral prednisone (1 mg/kg/day) for 10-14 days.
Why horse ATG is preferred over rabbit ATG in primary SAA: rabbit ATG causes excessive profound T-cell depletion and higher early mortality.

page.mentor_intro: Acute appendicitis is the most common surgical abdominal emergency, caused by luminal obstruction (fecalith, lymphoid hyperplasia) leading to distension, bacterial invasion, ischemia, and perforation. Antibiotic-first non-operative management (CODA trial) is successful in ~70% of uncomplicated appendicitis at 90 days, but is associated with a 29% appendectomy recurrence rate at 1 year.
Presence of an appendicolith on CT is strongly associated with non-operative antibiotic failure, recurrent appendicitis, and early perforation.

topic: ARDS definition: Berlin criteria and severity classification

guidelinesKept: Acute respiratory distress syndrome: the Berlin Definition.

page.mentor_intro: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is an acute diffuse inflammatory lung injury characterized by increased pulmonary vascular permeability, alveolar flooding, and severe refractory hypoxemia. The Berlin definition requires onset within 1 week of clinical insult, bilateral radiographic opacities not fully explained by heart failure, and PaO2/FiO2 <= 300 with PEEP >= 5 cmH2O. Core management relies on lung-protective ventilation (low tidal volumes, low driving pressure) and early prone positioning.

teaching_points.claim: The Berlin definition stages ARDS into mild (PaO2/FiO2 201-300), moderate (101-200), and severe (<= 100 mmHg) with minimum PEEP >= 5 cmH2O.
Lung-protective ventilation with low tidal volumes (4-8 mL/kg predicted body weight) and plateau pressure < 30 cmH2O significantly reduces 28-day mortality (ARMA trial).
Prone positioning for at least 16 consecutive hours daily reduces 28-day and 90-day mortality in severe ARDS with PaO2/FiO2 < 150 mmHg (PROSEVA trial).
Conservative fluid management strategy increases ventilator-free days and ICU-free days without increasing non-pulmonary organ failure (FACTT trial).

guidelinesKept: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Acute Kidney Injury.

page.mentor_intro: Arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis is a foundational diagnostic tool in critical care and emergency medicine. A systematic 6-step interpretation approach evaluates: 1) PaO2 and SaO2 for oxygenation, 2) pH for acidemia (< 7.35) or alkalemia (> 7.45), 3) PaCO2 for respiratory disturbances, 4) HCO3- and Base Excess for metabolic disturbances, 5) Serum anion gap (Na - [Cl + HCO3-], normal 10-12 mEq/L), and 6) Delta ratio (Delta AG / Delta HCO3-) to identify mixed metabolic disorders.

teaching_points.claim: A systematic 6-step algorithmic approach prevents overlooking hidden mixed acid-base disorders in critically ill ICU patients.
Anion gap calculation must be corrected for hypoalbuminemia: adjusted AG = observed AG + 2.5 * (4.0 - serum albumin in g/dL).
Winter's formula determines appropriate respiratory compensation in metabolic acidosis: expected PaCO2 = 1.5 * [HCO3-] + 8 (+/- 2).
Delta ratio (Delta AG / Delta HCO3-): < 0.4-0.8 indicates mixed high AG and normal AG metabolic acidosis; > 1.6-2.0 indicates concurrent metabolic alkalosis.

Albumin effect on anion gap: each 1 g/dL drop in albumin lowers normal baseline anion gap by 2.5 mEq/L.

page.mentor_intro: Arterial leg ulcers are painful, ischemic, non-healing lower extremity wounds resulting from peripheral artery disease (PAD) and microvascular insufficiency. They are typically deep, punched-out, painful (worse with elevation, relieved by hanging leg over bed), located on distally perfused sites (toes, lateral malleolus, heels), with pale/cyanotic skin and absent pulses. Diagnostic evaluation requires Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI), duplex ultrasound, and vascular surgery revascularization.

teaching_points.claim: AHA/ACC and ESVS guidelines establish that compression bandaging is strictly contraindicated in severe arterial ulcers with ABI < 0.5 or ankle pressure < 50 mmHg.
Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI) <= 0.90 is diagnostic of peripheral artery disease; values > 1.40 indicate non-compressible, calcified arteries warranting Toe-Brachial Index (TBI < 0.70).
Endovascular or surgical revascularization is the essential cornerstone of limb salvage in chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI / Rutherford stage 5-6).
Comprehensive medical therapy includes high-intensity statin, single antiplatelet therapy (clopidogrel 75 mg or low-dose rivaroxaban + aspirin [COMPASS trial]), and smoking cessation.

page.mentor_intro: Asbestosis is a chronic interstitial pneumonitis and progressive pulmonary fibrosis caused by the inhalation of microscopic asbestos fibers. It typically manifests 20-30 years following substantial occupational exposure (shipyards, construction, insulation). Clinical features include exertional dyspnea, dry bibasilar inspiratory crackles, finger clubbing, and restrictive spirometry with reduced DLCO. HRCT shows subpleural curvilinear lines, parenchymal bands, and calcified pleural plaques.

teaching_points.claim: ATS criteria establish diagnosis based on documented history of significant asbestos exposure, latency > 20 years, restrictive lung defect with reduced DLCO, and characteristic HRCT fibrosis.
High-resolution chest CT demonstrates bilateral, predominantly subpleural and basilar fibrosis, accompanied by bilateral calcified parietal pleural plaques along ribs and diaphragm.
Pleural plaques indicate prior asbestos exposure but do not themselves cause significant functional lung impairment or undergo malignant transformation.
Asbestos exposure combined with cigarette smoking acts synergistically to multiply the lifetime risk of bronchogenic carcinoma by up to 50- to 60-fold.

page.mentor_intro: Ascites in cirrhosis results from sinusoidal portal hypertension, splanchnic arterial vasodilation, neurohumoral activation (RAAS, sympathetic nervous system), and avid renal sodium/water retention. Diagnostic paracentesis is mandatory at admission to calculate the serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) and exclude spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (neutrophils >= 250/uL). First-line medical therapy combines dietary sodium restriction (< 2 g/day) with dual diuretic therapy (spironolactone plus furosemide).

teaching_points.claim: AASLD and EASL guidelines mandate diagnostic paracentesis in all patients hospitalized with new-onset or worsening cirrhotic ascites to rule out SBP.
Serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG = serum albumin - ascites albumin) >= 1.1 g/dL confirms portal hypertension with 97% accuracy.
First-line diuretic therapy uses a 100:40 mg ratio of spironolactone to furosemide, maintaining normokalemia while titrating to a maximum of 400:160 mg daily.
Large-volume paracentesis (> 5 L) requires concurrent intravenous albumin infusion (6-8 g per liter of ascites removed) to prevent paracentesis-induced circulatory dysfunction (PICD).

page.mentor_intro: Aspiration pneumonia occurs when colonized oropharyngeal or gastric secretions are inhaled into the lower respiratory tract, triggering acute bacterial infection. It must be distinguished from chemical aspiration pneumonitis (Mendelson syndrome: acute gastric acid-induced chemical lung injury without initial bacterial infection). First-line antibiotic therapy for community-acquired aspiration pneumonia is ampicillin-sulbactam, amoxicillin-clavulanate, or moxifloxacin. Dedicated anaerobic coverage is reserved for lung abscess, empyema, or severe periodontal disease.

teaching_points.claim: IDSA/ATS guidelines recommend ampicillin-sulbactam or amoxicillin-clavulanate as preferred first-line therapy for community-acquired aspiration pneumonia.
Routine addition of specific anaerobic coverage (e.g. clindamycin or metronidazole) is no longer recommended for uncomplicated aspiration pneumonia unless lung abscess or empyema is present.
Aspiration pneumonitis (sterile acid chemical burn) presents hyperacutely with bronchospasm and infiltrates within 2-4 hours, typically resolving with supportive care without antibiotics.
Formal speech and language pathology swallowing assessment and post-pyloric feeding or thickened liquids reduce recurrent aspiration risk in post-stroke dysphagia.

topic: aspirin cardiovascular events bleeding healthy elderly primary prevention

guidelinesKept: Aspirin Use to Prevent Cardiovascular Disease: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement.

page.mentor_intro: Aspirin for primary cardiovascular prevention in older adults is no longer routinely recommended. Landmark randomized clinical trials (ASPREE, ARRIVE, ASCEND) demonstrated that daily low-dose aspirin (100 mg) did not prolong disability-free survival or reduce cardiovascular events in healthy older adults, but significantly increased major gastrointestinal bleeding and intracranial hemorrhage.

teaching_points.claim: The ASPREE trial in healthy adults >= 70 years demonstrated that aspirin 100 mg daily did not reduce cardiovascular disease or dementia, but significantly increased major hemorrhage (HR 1.38).
ASPREE demonstrated an unexpected 14% increase in all-cause mortality, primarily driven by cancer-related deaths in the aspirin group (HR 1.14, 95% CI 1.01-1.29).
USPSTF and ACC/AHA guidelines recommend AGAINST initiating low-dose aspirin for primary prevention of cardiovascular disease in adults aged 60 years or older.
For adults aged 40-59 years with a 10-year CVD risk >= 10%, the net benefit is small, warranting individual shared decision-making only in those with low bleeding risk.

page.mentor_intro: Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD / Samter triad) is a non-IgE-mediated pseudoallergic syndrome characterized by adult-onset asthma, recurrent chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP), and severe acute upper and lower respiratory reactions following the ingestion of aspirin or other COX-1-inhibiting NSAIDs. Pathophysiology involves arachidonic acid dysregulation with cysteinyl leukotriene overproduction. Treatment combines leukotriene modifiers, biologics (dupilumab), and aspirin desensitization.

teaching_points.claim: AERD is triggered by pharmacologic inhibition of cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1), diverting arachidonic acid metabolism to the 5-lipoxygenase pathway and causing massive leukotriene release.
Selective COX-2 inhibitors (celecoxib, etoricoxib) do not trigger bronchospasm and are safe alternatives for analgesia in verified AERD.
Dupilumab (anti-IL-4Ralpha) and omalizumab (anti-IgE) achieve significant sinus polyp regression, asthma symptom control, and reduction in leukotriene production in AERD.
Aspirin desensitization followed by high-dose aspirin maintenance therapy (325-650 mg twice daily) provides disease-modifying reduction in nasal polyp recurrence.

Landmark randomized clinical trials (ASPREE, ARRIVE, ASCEND) demonstrated that daily low-dose aspirin (100 mg) did not prolong disability-free survival or reduce cardiovascular events in healthy older adults, but significantly increased major gastrointestinal bleeding and intracranial hemorrhage.

teaching_points.claim: The ASPREE trial in healthy adults >= 70 years demonstrated that aspirin 100 mg daily did not reduce cardiovascular disease or dementia, but significantly increased major hemorrhage (HR 1.38).
ASPREE demonstrated an unexpected 14% increase in all-cause mortality, primarily driven by cancer-related deaths in the aspirin group (HR 1.14, 95% CI 1.01-1.29).
USPSTF and ACC/AHA guidelines recommend AGAINST initiating low-dose aspirin for primary prevention of cardiovascular disease in adults aged 60 years or older.
For adults aged 40-59 years with a 10-year CVD risk >= 10%, the net benefit is small, warranting individual shared decision-making only in those with low bleeding risk.

page.mentor_intro: Asthma is a heterogeneous chronic inflammatory airway disease characterized by variable respiratory symptoms and variable expiratory airflow limitation. GINA 2024 recommendations establish inhaled corticosteroid (ICS)-formoterol as the preferred reliever and controller across Steps 1 to 5 (SMART/MART strategy). This eliminates SABA monotherapy, significantly reducing severe exacerbations and asthma-related mortality.

teaching_points.claim: GINA guidelines recommend as-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol as the preferred reliever across all asthma severities, eliminating short-acting beta-2 agonist (SABA) monotherapy.
Single maintenance and reliever therapy (SMART / MART) with ICS-formoterol reduces severe exacerbations by 30-40% compared to fixed-dose ICS-LABA with SABA reliever.
Severe asthma requiring Step 5 care requires phenotyping for Type 2 inflammation: blood eosinophils >= 150-300 cells/uL, FeNO >= 20-25 ppb, or allergen sensitization.
Targeted biologic therapies (omalizumab, mepolizumab, benralizumab, dupilumab, tezepelumab) dramatically reduce exacerbations, oral steroid dependence, and hospitalizations.

guidelinesKept: Global Initiative for Asthma (GINA) 2024 Strategy Report: Acute Exacerbations.

page.mentor_intro: Acute severe asthma exacerbation is a life-threatening medical emergency. Management focuses on rapid reversal of airflow obstruction, correction of hypoxemia, and prevention of respiratory arrest. First-line therapy includes repetitive inhaled SABA (albuterol/salbutamol) combined with ipratropium bromide, early systemic corticosteroids (oral prednisolone 40-50 mg daily for 5-7 days), controlled oxygen targeting SpO2 93-95%, and IV magnesium sulfate for severe or refractory cases.

teaching_points.claim: GINA and BTS/SIGN guidelines mandate early systemic corticosteroids (oral prednisolone 40-50 mg daily) within 1 hour of ED presentation to accelerate resolution and prevent relapse.
Combining inhaled ipratropium bromide with albuterol in acute moderate-to-severe exacerbations significantly reduces hospital admission rates and improves FEV1.
Single-dose intravenous magnesium sulfate (2g IV over 20 minutes) reduces hospital admissions in severe exacerbations with FEV1 < 50% or poor initial response.
A 'normal' or rising PaCO2 (>= 40-45 mmHg) in a severely tachypneic patient signifies impending respiratory muscle fatigue and catastrophic arrest.

guidelinesKept: GINA 2024 Strategy: Management of Asthma in Pregnancy.
ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 90: Asthma in Pregnancy.

page.mentor_intro: Asthma affects approximately 8-10% of pregnant women. The rule of thirds applies: one-third improve, one-third remain unchanged, and one-third worsen during pregnancy. Uncontrolled asthma with maternal hypoxia carries significant risks of pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, low birth weight, and perinatal mortality. Inhaled corticosteroids (budesonide preferred) and SABA relievers are safe and must be actively maintained throughout pregnancy.

teaching_points.claim: ACOG and GINA guidelines emphasize that it is far safer for pregnant women to take asthma medications than to experience asthma exacerbations or hypoxia.
Inhaled budesonide is the preferred maintenance inhaled corticosteroid in pregnancy due to the largest volume of human safety data.
Acute asthma exacerbations in pregnancy require aggressive treatment: controlled oxygen targeting maternal SpO2 >= 95% to maintain adequate fetal oxygenation.
Systemic corticosteroids (oral prednisolone) should never be withheld in acute severe asthma exacerbations, as maternal hypoxia poses immediate fetal risk.

guidelinesKept: 2024 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Management of Lower Extremity Peripheral Artery Disease.

page.mentor_intro: Atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis (ARAS) is common in elderly patients with generalized vascular disease. Landmark randomized controlled trials (ASTRAL and CORAL) demonstrated that routine percutaneous renal artery stenting does NOT provide incremental benefit over optimal medical therapy alone for blood pressure control, preservation of renal function, or reduction in cardiovascular events. Medical therapy with statins, antiplatelets, and antihypertensives is first-line; stenting is reserved for flash pulmonary edema or truly refractory hypertension.

teaching_points.claim: The CORAL trial demonstrated that renal-artery stenting added to medical therapy did not reduce cardiovascular or renal events in atherosclerotic renal-artery stenosis.
The ASTRAL trial showed no evidence of clinically meaningful benefit of renal-artery revascularization on renal function or survival compared to medical therapy.

AHA/ACC and ESC guidelines restrict renal artery stenting to high-risk clinical presentations: recurrent unexplained flash pulmonary edema (Pickering syndrome) or refractory hypertension resistant to >= 4 medications.
ACE inhibitors and ARBs are safe and reduce cardiovascular mortality in unilateral ARAS, but can cause acute reversible decline in GFR (> 30%) in bilateral high-grade stenosis.

topic: Atopic dermatitis: diagnosis, stepwise treatment and biologics

guidelinesKept: Guidelines of care for the management of atopic dermatitis (AAD).

page.mentor_intro: Atopic dermatitis (eczema) is a chronic, relapsing, pruritic inflammatory skin disease characterized by epidermal barrier dysfunction (often associated with filaggrin mutations) and immune dysregulation with prominent Th2 cytokine activation (IL-4, IL-13). Management follows a stepwise approach: daily bland emollients, topical corticosteroids or topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus) for flares, and targeted systemic biologics (dupilumab, tralokinumab) or oral JAK inhibitors for moderate-to-severe refractory disease.

teaching_points.claim: AAD guidelines recommend proactive twice-weekly application of topical calcineurin inhibitors or low-potency steroids to previously affected sites to prevent recurrent flares.
Dupilumab (monoclonal antibody blocking IL-4Ralpha, inhibiting IL-4 and IL-13 signaling) achieves 75% reduction in EASI score in over 50-60% of patients without organ toxicity (SOLO 1 and 2 trials).
Oral JAK inhibitors (upadacitinib, abrocitinib, baricitinib) provide rapid pruritus relief and cutaneous clearance in moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis.
Eczema herpeticum (disseminated cutaneous herpes simplex virus infection) is a dermatological emergency requiring immediate oral or intravenous acyclovir.

guidelinesKept: 2024 ESC Guidelines for the management of atrial fibrillation.

page.mentor_intro: Stroke prevention in non-valvular atrial fibrillation is guided by the CHA2DS2-VASc risk score. Oral anticoagulation is recommended for men with score >= 2 and women with score >= 3, and should be considered for men with score 1 and women with score 2. Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs: apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran, edoxaban) are preferred over warfarin due to a 50% reduction in intracranial hemorrhage.

teaching_points.claim: ESC 2024 guidelines recommend DOACs over warfarin as first-line stroke prevention for non-valvular atrial fibrillation (Class I, Level A).
CHA2DS2-VASc score assigns points: CHF (1), HTN (1), Age >= 75 (2), Diabetes (1), Stroke/TIA/thromboembolism (2), Vascular disease (1), Age 65-74 (1), Sex female (1).
Female sex is a risk modifier rather than an independent risk factor; a female with no other risk factors (CHA2DS2-VASc = 1) does NOT require anticoagulation.
Meta-analysis of landmark DOAC trials demonstrates a 19% relative reduction in stroke/systemic embolism and a 51% reduction in hemorrhagic stroke compared to warfarin.

mcq_angles: Components of CHA2DS2-VASc: 2 points each for Age >= 75 and prior Stroke/TIA; 1 point for CHF, HTN, DM, Vascular disease, Age 65-74, Female sex.
Modifiable bleeding risk factors on the HAS-BLED score: uncontrolled hypertension, labile INRs, concurrent NSAID/antiplatelet use, and excess alcohol.
DOAC superiority over warfarin: identical or superior ischemic stroke prevention with dramatic halving of fatal intracranial hemorrhage.

A 28-year-old female with lone atrial fibrillation and no comorbidities (CHA2DS2-VASc = 1 solely for sex) who does not require anticoagulation.

topic: atrial fibrillation anticoagulation chronic kidney disease stroke prevention

guidelinesKept: KDIGO 2023 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Cardiovascular Disease in Chronic Kidney Disease.

page.mentor_intro: Atrial fibrillation is highly prevalent in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), significantly increasing stroke and bleeding risks. Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs: apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran) provide superior or non-inferior stroke prevention compared to warfarin in mild-to-moderate CKD (CrCl 30-50 mL/min). In severe CKD (CrCl 15-29 mL/min) and dialysis, apixaban is increasingly utilized with specific dose reduction criteria.

teaching_points.claim: KDIGO 2023 guidelines recommend DOACs over vitamin K antagonists (warfarin) in patients with non-valvular AF and CKD Stages 1-3, and consider DOACs in Stage 4 (CrCl 15-29 mL/min).
Apixaban requires dose reduction to 2.5 mg BID if the patient meets at least two of the following criteria: age >= 80 years, body weight <= 60 kg, or serum creatinine >= 1.5 mg/dL (133 umol/L).
Warfarin in advanced CKD and dialysis accelerates vascular calcification and calcific uremic arteriolopathy (calciphylaxis) by inhibiting vitamin K-dependent matrix Gla protein.
Dabigatran is 80% renally eliminated and is contraindicated when CrCl < 30 mL/min in European guidelines.

topic: Atrial fibrillation catheter ablation and early rhythm control

guidelinesKept: 2024 ESC Guidelines for the management of atrial fibrillation.

page.mentor_intro: Atrial fibrillation management has shifted towards early rhythm control to prevent adverse cardiovascular outcomes and structural atrial remodeling. The landmark EAST-AFNET 4 trial demonstrated that early rhythm control (antiarrhythmic drugs or catheter ablation within 1 year of diagnosis) significantly reduced cardiovascular death, stroke, and hospitalizations compared to usual care. Catheter ablation is superior to antiarrhythmic drugs for maintaining sinus rhythm and improving quality of life, especially in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (CASTLE-AF).

teaching_points.claim: The EAST-AFNET 4 trial demonstrated that early rhythm control initiated within 1 year of AF diagnosis reduced cardiovascular death, stroke, or heart failure hospitalization by 21%.
Catheter ablation (pulmonary vein isolation) is superior to antiarrhythmic drug therapy for preventing recurrent AF and reducing heart failure mortality in HFrEF (CASTLE-AF trial).
ESC 2024 guidelines recommend pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) as first-line rhythm control for paroxysmal AF in symptomatic patients as an alternative to antiarrhythmic drugs (Class I, Level A).
Successful catheter ablation does NOT eliminate the need for oral anticoagulation, which must be continued indefinitely based on baseline CHA2DS2-VASc risk score.

topic: Atypical pneumonia pathogens: Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila, Q fever (Coxiella): diagnosis and treatment

guidelinesKept: Diagnosis and Treatment of Adults with Community-acquired Pneumonia: Official ATS/IDSA Guideline.
European Respiratory Society guidelines on the management of adult community-acquired pneumonia.

page.mentor_intro: Atypical pneumonia is caused by organisms that lack a peptidoglycan cell wall (Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae) or are obligate/facultative intracellular pathogens (Legionella pneumophila, Coxiella burnetii [Q fever]). Because they lack cell walls, beta-lactam antibiotics are completely ineffective. Diagnostic workup uses urinary antigen testing (for Legionella pneumophila serogroup 1) and respiratory multiplex PCR. First-line therapy relies on macrolides (azithromycin), respiratory fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin), or tetracyclines (doxycycline).

teaching_points.claim: Beta-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins) are inherently inactive against Mycoplasma and Chlamydia due to the absence of a bacterial peptidoglycan cell wall.
Legionella urinary antigen testing is rapid, specific (> 95%), and detects Legionella pneumophila serogroup 1 (responsible for 70-80% of community-acquired legionellosis).
IDSA/ATS guidelines recommend respiratory fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) or azithromycin as first-line treatment for Legionnaires' disease.

Extrapulmonary manifestations: Mycoplasma is associated with cold agglutinin autoimmune hemolytic anemia, erythema multiforme, and bullous myringitis; Legionella causes hyponatremia, diarrhea, and confusion.

sources.title: Diagnosis and Treatment of Adults with Community-acquired Pneumonia: Official ATS/IDSA Guideline.

Legionella clinical triad: high fever with relative bradycardia (Faget sign), gastrointestinal symptoms (watery diarrhea), and laboratory hyponatremia / transaminitis.
Treatment of choice for Q fever (Coxiella burnetii): oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 14 days.

topic: Autoantibody panel interpretation: ANA, ENA, dsDNA, ANCA, RF, anti-CCP clinical utility

guidelinesKept: 2019 European League Against Rheumatism/American College of Rheumatology classification criteria for systemic lupus erythematosus.
2021 American College of Rheumatology Guideline for the Treatment of Rheumatoid Arthritis.

page.mentor_intro: Autoantibody panels are essential diagnostic instruments in systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases (SARD), but must be interpreted strictly within the pre-test clinical context to avoid false-positive misdiagnoses. Antinuclear antibody (ANA) testing by indirect immunofluorescence on HEp-2 cells is the gold standard screening test (positive at >= 1:160). Downstream extractable nuclear antigen (ENA) testing differentiates specific diseases: anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm (SLE), anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB (Sjögren/SLE/congenital heart block), anti-Scl-70 (diffuse systemic sclerosis), anti-centromere (limited systemic sclerosis), anti-Jo-1 (myositis), anti-CCP and RF (rheumatoid arthritis), and ANCA (systemic vasculitis).

teaching_points.claim: EULAR/ACR 2019 criteria mandate positive ANA by HEp-2 immunofluorescence at a titer >= 1:80 as the required entry criterion for the classification of SLE.
Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies have high diagnostic specificity (> 96%) for rheumatoid arthritis and predict progressive radiographic erosive joint damage.
Anti-dsDNA antibody titers correlate with disease activity and active lupus nephritis; falling complement (C3, C4) alongside rising anti-dsDNA signals an impending clinical flare.
Anti-Ro/SSA antibodies in pregnant women cross the placenta and carry a 2% risk of causing neonatal lupus erythematosus and irreversible congenital complete heart block in the fetus.

mcq_angles: Entry criterion for SLE: ANA >= 1:80 (sensitivity > 98%); if ANA is negative, SLE is excluded in > 99% of cases.

Specific antibody associations: Anti-Sm (most specific for SLE, 99%), Anti-Ro/SSA (Sjögren, subacute cutaneous lupus, congenital heart block), Anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase I, diffuse scleroderma with ILD).
Serological flare monitoring in lupus: rising anti-dsDNA titers coupled with declining serum C3/C4 levels indicate activation of the classical complement cascade.

topic: Autoimmune encephalitis: Anti-NMDA receptor, LGI1, Caspr2 antibody profiles

guidelinesKept: A clinical approach to diagnosis of autoimmune encephalitis (Graus Criteria).
EFNS guidelines on the management of autoimmune encephalitis.

page.mentor_intro: Autoimmune encephalitis (AIE) is a rapidly progressive inflammatory brain disease caused by autoantibodies directed against neuronal cell-surface synaptic antigens (e.g. NMDA receptor, LGI1, Caspr2) or intracellular onconeural antigens (Hu, Ma2). It presents subacutely (< 3 months) with altered mental status, memory deficits, psychiatric disturbances, refractory seizures, movement disorders, and autonomic instability. First-line immunotherapy consists of high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone, IVIG, or plasma exchange, alongside screening for occult systemic tumors (e.g. ovarian teratoma in anti-NMDAR).

teaching_points.claim: Graus consensus diagnostic criteria establish clinical algorithms for definite autoimmune encephalitis based on subacute onset, CSF pleocytosis or oligoclonal bands, MRI T2/FLAIR hyperintensity, and autoantibodies.

Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis typically affects young females, presenting with a multistage progression (psychosis, memory loss, seizures, movement disorders, hypoventilation) and is associated with ovarian teratoma in ~40%.
Anti-LGI1 encephalitis characteristically presents in older adults with pathognomonic faciobrachial dystonic seizures (FBDS) and hyponatremia (SIADH), responding dramatically to early immunotherapy.
Second-line immunotherapy with rituximab or cyclophosphamide is recommended if there is inadequate clinical response within 10-14 days of first-line therapies.

Ovarian teratoma screening: transvaginal ultrasound and pelvic MRI are mandatory in all females diagnosed with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis (prompt surgical excision speeds neurological recovery).
CSF vs serum testing sensitivity: Anti-NMDAR testing in CSF has higher sensitivity and lower false-positive rates than serum; Anti-LGI1 is frequently positive in serum.

guidelinesKept: British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines for the management of iron deficiency and autoimmune gastritis.
Management of epithelial precancerous conditions and lesions in the stomach (MAPS II): European guidelines.

page.mentor_intro: Autoimmune gastritis (AIG) is a chronic, immune-mediated, organ-specific gastritis directed against gastric parietal cells and their secretory products (H+/K+-ATPase and intrinsic factor). It causes selective destruction of the oxyntic mucosa in the gastric body and fundus, sparing the antrum. Destruction of parietal cells causes achlorhydria (triggering hypergastrinemia and enterochromaffin-like [ECL] cell hyperplasia) and loss of intrinsic factor, producing vitamin B12 malabsorption (pernicious anaemia). Management involves lifelong parenteral or high-dose oral vitamin B12 replacement, iron repletion, and endoscopic surveillance for gastric neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) and adenocarcinoma.

teaching_points.claim: Destruction of gastric parietal cells leads to achlorhydria, high fasting serum gastrin, and lack of intrinsic factor causing vitamin B12 deficiency (pernicious anemia).
Anti-parietal cell antibodies (APCA) are sensitive (80-90%) but less specific; anti-intrinsic factor antibodies (AIFA) have high diagnostic specificity (> 98%) for pernicious anemia.
Endoscopic surveillance (MAPS II guidelines) is recommended every 3-5 years due to increased risks of Type 1 gastric neuroendocrine tumors (from hypergastrinemia) and gastric adenocarcinoma.

Vitamin B12 deficiency produces megaloblastic anemia and subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord (posterior and lateral column demyelination); folic acid alone masks anemia while allowing neurological damage to progress.

mcq_angles: The folate trap: treating megaloblastic anemia with folate without B12 corrects the CBC but precipitates or accelerates irreversible subacute combined degeneration.
Histological sparing: AIG involves the gastric body and fundus (oxyntic mucosa) while sparing the antrum (unlike H. pylori pangastritis).
Concurrent autoimmune conditions: up to 30-40% of AIG patients have autoimmune thyroid disease (Hashimoto thyroiditis; Schmidt syndrome/autoimmune polyglandular syndrome).

guidelinesKept: First international consensus on the diagnosis and management of autoimmune hemolytic anemia in adults.

page.mentor_intro: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (AIHA) is an immune-mediated disorder characterized by antibody-mediated destruction of red blood cells. It is classified into warm AIHA (wAIHA; 70-80% of cases, IgG-mediated, optimal binding at 37C, extravascular clearance in the spleen) and cold agglutinin disease (CAD; 15-20%, IgM-mediated, binding at 0-4C, classical complement-mediated intravascular and hepatic clearance). Diagnosis requires hemolytic markers (elevated LDH, indirect bilirubin, reticulocytosis, undetectable haptoglobin) and a positive direct antiglobulin test (DAT/Coombs). First-line therapy for wAIHA is oral prednisone (1 mg/kg/day); second-line is rituximab.

teaching_points.claim: First-line therapy for warm AIHA is oral prednisone (1 mg/kg/day for 3-4 weeks, then slow taper), achieving initial response in 70-80% of patients.
Rituximab (375 mg/m2 weekly x 4 or fixed 1000 mg x 2) is the preferred second-line therapy for warm AIHA refractory to or dependent on corticosteroids.
Cold agglutinin disease is mediated by IgM antibodies that fix complement; corticosteroids and splenectomy are clinically ineffective and should not be used in primary CAD.
Sutimlimab, a humanized monoclonal antibody inhibiting complement component C1s, produces rapid and sustained cessation of complement-mediated hemolysis in CAD (CARDINAL trial).

sources.title: First international consensus on the diagnosis and management of autoimmune hemolytic anemia in adults.

uncertainties: Indications and timing for splenectomy in multirefractory warm AIHA in the modern biologic era.

mcq_angles: Direct Antiglobulin Test (DAT) pattern differentiation: Warm AIHA = positive for IgG alone or IgG + C3d; Cold Agglutinin Disease = positive for C3d alone (IgM dissociates at warm temperatures).
Why steroids fail in CAD: IgM-complement binding occurs in peripheral extremities and red cells are cleared in liver via C3b/C4b, which corticosteroids do not suppress.
Thrombosis risk in AIHA: active hemolysis releases free hemoglobin that scavenges nitric oxide, creating a severe hypercoagulable state requiring VTE prophylaxis.

A 67-year-old with acrocyanosis (painful blue discoloration of ears, nose, fingers on cold exposure) and hemolytic anemia whose DAT is positive for C3d alone.

guidelinesKept: AASLD Practice Guidelines: Diagnosis and Management of Autoimmune Hepatitis.

page.mentor_intro: Autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) is a chronic, progressive necroinflammatory liver disease characterized by circulating autoantibodies, hypergammaglobulinemia (elevated IgG), and interface hepatitis on liver biopsy. Type 1 AIH (ANA and/or anti-smooth muscle antibodies [ASMA]) occurs at any age; Type 2 AIH (anti-liver-kidney microsomal 1 [anti-LKM1] or anti-LC1) occurs predominantly in children and young females. Standard first-line remission induction therapy combines systemic corticosteroids (prednisone/prednisolone) with azathioprine as a steroid-sparing agent.

teaching_points.claim: AASLD and EASL guidelines recommend combination therapy with prednisone (starting 30-40 mg daily) and azathioprine (1-2 mg/kg daily) to induce and maintain biochemical remission.

Oral budesonide (9 mg daily) combined with azathioprine is an effective first-line induction alternative in non-cirrhotic AIH, offering 90% first-pass hepatic metabolism with fewer steroid side effects.
Budesonide is strictly contraindicated in patients with established cirrhosis or portosystemic shunting due to reduced hepatic metabolism causing severe systemic corticosteroid toxicities.
Thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) and NUDT15 genotype/phenotype testing should be performed prior to azathioprine initiation to prevent life-threatening myelosuppression.

Second-line immunosuppression: mycophenolate mofetil vs tacrolimus in azathioprine-intolerant patients.
mcq_angles: Diagnostic criteria: elevated IgG, positive autoantibodies (ANA/ASMA in Type 1; anti-LKM1 in Type 2), interface hepatitis with dense portal plasma cell infiltrates on biopsy, absence of viral hepatitis.
Budesonide contraindication: cirrhosis; portosystemic shunts bypass hepatic first-pass clearance, flooding systemic circulation.
Definition of complete biochemical remission: complete normalization of serum transaminases (AST and ALT) AND serum IgG to within normal limits.

guidelinesKept: International consensus diagnostic criteria for autoimmune pancreatitis: guidelines of the International Association of Pancreatology.
